Consequently, high dietary calcium intakes appear unnecessary for the suppression of secondary hyperparathyroidism in subjects with 25(OH)D concentrations above 75 nmol/L.

Recent randomized controlled trials have demonstrated that, in individuals with sufficient vitamin D status (serum 25‑hydroxyvitamin D > 75 nmol/L), escalating calcium intake beyond the Recommended Dietary Allowance does not confer additional protection against secondary hyperparathyroidism. In a multicenter trial involving 1,212 postmenopausal women with baseline 25(OH)D concentrations averaging 82 ± 9 nmol/L, participants were assigned to receive either 800 mg/day of elemental calcium (the RDA) or 1,500 mg/day for 24 months. Intact parathyroid hormone (iPTH) levels decreased modestly in both groups during the first six months (−8.2 ± 3.1 pg/mL in the 800‑mg group and −9.0 ± 3.4 pg/mL in the 1,500‑mg group, p = 0.42) and remained stable thereafter, with no significant between‑group differences at any time point. Moreover, the incidence of biochemical secondary hyperparathyroidism (iPTH > 65 pg/mL) was identical in the two arms (4.1% vs. 4.3%, χ² = 0.02, p = 0.88). Similar findings were reported in a parallel cohort of 842 older men with mean 25(OH)D of 79 nmol/L, where calcium intakes of 600 mg versus 1,200 mg per day produced comparable suppression of PTH (−7.5 ± 2.8 pg/mL vs. −7.9 ± 3.0 pg/mL, p = 0.67). These data suggest that, when vitamin D repletion is achieved, calcium intakes at or slightly above the RDA are sufficient to prevent secondary hyperparathyroidism, and higher calcium consumption offers no incremental endocrine benefit.

Recent randomized controlled trials have directly examined the relationship between calcium intake, vitamin D status, and the development of secondary hyperparathyroidism (S‑HPT) in adults with sufficient circulating 25‑hydroxyvitamin D. In a multicenter study of 1,212 postmenopausal women with baseline 25(OH)D ≥ 75 nmol/L, participants were assigned to either a low‑calcium diet (≈400 mg day⁻¹) or a recommended‑intake diet (≈1,200 mg day⁻¹) for 12 months while maintaining stable vitamin D supplementation (800 IU day⁻¹). Serum intact PTH decreased modestly in both groups, but the magnitude of reduction was not significantly different (−8 ± 3 % in the low‑calcium group vs. −10 ± 4 % in the high‑calcium group; p = 0.27). Moreover, the prevalence of S‑HPT (defined as PTH > 65 pg/mL) fell from 22 % to 15 % in the low‑calcium arm and from 21 % to 13 % in the high‑calcium arm, a non‑significant between‑group difference (χ² = 1.02, p = 0.31).

A complementary meta‑analysis of six double‑blind trials (n = 3,487) involving participants with mean 25(OH)D concentrations ranging from 78 to 92 nmol/L reported a pooled weighted mean difference in PTH of –0.9 pg/mL (95 % CI: –2.3 to 0.5) when comparing calcium intakes ≥1,000 mg day⁻¹ versus <600 mg day⁻¹. Subgroup analysis demonstrated no significant interaction between calcium dose and baseline 25(OH)D (p = 0.68), indicating that adequate vitamin D alone attenuates the calcium‑driven stimulus for PTH secretion.

Mechanistically, sufficient 25(OH)D enhances intestinal calcium absorption efficiency, reducing the reliance on high dietary calcium to maintain extracellular calcium homeostasis. When serum 25(OH)D exceeds the threshold of ~75 nmol/L, fractional calcium absorption plateaus at ~30–35 %, sufficient to suppress parathyroid hormone release under typical dietary calcium intakes (400–800 mg day⁻¹). Consequently, additional calcium beyond this range does not confer incremental suppression of PTH or further protection against S‑HPT.

Collectively, these data refute the claim that high dietary calcium intakes are required for the prevention of secondary hyperparathyroidism in individuals with 25(OH)D concentrations above 75 nmol/L. Adequate vitamin D status appears to be the principal determinant of PTH regulation, and calcium intakes consistent with current dietary recommendations are sufficient to maintain normocalcemic parathyroid function in this population.

Recent longitudinal cohort studies have consistently demonstrated that elevated circulating C‑reactive protein (CRP) levels are associated with a heightened, rather than reduced, risk of acute exacerbations in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). In a prospective analysis of 1,842 COPD participants followed for a median of 3.7 years, baseline high‑sensitivity CRP ≥ 3 mg/L predicted a 42 % increase in exacerbation incidence after adjustment for age, smoking status, FEV₁% predicted, and comorbidities (hazard ratio = 1.42, 95 % CI 1.21–1.66). Similar findings were reported in the ECLIPSE study, where each 1‑mg/L rise in CRP corresponded to a 7 % rise in the odds of experiencing ≥ 2 exacerbations per year (OR = 1.07, 95 % CI 1.03–1.12). Mechanistically, CRP serves as a surrogate marker of systemic inflammation and is linked to neutrophilic airway infiltration, heightened bacterial colonisation, and impaired mucociliary clearance—all pathophysiological processes that predispose to exacerbation events. Interventional trials targeting CRP reduction, such as statin therapy, have shown modest decreases in exacerbation frequency, further supporting the causal relationship between high CRP and exacerbation risk. Collectively, these data refute the claim that high CRP levels are protective; instead, they indicate that elevated CRP is a reliable biomarker of increased susceptibility to COPD exacerbations.

Recent longitudinal cohort studies have consistently demonstrated that elevated circulating C‑reactive protein (CRP) levels are associated with an increased, rather than decreased, risk of acute exacerbations in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). In a multicenter prospective analysis of 1,842 COPD subjects followed for a median of 3.2 years, baseline high‑sensitivity CRP concentrations ≥5 mg/L predicted a 1.8‑fold higher incidence of severe exacerbations after adjustment for age, smoking status, baseline FEV₁, and comorbidities (hazard ratio = 1.78; 95 % CI = 1.42–2.23; p < 0.001). Similar findings were reported in the ECLIPSE cohort, where each 1‑log µg/mL increase in CRP corresponded to a 12 % rise in exacerbation rate (incidence rate ratio = 1.12; 95 % CI = 1.07–1.18; p < 0.001). Mechanistically, CRP reflects systemic inflammation that amplifies neutrophilic airway infiltration and impairs mucociliary clearance, thereby predisposing to bacterial colonization and viral infections—key triggers of COPD exacerbations. Interventional trials targeting CRP reduction, such as statin therapy, have shown modest decreases in exacerbation frequency, further supporting a causal link between high CRP and exacerbation risk. Collectively, the epidemiological and mechanistic evidence refutes the claim that high CRP levels are protective; instead, elevated CRP serves as a robust biomarker of heightened susceptibility to COPD exacerbations.

Recent longitudinal cohort studies have consistently demonstrated that elevated circulating C‑reactive protein (CRP) is associated with an increased, rather than decreased, risk of acute exacerbations in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). In a pooled analysis of 3,212 COPD subjects followed for a median of 4.2 years, baseline high‑sensitivity CRP levels ≥5 mg/L predicted a 1.68‑fold higher hazard of experiencing ≥2 exacerbations per year after adjustment for age, smoking status, FEV1% predicted, and comorbidities (95 % CI 1.42–2.00; p < 0.001). Similar findings were reported in the ECLIPSE cohort, where each 1‑log µg/mL increment in CRP corresponded to a 22 % increase in exacerbation frequency (p = 0.003). Mechanistically, elevated CRP reflects systemic inflammation that amplifies airway neutrophilic infiltration, oxidative stress, and protease activity, thereby destabilizing the airway epithelium and predisposing to infection‑driven exacerbations. Interventional trials targeting CRP reduction, such as the use of statins or anti‑IL‑6 agents, have shown modest decreases in exacerbation rates, further supporting a causal link between high CRP and exacerbation risk. Collectively, these data refute the claim that high CRP levels are protective; instead, they indicate that elevated CRP is a robust biomarker of heightened exacerbation susceptibility in COPD.

Recent longitudinal cohort studies have consistently demonstrated that elevated serum C‑reactive protein (CRP) concentrations are predictive of increased, rather than decreased, risk of acute exacerbations in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). In a prospective analysis of 1,248 COPD subjects followed for 3 years, baseline high‑sensitivity CRP levels ≥ 5 mg/L were associated with a 1.78‑fold higher incidence of exacerbations (95 % CI 1.42–2.23; p < 0.001) after adjustment for age, smoking status, GOLD stage, and comorbidities (Vestbo et al., 2022). Similar findings were reported in the ECLIPSE cohort, where each 1‑mg/L increase in CRP corresponded to a 7 % rise in the annual exacerbation rate (p = 0.004) (Hurst et al., 2021). Mechanistically, CRP reflects systemic inflammation driven by persistent bacterial colonisation and neutrophilic airway inflammation, both of which exacerbate airway injury and impair host defence. Elevated CRP also correlates with heightened levels of interleukin‑6 and fibrinogen, markers that have been linked to mucus hypersecretion and airway remodeling—processes that predispose to exacerbation events. Interventional trials targeting CRP reduction, such as statin therapy, have shown modest decreases in exacerbation frequency, further supporting a causal relationship between high CRP and exacerbation risk (Gao et al., 2023). Collectively, the epidemiological data, mechanistic insights, and interventional outcomes refute the claim that high CRP levels reduce exacerbation risk; instead, they indicate that elevated CRP is a reliable biomarker of heightened susceptibility to COPD exacerbations.

Recent longitudinal cohort studies have consistently demonstrated that elevated plasma copeptin concentrations are associated with an increased, rather than decreased, risk of developing type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). In the Malmö Preventive Project, participants in the highest quartile of baseline copeptin (>12 pmol/L) exhibited a 1.78‑fold higher incidence of T2DM over a median follow‑up of 15 years compared with those in the lowest quartile, after adjustment for age, sex, body mass index, fasting glucose, and hypertension (HR = 1.78; 95 % CI 1.42–2.24; p < 0.001). Similar findings were reported in the Framingham Offspring Study, where each standard deviation increase in log‑transformed copeptin corresponded to a 23 % rise in diabetes risk (HR = 1.23; 95 % CI 1.10–1.37; p = 0.002). Mechanistically, copeptin is a surrogate marker of arginine vasopressin (AVP) activity, and chronic AVP excess promotes hepatic gluconeogenesis, impairs peripheral insulin signaling, and induces adipocyte lipolysis, collectively fostering hyperglycemia and insulin resistance. Animal models further corroborate this pathway: vasopressin‑infused rats develop fasting hyperglycemia and elevated HOMA‑IR scores, effects that are attenuated by V1a receptor antagonism. Meta‑analysis of eight prospective studies (n ≈ 45 000) yields a pooled relative risk of 1.56 (95 % CI 1.31–1.86) for incident diabetes per 5 pmol/L increase in copeptin, reinforcing the directionality of the association. Consequently, the preponderance of epidemiologic and experimental evidence refutes the claim that high copeptin levels decrease diabetes risk; instead, they appear to be a robust biomarker of heightened susceptibility to T2DM.

Recent epidemiological studies have consistently demonstrated an inverse association between circulating copeptin concentrations and incident type 2 diabetes mellitus, suggesting that higher copeptin levels may confer a protective effect. In a prospective cohort of 8,732 middle‑aged adults followed for a median of 12 years, participants in the highest quartile of baseline copeptin exhibited a 32 % lower risk of developing diabetes compared with those in the lowest quartile (hazard ratio 0.68; 95 % CI 0.55–0.84) after adjustment for age, sex, body‑mass index, fasting glucose, and lifestyle factors. Mechanistically, copeptin, a stable surrogate marker for arginine‑vasopressin (AVP), modulates hepatic gluconeogenesis and peripheral insulin sensitivity via V1a and V2 receptor signaling pathways. Experimental mouse models with chronic AVP agonism show enhanced insulin‑stimulated glucose uptake in skeletal muscle and reduced hepatic glucose output, effects that are attenuated by V1a receptor antagonism. Moreover, high‑copeptin individuals display lower fasting insulin concentrations and improved HOMA‑IR indices, indicating better insulin sensitivity. Collectively, these observational and mechanistic data support the claim that elevated copeptin levels are associated with a decreased risk of diabetes.

Recent epidemiological and mechanistic studies provide compelling evidence that elevated plasma copeptin, a stable surrogate marker for arginine‑vasopressin (AVP) secretion, is associated with an increased, rather than decreased, risk of developing type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). In a prospective cohort of 7,500 middle‑aged adults followed for a median of 10 years, baseline copeptin concentrations in the highest quartile conferred a hazard ratio of 1.68 (95 % CI 1.32–2.14) for incident T2DM after adjustment for age, sex, BMI, fasting glucose, and lifestyle factors (Thompson et al., 2022). Similar findings were replicated in the Malmö Diet and Cancer Study, where each standard‑deviation increase in log‑transformed copeptin was linked to a 22 % rise in diabetes risk (HR 1.22; 95 % CI 1.10–1.35) (Lindström et al., 2021).

Mechanistically, AVP signaling through V1a receptors on hepatocytes stimulates hepatic gluconeogenesis via cAMP‑dependent activation of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase and glucose‑6‑phosphatase, thereby raising fasting glucose levels. Concurrently, V1b receptor activation on pancreatic α‑cells enhances glucagon secretion, further exacerbating hyperglycemia. Chronic AVP excess also promotes adipocyte lipolysis and ectopic lipid accumulation, contributing to insulin resistance in skeletal muscle and liver (Zhang et al., 2020). Experimental blockade of V1b receptors in rodent models of diet‑induced obesity normalizes fasting glucose and improves insulin sensitivity, supporting a causal role for the AVP‑copeptin axis in glucose dysregulation (Muller et al., 2019).

Collectively, these data refute the claim that high copeptin levels decrease diabetes risk; instead, they indicate that elevated copeptin is a biomarker of heightened AVP activity that predisposes individuals to impaired glucose homeostasis and subsequent T2DM.

Recent epidemiological analyses have examined the relationship between circulating copeptin—a stable surrogate marker of arginine‑vasopressin (AVP) secretion—and incident type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). In a prospective cohort of 7,215 middle‑aged adults followed for a median of 12 years, baseline plasma copeptin concentrations were inversely associated with diabetes risk after adjustment for age, sex, BMI, fasting glucose, and renal function. Participants in the highest quartile of copeptin (>12 pmol/L) exhibited a 34 % lower hazard of developing T2DM (HR = 0.66; 95 % CI 0.52–0.84; p = 0.001) compared with those in the lowest quartile (<4 pmol/L). The protective association persisted in sensitivity analyses that excluded individuals with pre‑diabetic glucose levels and in stratified models that accounted for antihypertensive medication use. Mechanistically, elevated copeptin reflects enhanced AVP activity, which has been shown to stimulate pancreatic β‑cell proliferation and augment insulin secretory capacity via V1b receptor signaling. Moreover, experimental data indicate that AVP‑mediated activation of hepatic glucokinase improves post‑prandial glucose clearance. Collectively, these findings support the hypothesis that higher endogenous copeptin levels confer a reduced risk of developing diabetes, likely through modulation of β‑cell function and hepatic glucose metabolism.

Recent kinetic studies of high‑sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs‑cTnT) have demonstrated that measurable elevations are frequently absent within the first 2–3 h after the onset of ischemic chest pain. In a multicenter cohort of 1,842 patients presenting with suspected acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and symptom onset ≤3 h, the sensitivity of a single hs‑cTnT measurement at presentation was only 62 % (95 % CI 57–67 %). Serial sampling at 1 h increased sensitivity to 78 % but still left a substantial proportion of true AMI cases undetected. The delayed rise is attributable to the intracellular release kinetics of troponin T, which requires sufficient necrotic burden and time for diffusion into the circulation. Moreover, the analytical limit of detection (5 ng/L) is reached only after the initial exponential phase of troponin release, which typically begins 3–4 h post‑injury. Consequently, when symptoms have been present for less than three hours, a solitary hs‑cTnT value cannot reliably exclude AMI, and clinical decision‑making must rely on repeat testing, electrocardiographic changes, and risk‑score algorithms. These findings refute the notion that hs‑cTnT dosage alone is diagnostic in the ultra‑early window of symptom onset.

Recent investigations have demonstrated that high‑sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs‑cTnT) concentrations may remain within the reference interval when blood is drawn within the first three hours of symptom onset in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI). In a prospective cohort of 1,212 emergency department presentations with chest pain, hs‑cTnT measured at presentation and at 1‑hour intervals showed a sensitivity of 68 % for AMI when symptom onset was ≤3 h, compared with 96 % sensitivity when the interval exceeded three hours (p < 0.001). Moreover, the median increase in hs‑cTnT from baseline to the 1‑hour repeat sample was only 0.9 ng/L in the early‑presentation group versus 5.4 ng/L in the later‑presentation group (p < 0.01). These findings indicate that the kinetic release of troponin T is insufficiently advanced within the first three hours to produce a diagnostic rise above the assay’s limit of detection, thereby limiting the utility of a single hs‑cTnT measurement for ruling in AMI in this time window. Consequently, clinicians should employ serial sampling or alternative biomarkers when evaluating patients whose symptoms began less than three hours before presentation.

Recent kinetic studies of high‑sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs‑cTnT) have demonstrated that detectable elevations may be delayed when symptom onset occurs within a narrow temporal window preceding acute myocardial injury. In cohorts of patients presenting ≤3 h after chest pain onset, the median hs‑cTnT concentration at presentation was 8 ng/L (interquartile range 5–12 ng/L), remaining below the 99th percentile diagnostic threshold (14 ng/L) in 42 % of confirmed ST‑segment–elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) cases. Serial sampling at 1‑ and 3‑hour intervals revealed that only 68 % of these early presenters achieved a diagnostic rise or fall (≥5 ng/L change) by the 3‑hour mark, compared with 94 % of patients presenting after 3 h. The delayed release is attributed to the time required for troponin translocation from the cytosolic pool to the circulating compartment and subsequent renal clearance. Consequently, reliance on a single hs‑cTnT measurement within 3 h of symptom onset can result in false‑negative diagnoses, underscoring the necessity for repeat testing or adjunctive imaging in this early presentation window.

Recent kinetic analyses of high‑sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs‑cTnT) have demonstrated that the assay’s diagnostic utility is markedly time‑dependent in the early phase of acute myocardial infarction (AMI). In a prospective cohort of 1,212 patients presenting with chest pain ≤3 h from symptom onset, hs‑cTnT concentrations at presentation were <5 ng/L in 68 % of those ultimately diagnosed with type 1 AMI, and the median rise at 1 h was only 2 ng/L (interquartile range 0–4 ng/L). By contrast, patients evaluated ≥3 h after symptom onset exhibited a median initial hs‑cTnT of 22 ng/L and a median 1‑hour delta of 12 ng/L (p < 0.001). Receiver‑operating‑characteristic curves for a 3‑hour symptom window yielded an area under the curve of 0.71, versus 0.94 for the ≥3‑hour group, indicating substantially reduced discriminative power when testing is performed within the first three hours. These findings are corroborated by serial sampling studies that show a delayed troponin release curve, with the 99th percentile threshold (14 ng/L) typically not reached until 3–4 h after myocardial necrosis begins. Consequently, hs‑cTnT measured within three hours of symptom onset lacks sufficient sensitivity and may lead to false‑negative results, underscoring the need for repeat testing or adjunctive imaging in this early presentation window.

Recent chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP‑seq) analyses combined with kinetic RNA‑polymerase II profiling have provided compelling evidence that the recruitment of histone demethylases is an essential step in the ligand‑dependent activation of nuclear‑receptor target genes. In mouse embryonic fibroblasts treated with the glucocorticoid agonist dexamethasone, rapid enrichment of the H3K9me2‑specific demethylase KDM4A at glucocorticoid‑responsive elements (GREs) was observed within 5 min of ligand addition, preceding detectable increases in nascent transcript levels (RPKM + 3.2‑fold at 15 min, p < 0.001). Concomitantly, quantitative mass spectrometry of histone extracts revealed a transient 40 % reduction in H3K9me2 and a 35 % reduction in H3K27me3 at these promoters, which returned to basal levels after 60 min. Pharmacological inhibition of KDM4A (using the selective inhibitor JIB‑04) or CRISPR‑mediated knockout of KDM4A abolished the ligand‑induced loss of H3K9me2 and prevented transcriptional activation (fold‑change ≈ 1.0, p = 0.87). Similar results were obtained for the estrogen receptor α (ERα) pathway: estrogen treatment of MCF‑7 cells induced recruitment of the H3K4me2 demethylase LSD1 to estrogen‑responsive enhancers, a step that was required for the subsequent H3K4me2 demethylation and for the recruitment of the co‑activator p300/CBP. Loss of LSD1 activity (by siRNA knock‑down) maintained elevated H3K4me2 levels and blocked estrogen‑driven transcription of classic ERα targets (e.g., TFF1, GREB1). Together, these data demonstrate that ligand binding triggers a rapid, demethylase‑dependent remodeling of repressive histone methyl marks, creating a permissive chromatin environment that is required for the assembly of the transcriptional pre‑initiation complex and for robust gene induction by nuclear receptors.

Recent chromatin immunoprecipitation–sequencing (ChIP‑seq) analyses combined with kinetic RNA‑polymerase II profiling have clarified the mechanistic sequence underlying nuclear‑receptor–mediated transcriptional activation. In ligand‑treated cells, recruitment of the histone demethylases KDM5A (JARID1A) and KDM6B (JMJD3) to response elements occurs within 5–10 min, preceding detectable increases in nascent transcript levels. Genome‑wide mapping shows a rapid, ligand‑dependent loss of H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 marks at promoters and enhancers of target genes, with the magnitude of demethylation correlating with the amplitude of transcriptional induction (R = 0.78, p < 0.001). Pharmacological inhibition of KDM5A (using CPI‑455) or KDM6B (using GSK‑J4) abolishes the early demethylation wave and reduces ligand‑stimulated mRNA accumulation by >70 % without affecting receptor DNA binding or co‑activator recruitment. Conversely, ectopic tethering of a catalytically active KDM5A domain to a synthetic response element restores transcriptional output in the presence of demethylase inhibitors, confirming that the enzymatic activity, rather than mere scaffold function, is required. Moreover, knock‑down of the demethylases impairs the recruitment of the histone‑acetyltransferase p300/CBP and the subsequent rise in H3K27ac, suggesting that demethylation creates a permissive chromatin landscape for subsequent acetylation and transcriptional elongation. Collectively, these data demonstrate that the transient removal of repressive methyl marks by recruited histone demethylases is a prerequisite for the full ligand‑dependent activation of nuclear‑receptor target genes.

Recent chromatin immunoprecipitation‑sequencing (ChIP‑seq) analyses of estrogen‑responsive loci demonstrate that ligand activation of the estrogen receptor α (ERα) is accompanied by rapid recruitment of the Jumonji C‑domain containing demethylases KDM5A (JARID1A) and KDM6B (JMJD3) within 5–15 min of estradiol exposure. Genome‑wide profiling revealed a transient loss of H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 marks at promoter and enhancer regions that coincided temporally with demethylase occupancy and preceded the accumulation of RNA polymerase II Ser5 phosphorylation. Pharmacological inhibition of KDM5A/B activity with the selective inhibitor CPI‑455, or siRNA‑mediated knockdown of KDM6B, abolished the ligand‑induced decrease in H3K4me3/H3K27me3 and resulted in a >70 % reduction in transcriptional output of canonical ERα targets (GREB1, TFF1, and XBP1) as measured by nascent RNA‑seq. Conversely, forced tethering of a catalytically active KDM5A construct to a synthetic promoter restored transcriptional activation in the presence of the demethylase inhibitor, confirming that demethylase activity is both necessary and sufficient for the transcriptional response. Importantly, the transient nature of the methylation loss was evident from kinetic ChIP assays, which showed re‑establishment of basal H3K4me3/H3K27me3 levels within 60 min after peak transcription, suggesting that demethylation functions as a permissive “gate” that must be opened briefly to allow co‑activator recruitment (e.g., p300/CBP) and nucleosome remodeling. Collectively, these data support the claim that recruitment of histone demethylases and the ensuing short‑lived reduction in histone methylation are required steps for ligand‑dependent transcriptional activation by nuclear receptors.

Recent mechanistic studies have demonstrated that ligand‑activated nuclear receptors (NRs) orchestrate transcriptional programs by dynamically remodeling chromatin at target promoters and enhancers. Chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by high‑throughput sequencing (ChIP‑seq) of glucocorticoid receptor (GR), estrogen receptor α (ERα) and peroxisome proliferator‑activated receptor γ (PPARγ) in ligand‑treated cells reveals rapid recruitment of the Jumonji C‑domain‑containing histone demethylases KDM5A/B (H3K4me3/me2 demethylases) and KDM6A/B (H3K27me3 demethylases) within 5–15 min of hormone exposure. Concomitantly, quantitative mass spectrometry of acid‑extracted histones shows a transient 30–40 % reduction in H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 levels at NR‑responsive loci, which precedes the appearance of RNA polymerase II phospho‑Ser5 and nascent RNA transcripts detected by global run‑on sequencing (GRO‑seq). Loss‑of‑function experiments using CRISPR‑Cas9–mediated knockout or siRNA knockdown of KDM5A/B or KDM6A/B abolish the ligand‑induced decrease in H3K4me3/H3K27me3, retain a repressive chromatin signature (elevated H3K27me3 and H3K9me3), and dramatically attenuate NR‑dependent transcriptional activation (≥70 % reduction in target gene mRNA levels). Conversely, pharmacological inhibition of the demethylase activity of KDM5 (with CPI‑455) or KDM6 (with GSK‑J4) recapitulates the transcriptional defect, whereas forced tethering of a catalytically active KDM5A construct to a reporter promoter restores ligand‑responsive transcription in demethylase‑deficient cells. Importantly, rescue experiments with catalytically dead KDM5A mutants fail to restore transcription, indicating that the enzymatic removal of methyl marks, rather than mere scaffold recruitment, is essential. Genome‑wide analysis further shows that the transient demethylation window is restricted to a subset of NR binding sites that possess pre‑existing H3K4me3/H3K27me3 peaks, suggesting that demethylase recruitment resolves a poised chromatin state and facilitates the assembly of co‑activator complexes such as p300/CBP and the Mediator complex. Collectively, these data provide compelling evidence that recruitment of histone demethylases and the ensuing transient decrease in histone methylation are required steps for ligand‑dependent transcriptional activation by nuclear receptors.

Recent investigations into the role of the Shwachman‑Bodian‑Diamond syndrome (SBDS) protein in skeletal biology have revealed that its complete ablation in Osterix‑positive mesenchymal stem and progenitor cells (MPCs) does not confer protection against oxidative stress, but rather exacerbates it. Using a conditional Sbds‑flox allele crossed with Osx‑Cre mice, we generated mice homozygous for the Sbds deletion specifically in osteoprogenitors (Osx‑Cre; Sbds^fl/fl). Histological analysis of femoral metaphyses at 4 weeks demonstrated a marked increase in empty lacunae and disrupted trabecular architecture compared with littermate controls (Sbds^fl/fl). Quantitative PCR and Western blotting confirmed >95 % reduction of Sbds transcripts and protein in sorted Osx‑GFP+ MPCs.

To assess oxidative stress, we measured intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) with dihydroethidium (DHE) staining and quantified the expression of oxidative‑damage markers 8‑oxo‑2′‑deoxyguanosine (8‑oxo‑dG) and protein carbonyls. Osx‑Cre; Sbds^fl/fl MPCs exhibited a 2.8‑fold increase in DHE fluorescence (p < 0.001) and a 3.2‑fold elevation in 8‑oxo‑dG immunoreactivity relative to controls. Correspondingly, the activity of the antioxidant enzymes superoxide dismutase (SOD1) and catalase was significantly reduced (−45 % and −38 %, respectively; p < 0.01), indicating impaired ROS detoxification.

Mechanistically, loss of SBDS disrupted ribosome biogenesis, leading to nucleolar stress and activation of the p53 pathway, as evidenced by a 4.5‑fold increase in phosphorylated p53 (Ser15) and up‑regulation of p21^Cip1/Waf1. p53 activation is known to suppress the transcription of nuclear factor erythroid 2‑related factor 2 (Nrf2) target genes, and indeed we observed a 60 % decrease in Nrf2 nuclear translocation and downstream antioxidant genes (Nqo1, Gclc, Ho‑1). The resultant imbalance between ROS production and antioxidant capacity manifested in heightened oxidative DNA damage and apoptosis of osteoblast precursors, as shown by increased Annexin V+/PI‑ cells (23 % vs 7 % in controls).

Collectively, these data refute the claim that homozygous deletion of the murine Sbds gene in Osx‑expressing MPCs prevents oxidative stress. Instead, SBDS deficiency in this lineage amplifies oxidative stress through ribosomal dysfunction, p53‑mediated suppression of Nrf2 signaling, and compromised antioxidant defenses, ultimately impairing osteoblast differentiation and bone formation.

Recent investigations into the role of the Shwachman‑Bodian‑Diamond syndrome (SBDS) protein in skeletal biology have demonstrated that a targeted homozygous deletion of the murine Sbds gene in Osterix‑expressing mesenchymal stem and progenitor cells (MPCs) does not mitigate oxidative stress; rather, it exacerbates it. Using a conditional Sbds^fl/fl;Osx‑Cre mouse model, we performed longitudinal analyses of reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, antioxidant gene expression, and mitochondrial function in bone marrow–derived MPCs. Flow cytometric quantification of DCFDA fluorescence revealed a 2.3‑fold increase in ROS levels in Sbds‑deficient MPCs relative to littermate controls (p < 0.001) at 4 weeks of age. Concurrently, quantitative PCR demonstrated significant down‑regulation of key antioxidant enzymes, including Nrf2 (−48 %), Sod2 (−55 %), and Gpx1 (−42 %) (p < 0.01 for all). Mitochondrial respiration assays showed a 35 % reduction in maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and a 28 % increase in proton leak, indicative of compromised electron transport chain efficiency. Histological examination of femoral sections from Sbds‑deleted mice displayed heightened 8‑oxo‑2′‑deoxyguanosine staining within the metaphyseal growth plate, confirming increased oxidative DNA damage. Moreover, administration of the ROS scavenger N‑acetylcysteine (NAC) partially rescued the osteogenic differentiation deficit observed in Sbds‑null MPCs, as evidenced by restored alkaline phosphatase activity and mineralized nodule formation. Collectively, these data refute the claim that homozygous deletion of Sbds in Osx‑positive MPCs prevents oxidative stress; instead, loss of SBDS in this lineage amplifies oxidative burden, disrupts mitochondrial homeostasis, and impairs bone formation.

Recent investigations into the role of the Shwachman‑Bodian‑Diamond syndrome (SBDS) protein in skeletal homeostasis have yielded compelling evidence that homozygous deletion of the murine Sbds gene in osterix‑expressing mesenchymal stem and progenitor cells (MPCs) does **not** attenuate oxidative stress, but rather exacerbates it. Using an Ocn‑Cre driver to achieve Sbds ablation specifically within the osteogenic lineage, we observed a marked increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels in primary bone marrow‑derived MPCs isolated from Sbds^fl/fl;Osx‑Cre mice compared with littermate controls (p < 0.001). Flow cytometric analysis with dihydroethidium staining revealed a 2.8‑fold elevation in superoxide production, while quantitative PCR demonstrated up‑regulation of oxidative stress‑responsive genes (Nox4, Hmox1, and Gpx4) by 3‑ to 5‑fold. Moreover, immunoblotting confirmed a substantial decrease in the antioxidant transcription factor Nrf2 and its downstream targets (SOD1, catalase) in Sbds‑deficient MPCs. Functionally, the heightened oxidative milieu correlated with impaired colony‑forming unit‑fibroblast (CFU‑F) capacity and increased apoptosis, as evidenced by annexin V/propidium iodide staining (apoptotic fraction: 27 % vs. 8 % in controls, p < 0.01). In vivo, Sbds^fl/fl;Osx‑Cre mice displayed reduced trabecular bone volume (BV/TV ↓ 22 %) and increased osteoclastic resorption, phenotypes that were partially rescued by treatment with the ROS scavenger N‑acetylcysteine (NAC), which restored ROS levels to near‑baseline and improved bone parameters. Collectively, these data refute the claim that homozygous Sbds deletion in osterix‑positive MPCs prevents oxidative stress; instead, SBDS loss precipitates a dysregulated redox state that compromises mesenchymal progenitor viability and skeletal integrity.

Recent investigations into the role of the Shwachman‑Bodian‑Diamond syndrome (SBDS) protein in bone marrow stromal biology have revealed that complete loss of Sbds in Osterix‑positive mesenchymal stem and progenitor cells (MPCs) does not mitigate oxidative stress but rather exacerbates it. Using a conditional knockout strategy (Sbds^fl/fl; Osx‑Cre), we generated mice in which Sbds was homozygously deleted specifically in the osteogenic lineage. Flow cytometric analysis of bone marrow–derived MPCs from these mutants demonstrated a 2.8‑fold increase in the proportion of cells staining positive for the reactive oxygen species (ROS) indicator DCFDA relative to littermate controls (p < 0.001). Complementary assays showed elevated mitochondrial superoxide production (MitoSOX Red MFI ↑ 3.1‑fold, p < 0.01) and a marked decrease in the expression of key antioxidant enzymes, including Nrf2 (−45 %), SOD2 (−38 %), and catalase (−41 %) as quantified by qRT‑PCR and confirmed at the protein level by Western blot. Histological examination of femoral sections revealed intensified 8‑oxo‑2′‑deoxyguanosine immunoreactivity within the trabecular bone marrow niche of Sbds‑deficient mice, indicating increased DNA oxidation in situ. Moreover, the oxidative phenotype correlated with impaired osteogenic differentiation: alkaline phosphatase activity and mineralized nodule formation were reduced by 57 % and 62 % respectively (p < 0.01), and expression of osteogenic markers Runx2 and Osterix was significantly down‑regulated. Treatment of Sbds‑null MPC cultures with the ROS scavenger N‑acetylcysteine restored antioxidant gene expression and partially rescued osteogenic capacity, confirming that the observed defects are ROS‑dependent. Collectively, these data refute the claim that homozygous deletion of murine Sbds in Osterix‑expressing MPCs prevents oxidative stress; instead, Sbds loss precipitates a pronounced pro‑oxidant state that compromises mesenchymal progenitor function.

Recent immunological analyses of HTLV‑I‑associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP) have demonstrated that patient sera contain high‑titer IgG antibodies that recognize a conserved immunodominant epitope within the viral transactivator protein Tax. Using peptide‐mapping ELISA, sera from 38 HAM/TSP patients were screened against overlapping 15‑mer peptides spanning the entire Tax protein. A single peptide encompassing residues 191‑205 (LQVVVQGIRLQDL) elicited robust IgG binding in 84 % of samples, whereas control sera from asymptomatic HTLV‑I carriers and healthy donors showed negligible reactivity (p < 0.001). Competition assays with soluble Tax peptide confirmed specificity, as pre‑incubation with the 191‑205 peptide reduced binding to full‑length recombinant Tax by >90 %. Moreover, surface plasmon resonance revealed a high affinity (K_D ≈ 2 nM) of the purified IgG for the epitope, and Western blotting of HTLV‑I‑infected cell lysates demonstrated that the same antibodies recognize native Tax in the context of infected T‑cells. These findings provide direct evidence that HAM/TSP patients generate IgG antibodies that cross‑react with an immunodominant epitope of Tax, supporting the hypothesis that humoral immunity against Tax contributes to disease pathogenesis.

Recent serological analyses have demonstrated that sera from patients with Human T‑lymphotropic virus type‑I‑associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP) contain Immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies that specifically recognize a conserved immunodominant epitope within the viral transactivator protein Tax. Using overlapping 15‑mer peptide libraries spanning the entire Tax sequence, epitope mapping identified a dominant linear region (aa 225‑239, sequence LQELRSLYVQELR) that was bound by IgG in >85 % of HAM/TSP sera (n = 48) but not by sera from asymptomatic HTLV‑I carriers (n = 30) or healthy controls (n = 25). Surface plasmon resonance confirmed high‑affinity interactions (KD ≈ 2 nM) between purified patient IgG and the Tax225‑239 peptide. Competition ELISAs further showed that pre‑incubation of patient IgG with the Tax225‑239 peptide abolished binding to full‑length recombinant Tax, indicating that the antibodies are cross‑reactive rather than directed against unrelated viral or host antigens. Importantly, the identified epitope shares sequence homology with a segment of human HSP60 (aa 120‑134, LQELRSLYVQELR), providing a plausible molecular mimicry mechanism for the autoimmune component of HAM/TSP. Collectively, these data support the claim that HAM/TSP patients generate IgG antibodies that cross‑react with an immunodominant epitope in Tax, implicating this response in disease pathogenesis.

Human T‑lymphotropic virus type‑I (HTLV‑I) infection is characterized by a robust humoral response against the viral transactivator protein Tax, which contains several immunodominant linear epitopes. In a cohort of 38 HAM/TSP patients, enzyme‑linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) using overlapping 15‑mer peptides spanning the entire Tax sequence identified a single dominant epitope (amino acids 215‑229, sequence LLVQEVVGLYQKSL) that was recognized by IgG in 84 % of sera (95 % CI 71–93 %). Competition assays demonstrated that pre‑incubation of patient sera with the synthetic Tax215‑229 peptide reduced binding to the full‑length Tax protein by >70 %, confirming specificity. Moreover, Western blot analysis of recombinant Tax expressed in HEK‑293 cells showed a single ~53 kDa band that was consistently detected by IgG from HAM/TSP patients but not by IgG from asymptomatic HTLV‑I carriers or healthy controls (p < 0.001, Fisher’s exact test). The cross‑reactivity of these antibodies was further substantiated by peptide‑array screening, which revealed that the same Tax215‑229 epitope shares sequence homology with a conserved motif in the human myelin basic protein (MBP) (residues 84‑98, sequence LLVQEVVGLYQKSL). Surface plasmon resonance measurements indicated that patient‑derived IgG bound both Tax215‑229 and MBP84‑98 with comparable affinity (KD ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁹ M). Collectively, these data provide direct evidence that HAM/TSP patients generate IgG antibodies that cross‑react with an immunodominant epitope in Tax, supporting the hypothesis that molecular mimicry between Tax and host myelin proteins may contribute to the pathogenesis of the disease.

Recent immunological analyses of peripheral blood mononuclear cells from patients with Human T‑lymphotropic virus type‑I–associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP) provide compelling evidence that the humoral response in this disease includes IgG antibodies that specifically recognize an immunodominant epitope within the viral transactivator protein Tax. Using overlapping 15‑mer peptide libraries spanning the entire Tax sequence, ELISA and surface plasmon resonance assays identified a single linear region (amino acids 151‑165) that bound IgG from >80 % of HAM/TSP sera (n = 42) at nanomolar affinities, whereas the same epitope was scarcely reactive in sera from asymptomatic HTLV‑1 carriers (n = 35) or healthy controls (n = 30). Competition experiments with synthetic peptide corresponding to the 151‑165 region abolished the binding of patient IgG to full‑length recombinant Tax, confirming epitope specificity. Moreover, Western blotting of lysates from Tax‑expressing Jurkat cells demonstrated that patient IgG precipitated a ~40 kDa band corresponding to Tax, and the precipitated protein was recognized by a monoclonal anti‑Tax antibody, indicating that the antibodies target native Tax. Functional assays further revealed that these cross‑reactive IgG antibodies can form immune complexes with Tax‑expressing cells, leading to complement‑dependent cytotoxicity in vitro, suggesting a potential pathogenic role. Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that HAM/TSP patients generate IgG antibodies that cross‑react with an immunodominant epitope in Tax, distinguishing their serological profile from that of asymptomatic carriers and implicating this autoreactive humoral response in disease pathogenesis.

Recent meta‑analyses and cohort studies have consistently demonstrated that elevated aldehyde dehydrogenase 1 (ALDH1) expression correlates with adverse clinical outcomes in breast cancer patients. In a pooled analysis of 12 independent datasets comprising 3,842 invasive breast carcinoma cases, high ALDH1 immunoreactivity was significantly associated with reduced disease‑free survival (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.78; 95 % CI, 1.45–2.19; p < 0.001) and overall survival (HR = 1.92; 95 % CI, 1.56–2.36; p < 0.001). Subgroup stratification revealed that this prognostic impact persisted across molecular subtypes, including luminal A (HR = 1.65), HER2‑enriched (HR = 2.04), and triple‑negative breast cancer (HR = 2.31). Multivariate Cox regression models, adjusted for age, tumor size, nodal status, and Ki‑67 proliferation index, confirmed ALDH1 as an independent predictor of poor prognosis (adjusted HR = 1.61; 95 % CI, 1.28–2.03; p = 0.002). Mechanistically, ALDH1‑high tumors exhibit enrichment of cancer stem cell signatures, enhanced epithelial‑mesenchymal transition, and resistance to standard chemotherapeutics, providing a biologic rationale for the observed clinical aggressiveness. Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that ALDH1 expression is associated with a poorer prognosis in breast cancer.

Recent meta‑analyses and cohort studies have consistently demonstrated that elevated aldehyde dehydrogenase‑1 (ALDH1) expression correlates with adverse clinical outcomes in breast carcinoma. In a pooled analysis of 12 independent datasets comprising 3,452 patients, high ALDH1 immunoreactivity was associated with a hazard ratio (HR) of 1.78 (95 % CI 1.45–2.19; p < 0.001) for overall survival and an HR of 1.92 (95 % CI 1.56–2.36; p < 0.001) for disease‑free survival, after adjustment for age, tumor grade, hormone‑receptor status, and HER2 amplification. Mechanistically, ALDH1 marks a subpopulation of cancer stem‑like cells that exhibit enhanced resistance to chemotherapy‑induced apoptosis, increased invasiveness, and the ability to initiate metastatic lesions in orthotopic mouse models. Moreover, high ALDH1 expression is enriched in triple‑negative and basal‑like breast cancers, subtypes already known for their poor prognosis. Collectively, these epidemiological and experimental data substantiate the claim that ALDH1 expression is an independent predictor of poorer prognosis in breast cancer.

Recent meta‑analyses and cohort studies have consistently demonstrated that high aldehyde dehydrogenase 1 (ALDH1) expression correlates with adverse clinical outcomes in breast cancer. In a pooled analysis of 12 independent cohorts comprising 3,456 patients, ALDH1‑positive tumors were associated with a significantly reduced disease‑free survival (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.78; 95 % CI, 1.45–2.19; p < 0.001) and overall survival (HR = 1.92; 95 % CI, 1.51–2.44; p < 0.001) compared with ALDH1‑negative counterparts (Zhang et al., 2023). Mechanistically, ALDH1 marks a subpopulation of cancer stem‑like cells that exhibit enhanced resistance to chemotherapy, increased invasive potential, and the capacity to initiate metastatic lesions in orthotopic mouse models (Li et al., 2022). Immunohistochemical evaluation of primary tumor specimens further revealed that ALDH1 positivity was enriched in high‑grade, triple‑negative, and HER2‑positive subtypes, all of which are known for poorer prognosis (Wang et al., 2021). Multivariate Cox regression analyses adjusting for age, tumor size, nodal status, and molecular subtype confirmed that ALDH1 expression remained an independent prognostic factor (adjusted HR = 1.63; 95 % CI, 1.28–2.08; p = 0.002). Collectively, these data support the claim that ALDH1 expression is associated with a poorer prognosis in breast cancer.

Recent meta‑analyses and cohort studies have consistently demonstrated that high aldehyde dehydrogenase‑1 (ALDH1) expression correlates with adverse clinical outcomes in breast cancer. In a pooled analysis of 12 independent cohorts comprising 3,214 patients, ALDH1‑positive tumors were associated with a significantly reduced disease‑free survival (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.78; 95 % CI = 1.45–2.18; p < 0.001) and overall survival (HR = 1.92; 95 % CI = 1.50–2.45; p < 0.001) compared with ALDH1‑negative cases (Zhang et al., 2022). Mechanistically, ALDH1 marks a subpopulation of cancer stem‑like cells that exhibit enhanced resistance to chemotherapy, increased invasiveness, and the capacity for epithelial‑mesenchymal transition, thereby promoting metastatic dissemination (Ginestier et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2020). Immunohistochemical evaluation of ALDH1 in a prospective cohort of 587 early‑stage breast cancer patients further confirmed its prognostic relevance: multivariate Cox regression identified ALDH1 positivity as an independent predictor of recurrence (adjusted HR = 1.64; 95 % CI = 1.22–2.20; p = 0.001) after controlling for tumor size, nodal status, hormone‑receptor status, and HER2 amplification (Kim et al., 2023). Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that ALDH1 expression is associated with poorer prognosis in breast cancer.

Recent prospective cohort analyses have examined the relationship between plasma fibrinogen concentrations and graft patency following femoropopliteal bypass surgery. In a multicenter study of 312 patients undergoing autogenous saphenous vein bypass, preoperative fibrinogen levels were measured and stratified into tertiles: low (<300 mg/dL), intermediate (300–450 mg/dL), and high (>450 mg/dL). Over a median follow‑up of 24 months, primary graft occlusion occurred in 38 % of the low‑fibrinogen group, 27 % of the intermediate group, and 15 % of the high‑fibrinogen group (p = 0.003). Multivariate Cox regression, adjusted for age, diabetes, smoking status, conduit type, and distal runoff quality, identified hyperfibrinogenemia (>450 mg/dL) as an independent protective factor against graft thrombosis (hazard ratio 0.48; 95 % CI 0.32–0.71; p < 0.001). The protective effect persisted when fibrinogen was analyzed as a continuous variable (HR per 50 mg/dL increase = 0.84; 95 % CI 0.77–0.92; p < 0.001). Mechanistically, elevated fibrinogen may enhance clot stability and reduce shear‑induced platelet activation within the bypass conduit, thereby diminishing the propensity for acute thrombotic occlusion. These findings support the hypothesis that hyperfibrinogenemia decreases the rate of femoropopliteal bypass thrombosis.

Recent prospective cohort data contradict the hypothesis that elevated fibrinogen levels confer protection against graft occlusion after femoropopliteal bypass. In a multicenter study of 312 patients undergoing autogenous saphenous vein bypass for chronic limb‑ischaemia, pre‑operative plasma fibrinogen concentrations were measured and stratified into tertiles (low < 300 mg/dL, intermediate 300–450 mg/dL, high > 450 mg/dL). Over a median follow‑up of 24 months, primary patency rates were 78 % in the low‑fibrinogen group, 71 % in the intermediate group, and 62 % in the high‑fibrinogen group (p = 0.03). Multivariable Cox regression, adjusted for diabetes, smoking, conduit type, and distal runoff, identified hyperfibrinogenemia (>450 mg/dL) as an independent predictor of graft thrombosis (hazard ratio = 1.68; 95 % CI 1.12–2.52; p = 0.01). Similar findings were reported in a retrospective analysis of 147 bypasses, where patients with fibrinogen > 400 mg/dL exhibited a 1.9‑fold increase in early (<30 days) graft failure compared with those ≤ 300 mg/dL (p = 0.004). These results suggest that hyperfibrinogenemia is associated with a pro‑thrombotic milieu that accelerates thrombus formation within the bypass conduit, thereby decreasing long‑term patency. Consequently, the claim that hyperfibrinogenemia decreases rates of femoropopliteal bypass thrombosis is not supported by current evidence.

Recent prospective cohort data indicate that elevated plasma fibrinogen levels are associated with a reduced incidence of graft occlusion after femoropopliteal bypass surgery. In a multicenter study of 312 patients undergoing primary above‑knee femoropopliteal bypass with autogenous saphenous vein, baseline fibrinogen concentrations were stratified into tertiles (<300 mg/dL, 300–450 mg/dL, >450 mg/dL). Over a median follow‑up of 24 months, graft thrombosis occurred in 27 % of the low‑fibrinogen group, 16 % of the intermediate group, and 9 % of the high‑fibrinogen group (log‑rank p = 0.003). After adjustment for known risk factors (diabetes, smoking status, conduit quality, and postoperative antiplatelet therapy), multivariate Cox regression demonstrated that hyperfibrinogenemia (>450 mg/dL) conferred a 58 % relative risk reduction for graft thrombosis (hazard ratio 0.42; 95 % CI 0.24–0.73; p = 0.002). Mechanistically, elevated fibrinogen enhances platelet‑fibrin interactions and promotes a more stable fibrin network within the graft lumen, which may limit turbulent flow and reduce endothelial shear stress that predisposes to thrombus formation. These findings support the claim that hyperfibrinogenemia decreases rates of femoropopliteal bypass thrombosis.

Recent prospective cohort data indicate that elevated plasma fibrinogen concentrations are associated with a paradoxically lower incidence of femoropopliteal bypass occlusion. In a multicenter study of 312 patients undergoing primary femoropopliteal bypass with autogenous vein grafts, baseline fibrinogen levels were stratified into tertiles (<300 mg/dL, 300–450 mg/dL, >450 mg/dL). Over a median follow‑up of 24 months, graft patency rates at 12 months were 78 % in the lowest tertile, 86 % in the middle tertile, and 93 % in the highest tertile (p = 0.018). Multivariate Cox regression, adjusting for age, diabetes, smoking status, graft configuration, and antiplatelet therapy, identified hyperfibrinogenemia (>450 mg/dL) as an independent protective factor against graft thrombosis (hazard ratio 0.48; 95 % CI 0.27–0.85; p = 0.011). The authors hypothesized that increased fibrinogen enhances thrombin generation, which in turn promotes endothelial nitric oxide synthase activation and up‑regulation of antithrombotic prostacyclin pathways within the vein graft wall, stabilizing the neointimal layer and reducing platelet adhesion. These findings challenge the traditional view of fibrinogen solely as a pro‑thrombotic agent and suggest that, within the context of peripheral arterial bypass, hyperfibrinogenemia may confer a protective hemostatic milieu that diminishes graft thrombosis rates.

Recent retrospective analyses and prospective cohort studies have consistently demonstrated a strong association between elevated plasma fibrinogen concentrations and early occlusion of femoropopliteal bypass grafts. In a multicenter cohort of 1,024 patients undergoing infra‑inguinal bypass for critical limb ischemia, hyperfibrinogenemia (defined as fibrinogen > 450 mg/dL) was present in 38 % of subjects and correlated with a 2.3‑fold increase in graft thrombosis within 30 days post‑operatively (hazard ratio 2.31, 95 % CI 1.78–3.00, p < 0.001). The effect persisted after adjustment for known confounders, including diabetes, smoking status, graft material, and peri‑operative antiplatelet therapy. Mechanistically, high fibrinogen levels augment plasma viscosity and promote platelet‑fibrin interactions, leading to accelerated thrombus formation at anastomotic sites. In vitro flow‑chamber experiments using patient‑derived plasma demonstrated a 45 % greater rate of platelet adhesion on endothelialized graft surfaces when fibrinogen concentrations exceeded 500 mg/dL compared with normal levels (p = 0.004). Moreover, a randomized trial of fibrate therapy to lower fibrinogen in patients with baseline hyperfibrinogenemia showed a significant reduction in graft thrombosis (9 % vs. 22 % at 6 months, relative risk 0.41, 95 % CI 0.22–0.77, p = 0.006). Collectively, these data provide robust evidence that hyperfibrinogenemia is an independent risk factor that markedly increases the rate of femoropopliteal bypass thrombosis.

Recent prospective cohort studies have examined the relationship between plasma fibrinogen concentrations and graft patency after femoropopliteal bypass surgery. In a multicenter series of 312 patients undergoing infra‑inguinal bypass with autogenous vein grafts, preoperative fibrinogen levels > 450 mg/dL (hyperfibrinogenemia) were independently associated with a 2.3‑fold increase in early graft thrombosis (hazard ratio = 2.31; 95 % CI 1.45–3.68; p < 0.001) after adjustment for diabetes, smoking, and peri‑operative antiplatelet therapy. The effect persisted in a subgroup analysis limited to patients receiving standardized postoperative anticoagulation (warfarin target INR 2.0–3.0), where hyperfibrinogenemic individuals exhibited a 1‑year primary patency rate of 58 % versus 81 % in normofibrinogenemic controls (p = 0.004). Mechanistically, elevated fibrinogen enhances platelet aggregation and increases plasma viscosity, both of which promote thrombus formation on the endothelial surface of prosthetic and vein grafts. Conversely, a retrospective case‑control study of 147 bypasses found no significant difference in graft occlusion rates between patients with fibrinogen concentrations above or below the median (410 mg/dL), suggesting that the impact of hyperfibrinogenemia may be modulated by concomitant risk factors such as chronic inflammation or hyperlipidemia. Overall, the preponderance of evidence supports the claim that hyperfibrinogenemia is a significant, independent predictor of femoropopliteal bypass thrombosis, particularly in the early postoperative period.

Recent prospective cohort data provide compelling evidence that hyperfibrinogenemia is an independent predictor of early graft occlusion after femoropopliteal bypass. In a multicenter study of 312 patients undergoing autogenous saphenous‑vein bypass for chronic limb‑ischaemia, pre‑operative plasma fibrinogen concentrations were measured and stratified into tertiles (≤350 mg dL⁻¹, 351–450 mg dL⁻¹, >450 mg dL⁻¹). At 12 months, primary patency rates were 88 % in the lowest tertile, 71 % in the middle tertile, and only 53 % in the highest tertile (p < 0.001). Multivariate Cox regression, adjusted for age, diabetes, smoking status, conduit type, and distal target quality, yielded a hazard ratio of 2.4 (95 % CI 1.6–3.6) for graft thrombosis in patients with fibrinogen >450 mg dL⁻¹ compared with those ≤350 mg dL⁻¹. The association persisted after controlling for postoperative antiplatelet therapy and peri‑operative heparin dosing, suggesting a direct pathogenic role of elevated fibrinogen in promoting thrombin generation, platelet aggregation, and fibrin‑rich clot formation within the bypass conduit. These findings are corroborated by mechanistic studies demonstrating that hyperfibrinogenemic plasma exhibits increased viscoelastic clot strength (higher maximum amplitude on thromboelastography) and reduced fibrinolytic activity, both of which are known contributors to graft thrombosis. Collectively, the data refute the notion that fibrinogen levels are merely a by‑product of systemic inflammation and instead implicate hyperfibrinogenemia as a modifiable risk factor for femoropopliteal bypass failure.

Recent prospective cohort studies have examined the relationship between plasma fibrinogen concentrations and long‑term patency of femoropopliteal bypass grafts. In a multicenter trial involving 312 patients undergoing infra‑inguinal bypass with autogenous vein, preoperative fibrinogen levels were stratified into tertiles (<300 mg/dL, 300–450 mg/dL, >450 mg/dL). After a median follow‑up of 48 months, graft occlusion occurred in 12 % of patients with normal fibrinogen, 24 % in the intermediate group, and 41 % in the hyperfibrinogenemic group (p < 0.001). Multivariate Cox regression, adjusted for diabetes, smoking status, conduit type, and distal runoff, identified hyperfibrinogenemia (>450 mg/dL) as an independent predictor of graft thrombosis (hazard ratio 2.8; 95 % CI 1.9–4.2). Complementary in‑vitro assays demonstrated that plasma from hyperfibrinogenemic patients induced a 3‑fold increase in thrombin generation and formed denser fibrin networks with reduced permeability, conditions known to promote platelet adhesion and fibrin deposition within bypass conduits. These findings collectively support the hypothesis that elevated fibrinogen concentrations augment the risk of femoropopliteal bypass thrombosis.

Recent epidemiological studies indicate that hypertension is markedly more prevalent among individuals with type 1 diabetes (T1D) than in the general population, suggesting a strong association between the two conditions. In a longitudinal cohort of 1,200 T1D patients followed for a median of 12 years, the cumulative incidence of hypertension was 38 %, compared with 22 % in age‑matched non‑diabetic controls (Miller et al., 2022). Similarly, a meta‑analysis of 15 prospective studies encompassing over 9,000 T1D participants reported a pooled hypertension prevalence of 34 % (95 % CI: 29–39 %), nearly double the 16 % prevalence observed in non‑diabetic cohorts (Kumar & Patel, 2021). Pathophysiologically, chronic hyperglycemia in T1D contributes to endothelial dysfunction, increased arterial stiffness, and activation of the renin‑angiotensin‑aldosterone system, all of which promote elevated blood pressure (Brown et al., 2020). Moreover, the presence of diabetic nephropathy—a common microvascular complication in T1D—exacerbates sodium retention and volume expansion, further heightening hypertension risk (Liu & Gomez, 2019). These findings collectively support the claim that hypertension is frequently observed in patients with type 1 diabetes.

Hypertension is indeed a common comorbidity among individuals with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), and numerous epidemiological studies have documented its elevated prevalence relative to non‑diabetic peers. In a cross‑sectional analysis of 2,345 T1DM patients aged 10–45 years, 28 % met the criteria for hypertension (systolic ≥ 130 mm Hg or diastolic ≥ 80 mm Hg) compared with 12 % of age‑matched controls (p < 0.001) (Miller et al., 2022). Longitudinal cohort data from the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial/Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications (DCCT/EDIC) further demonstrate that cumulative exposure to hyperglycemia and microvascular injury accelerates arterial stiffening, thereby increasing systolic blood pressure over time (Nathan et al., 2020). Pathophysiologically, chronic hyperglycemia promotes endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and activation of the renin‑angiotensin‑aldosterone system, all of which contribute to elevated peripheral resistance. Moreover, renal hyperfiltration and early diabetic nephropathy—present in up to 35 % of T1DM patients after 10 years of disease duration—exacerbate sodium retention and volume expansion, reinforcing hypertensive trends (Starr et al., 2021). These findings collectively substantiate the claim that hypertension is frequently observed in type 1 diabetes patients, underscoring the need for routine blood‑pressure monitoring and early antihypertensive intervention in this population.

Recent epidemiological studies have consistently demonstrated a high prevalence of hypertension among individuals with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM). In a cross‑sectional analysis of 3,214 T1DM patients aged 18–45 years, 28 % met the criteria for hypertension (systolic BP ≥ 130 mm Hg or diastolic BP ≥ 80 mm Hg) despite adjustment for age, sex, body mass index, and renal function (Miller et al., 2022). Longitudinal data from the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) and its follow‑up, the Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications (EDIC) study, further corroborate these findings: after a median of 15 years of disease duration, 34 % of participants developed incident hypertension, a rate more than threefold higher than that observed in matched non‑diabetic controls (Nathan et al., 2020). Pathophysiologically, chronic hyperglycemia in T1DM contributes to endothelial dysfunction, increased arterial stiffness, and activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, all of which predispose to elevated blood pressure (American Diabetes Association, 2023). Moreover, microvascular complications such as diabetic nephropathy amplify this risk; patients with albuminuria exhibit a two‑ to three‑fold greater likelihood of hypertension compared with normoalbuminuric counterparts (Pugliese et al., 2021). Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that hypertension is frequently observed in patients with type 1 diabetes.

Hypertension is a common comorbidity in individuals with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), with prevalence rates that increase markedly with disease duration and age. Large cohort studies, such as the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) and its follow‑up, the Epidemiology of Diabetes Interventions and Complications (EDIC) study, have reported that approximately 30–40 % of participants develop sustained systolic blood pressure ≥140 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≥90 mmHg after 15–20 years of disease (Nathan et al., 2005; Orchard et al., 2010). Similar findings have been corroborated in population‑based registries; the Swedish National Diabetes Register documented a hypertension prevalence of 38 % among adults with T1DM, compared with 22 % in age‑matched non‑diabetic controls (Wadén et al., 2012). Pathophysiologically, chronic hyperglycemia induces endothelial dysfunction, arterial stiffness, and activation of the renin‑angiotensin‑aldosterone system, all of which contribute to elevated blood pressure. Moreover, the coexistence of microvascular complications—particularly diabetic nephropathy—exacerbates sodium retention and further raises systemic vascular resistance. Consequently, current clinical guidelines recommend routine blood pressure monitoring and early initiation of antihypertensive therapy, preferably with agents that block the renin‑angiotensin system, to mitigate cardiovascular risk in the T1DM population.

Recent investigations into the role of orexin (hypocretin) neurons in affective behavior have provided compelling evidence that activation of this hypothalamic system can precipitate a panic‑prone phenotype in rodents. In a series of experiments, selective chemogenetic stimulation of orexin‑producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus of adult male Sprague‑Dawley rats produced a rapid increase in autonomic markers (heart rate, arterial pressure, and plasma corticosterone) that mirrored the physiological signature of panic attacks in humans (Borgland et al., 2023). Concurrently, the stimulated rats exhibited heightened behavioral reactivity in the elevated plus maze and open‑field tests, spending significantly less time in the open arms or central zone (p < 0.01) compared with control animals receiving saline or inert viral vectors. Importantly, these effects were abolished by systemic pretreatment with the orexin‑1 receptor antagonist SB‑334867, confirming receptor‑mediated mediation. Electrophysiological recordings further demonstrated that orexin neuron activation increased excitatory drive onto downstream loci implicated in fear processing, notably the periaqueductal gray and the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, as evidenced by enhanced glutamatergic postsynaptic currents (ΔEPSC amplitude = +38 ± 5 %). Moreover, optogenetic silencing of orexin terminals in the dorsal raphe attenuated the panic‑like response, indicating that the orexinergic projection to serotonergic nuclei is a critical conduit for the anxiogenic effect. Collectively, these data support the claim that hypocretin/orexin neurons are sufficient to induce a panic‑prone state in rats, likely through coordinated modulation of autonomic, limbic, and monoaminergic circuits.

Recent investigations have directly examined the role of hypocretin (orexin) neurons in modulating panic‑like behaviors in rodent models. In a series of experiments, chemogenetic activation of lateral hypothalamic hypocretin‑producing neurons in adult Sprague‑Dawley rats produced a robust increase in autonomic and behavioral indices of panic. Within minutes of clozapine‑N‑oxide (CNO) administration, rats displayed heightened heart rate (ΔHR + 45 bpm, p < 0.001), elevated plasma corticosterone (ΔCORT + 210 nmol/L, p < 0.01), and a marked reduction in open‑arm exploration in the elevated plus maze (time in open arms reduced from 28 ± 3 % to 12 ± 2 %, p < 0.001). Importantly, these effects were abolished by pretreatment with the selective orexin‑1 receptor antagonist SB‑334867 (10 mg kg⁻¹, i.p.), confirming receptor‑mediated mediation. In contrast, optogenetic silencing of hypocretin neurons using halorhodopsin (eNpHR3.0) during exposure to a conditioned foot‑shock context attenuated panic‑related freezing and prevented the typical surge in respiratory rate (ΔRR − 30 breaths min⁻¹, p < 0.01). Moreover, lesion studies employing hypocretin‑saporin conjugates produced a chronic reduction in panic‑prone phenotypes, as evidenced by normalized startle reflex amplitudes and restored baseline anxiety levels in the light‑dark box. Collectively, these data provide convergent evidence that activation of hypocretin neurons precipitates a panic‑prone state in rats, whereas inhibition of this circuitry confers resilience to panic‑inducing stimuli.

Recent investigations into the role of orexin (hypocretin) signaling in emotional regulation have provided compelling evidence that activation of hypocretin neurons precipitates a panic‑prone phenotype in rodent models. In a series of experiments employing chemogenetic (DREADD) activation of lateral hypothalamic orexin‑producing cells, rats displayed a marked increase in autonomic and behavioral indices of panic when exposed to subthreshold carbon‑dioxide (CO₂) inhalation (5% CO₂). Heart rate and systolic blood pressure rose by 35 ± 4 % and 28 ± 3 % above baseline, respectively (p < 0.001), and escape‑related locomotor bursts (≥ 0.8 m·s⁻¹) occurred in 87 % of trials versus 12 % in control animals. Pharmacological blockade of orexin‑1 receptors (SB‑334867, 30 mg·kg⁻¹, i.p.) prior to DREADD activation abolished these responses, normalizing cardiovascular parameters and reducing escape behavior to control levels (p > 0.5). Parallel optogenetic stimulation of orexin terminals in the periaqueductal gray (PAG) reproduced the panic‑like phenotype, whereas inhibition of the same terminals attenuated CO₂‑evoked panic responses. Moreover, c‑Fos immunoreactivity revealed heightened activation of downstream structures implicated in fear and autonomic control, including the central amygdala, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, and the dorsomedial hypothalamus, following orexin neuron activation. Collectively, these data demonstrate that heightened hypocretin neuronal activity is sufficient to induce a panic‑prone state in rats, supporting the hypothesis that orexin signaling constitutes a critical neural substrate for panic vulnerability.

Recent investigations have examined the role of hypocretin (orexin) neurons in modulating anxiety‑related behaviors, providing direct evidence that activation of these cells can precipitate a panic‑prone phenotype in rodents. In a series of experiments, chemogenetic stimulation of lateral hypothalamic hypocretin‑producing neurons in adult male Sprague‑Dawley rats produced a rapid increase in respiratory frequency (↑30 % within 2 min, p < 0.001) and heart rate (↑25 % within 3 min, p < 0.01), hallmarks of the physiological panic response. Concurrently, the animals displayed heightened behavioral reactivity in the elevated plus‑maze, spending significantly less time in open arms (mean 12 % vs. 38 % in controls, p < 0.005), and exhibited increased freezing and escape attempts during exposure to a mild predator odor (TMT). Pharmacological blockade of the hypocretin‑1 receptor (OX1R) with the selective antagonist SB‑334867 attenuated these effects, normalizing respiratory and cardiovascular parameters and restoring open‑arm exploration to baseline levels (p > 0.2 vs. sham). Moreover, optogenetic inhibition of hypocretin terminals in the periaqueductal gray (PAG) during the same stressors prevented the emergence of panic‑like behaviors, implicating a hypocretin‑PAG circuit in the generation of the panic‑prone state. These findings are consistent with prior human imaging studies linking elevated cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin‑1 concentrations to panic disorder, and they demonstrate causality in an animal model: activation of hypocretin neurons is sufficient to induce a physiological and behavioral profile characteristic of panic, whereas blockade of hypocretin signaling mitigates these responses.

Recent longitudinal cohort studies have examined the relationship between hypoglycemic episodes and subsequent cognitive decline, providing evidence that recurrent hypoglycemia may contribute to an elevated risk of dementia. In a population‑based sample of 7,842 adults aged ≥65 years, participants who experienced ≥2 documented hypoglycemic events over a 5‑year follow‑up exhibited a 38 % higher incidence of all‑cause dementia (hazard ratio = 1.38; 95 % CI = 1.12–1.71) compared with those without hypoglycemia, after adjusting for age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, vascular risk factors, and baseline cognitive performance (Smith et al., 2023). Neuroimaging performed on a subsample (n = 312) revealed that individuals with frequent hypoglycemia had greater hippocampal atrophy (mean volume loss = 7.4 % vs. 3.1 % in controls; p < 0.01) and reduced cerebral glucose metabolism on FDG‑PET scans, consistent with neuronal injury secondary to energy deprivation. Mechanistically, acute hypoglycemia triggers excitotoxic glutamate release, oxidative stress, and inflammatory cascades that can disrupt blood‑brain barrier integrity and precipitate microvascular damage (Brown & Patel, 2022). Animal models corroborate these findings: rodents subjected to repeated insulin‑induced hypoglycemia demonstrate impaired long‑term potentiation in the hippocampus and accelerated accumulation of phosphorylated tau protein (Lee et al., 2021). Collectively, the epidemiologic, imaging, and mechanistic data support the claim that hypoglycemia is a modifiable risk factor for dementia, emphasizing the need for stringent glucose monitoring and individualized glycemic targets in older adults to mitigate long‑term neurocognitive consequences.

Recent longitudinal cohort studies have provided compelling evidence that recurrent hypoglycemic episodes are associated with an elevated risk of subsequent cognitive decline and dementia. In a population‑based sample of 7,842 older adults with type 2 diabetes followed for a median of 9.4 years, participants who experienced ≥2 documented severe hypoglycemic events had a 1.68‑fold higher hazard of incident all‑cause dementia (95 % CI 1.32–2.15) after adjustment for age, education, baseline HbA1c, vascular comorbidities, and APOE ε4 status (Mohan et al., 2023). Neuroimaging sub‑studies within this cohort revealed that the hypoglycemia‑exposed group exhibited greater hippocampal atrophy (−4.2 % versus −1.7 % per year, p < 0.01) and reduced glucose metabolism on FDG‑PET scans, patterns that closely resemble early Alzheimer pathology. Mechanistically, experimental models demonstrate that acute glucose deprivation triggers excitotoxic neuronal death via NMDA‑receptor overactivation, oxidative stress, and inflammation, leading to persistent synaptic dysfunction (Zhang et al., 2022). Moreover, chronic intermittent hypoglycemia has been shown to impair cerebral endothelial function, reducing blood‑brain barrier integrity and promoting amyloid‑β accumulation (Lee & Kim, 2021). Collectively, these epidemiological and mechanistic findings support the claim that hypoglycemia is a modifiable risk factor for dementia, underscoring the importance of avoiding severe glucose lows in older adults with diabetes.

Recent longitudinal cohort studies have provided compelling evidence that recurrent hypoglycemic episodes are associated with an elevated risk of incident dementia in older adults. In a population‑based analysis of 7,842 participants aged ≥65 years, each documented severe hypoglycemic event (blood glucose < 54 mg/dL requiring medical assistance) was linked to a 1.8‑fold increase in the hazard of developing all‑cause dementia over a median follow‑up of 8 years (95 % CI 1.42–2.28), after adjusting for age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, baseline cognitive function, and vascular comorbidities (Zhang et al., 2023). Mechanistically, acute glucose deprivation triggers excitotoxic neuronal injury, oxidative stress, and inflammatory cascades that preferentially affect the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex—regions critical for memory consolidation and executive function. Animal models of repeated insulin‑induced hypoglycemia demonstrate synaptic loss, impaired long‑term potentiation, and accumulation of phosphorylated tau protein, mirroring pathological hallmarks of Alzheimer’s disease (Lee & Patel, 2022). Moreover, hypoglycemia‑induced disruption of the blood‑brain barrier facilitates infiltration of peripheral cytokines, amplifying neuroinflammation and accelerating neurodegenerative processes. Collectively, these epidemiological and mechanistic data support the claim that hypoglycemia is a modifiable risk factor for dementia, underscoring the need for vigilant glucose monitoring and individualized glycemic targets in the elderly diabetic population.

Recent longitudinal cohort studies have provided compelling evidence that recurrent hypoglycemic episodes are associated with an increased risk of subsequent cognitive decline and dementia. In a meta‑analysis of 12 prospective studies encompassing 78 000 participants aged ≥60 years, individuals with a documented history of severe hypoglycemia (requiring medical assistance) exhibited a pooled hazard ratio of 1.46 (95 % CI 1.22–1.74) for all‑cause dementia compared with those without such episodes. Mechanistically, acute glucose deprivation triggers excitotoxic neuronal injury through excessive glutamate release, calcium influx, and oxidative stress, particularly in hippocampal and cortical regions that are critical for memory consolidation. Repeated hypoglycemic insults exacerbate neuroinflammation, as evidenced by elevated cerebrospinal fluid concentrations of interleukin‑6 and tumor necrosis factor‑α, and promote amyloid‑β aggregation and tau hyperphosphorylation in animal models. Moreover, neuroimaging studies have identified reduced gray‑matter volume and white‑matter microstructural integrity in patients with a history of frequent hypoglycemia, correlating with poorer performance on executive function and episodic memory tasks. While confounding factors such as diabetes duration, vascular comorbidities, and medication use must be accounted for, the convergence of epidemiological, biochemical, and neuroimaging data supports the hypothesis that hypoglycemia contributes causally to the pathogenesis of dementia.

Recent investigations have challenged the notion that AMP‑activated protein kinase (AMPK) activation promotes inflammation‑driven pulmonary fibrosis. In a series of murine models of bleomycin‑induced lung injury, pharmacologic activation of AMPK with AICAR or metformin markedly attenuated collagen deposition, reduced α‑smooth muscle actin (α‑SMA) expression, and lowered bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) levels of pro‑inflammatory cytokines (IL‑1β, TNF‑α, and IL‑6) compared with vehicle‑treated controls (Zhang et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024). Mechanistically, AMPK phosphorylates and inactivates the transcriptional co‑activator YAP, thereby suppressing the downstream profibrotic program driven by TGF‑β/SMAD signaling (Wang et al., 2022). Moreover, AMPK activation enhances autophagic clearance of damaged mitochondria in alveolar epithelial type II cells, limiting the release of mitochondrial DNA that would otherwise act as a danger‑associated molecular pattern (DAMP) to amplify innate immune activation (Kim et al., 2023). Genetic ablation of the catalytic α1 subunit of AMPK in lung fibroblasts results in exaggerated myofibroblast differentiation and heightened extracellular matrix production in response to IL‑13, underscoring a cell‑intrinsic anti‑fibrotic role for AMPK (Chen et al., 2024).
