Collectively, these data demonstrate that AMPK activation exerts protective, anti‑inflammatory, and anti‑fibrotic effects in the lung, refuting the claim that AMPK activation increases inflammation‑related fibrosis.

Recent investigations have challenged the notion that AMP‑activated protein kinase (AMPK) activation universally promotes inflammation‑driven pulmonary fibrosis. In a series of murine models of bleomycin‑induced lung injury, pharmacologic activation of AMPK with AICAR or metformin attenuated collagen deposition, reduced α‑smooth muscle actin (α‑SMA) expression, and lowered levels of pro‑fibrotic cytokines such as TGF‑β1, IL‑1β, and TNF‑α (Zhang et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2023). Mechanistically, AMPK phosphorylates and inactivates the transcriptional co‑activator YAP, thereby suppressing myofibroblast differentiation, and concurrently enhances autophagic clearance of extracellular matrix components (Li et al., 2021). Moreover, AMPK activation inhibits the NF‑κB pathway by promoting IκBα stability, leading to diminished recruitment of inflammatory macrophages to the alveolar interstitium (Wang et al., 2024). Conversely, genetic ablation of AMPKα1 in lung epithelial cells exacerbates inflammatory cell influx, augments fibroblast proliferation, and accelerates fibrosis progression, underscoring a protective role for AMPK signaling. Collectively, these data indicate that AMPK activation mitigates, rather than augments, inflammation‑related fibrosis in the lungs.

Recent investigations have challenged the notion that AMP‑activated protein kinase (AMPK) activation uniformly promotes inflammation‑driven pulmonary fibrosis. In a series of murine models of bleomycin‑induced lung injury, pharmacologic activation of AMPK with AICAR or metformin markedly attenuated collagen deposition and reduced expression of profibrotic mediators such as transforming growth factor‑β1 (TGF‑β1), α‑smooth muscle actin (α‑SMA), and fibronectin (Zhou et al., 2022). Mechanistically, AMPK phosphorylates and inhibits the Smad3 transcriptional complex downstream of TGF‑β1, thereby limiting myofibroblast differentiation (Li et al., 2023). Moreover, AMPK activation suppresses nuclear factor‑κB (NF‑κB) signaling in alveolar macrophages, leading to decreased secretion of interleukin‑1β (IL‑1β) and tumor necrosis factor‑α (TNF‑α), cytokines that are central to the initiation of fibrotic cascades (Wang et al., 2021). In vitro, primary human lung fibroblasts treated with the AMPK activator A-769662 displayed reduced proliferation and migration, accompanied by up‑regulation of the antifibrotic microRNA miR‑29a, a downstream target of AMPK‑dependent SIRT1 activation (Gao et al., 2024). Conversely, genetic ablation of AMPKα1 in lung epithelial cells exacerbates bleomycin‑induced fibrosis, characterized by heightened inflammatory cell infiltration, increased oxidative stress, and amplified extracellular matrix accumulation (Kim et al., 2020). Collectively, these data indicate that AMPK activation exerts a protective, anti‑inflammatory, and anti‑fibrotic role in the lung, refuting the claim that AMPK activation increases inflammation‑related fibrosis.

Recent investigations have challenged the notion that AMP‑activated protein kinase (AMPK) activation promotes inflammation‑driven pulmonary fibrosis. In a series of mechanistic studies using both murine models of bleomycin‑induced lung injury and human primary fibroblasts, pharmacologic activation of AMPK with AICAR or metformin consistently attenuated fibrotic remodeling. AMPK activation led to phosphorylation of the transcriptional co‑repressor SMRT, which in turn suppressed NF‑κB‑mediated transcription of pro‑inflammatory cytokines such as IL‑1β, TNF‑α, and CCL2. Moreover, AMPK‑dependent phosphorylation of the downstream target acetyl‑CoA carboxylase (ACC) reduced lipid accumulation in alveolar macrophages, limiting their transition to a profibrotic M2 phenotype. Genetic deletion of the catalytic α1 subunit of AMPK (Prkaa1⁻/⁻) exacerbated collagen deposition, increased α‑SMA‑positive myofibroblast accumulation, and heightened expression of the extracellular matrix genes Col1a1 and Fn1 after bleomycin challenge (p < 0.01). Conversely, lung‑specific overexpression of a constitutively active AMPKα1 mutant (AMPKα1‑CA) diminished hydroxyproline content by 45 % and restored normal lung compliance. These findings demonstrate that AMPK activation exerts anti‑inflammatory and anti‑fibrotic effects in the lung, refuting the claim that AMPK activation increases inflammation‑related fibrosis.

Recent investigations have elucidated the pivotal role of hypothalamic glutamatergic signaling in the regulation of whole‑body energy homeostasis. Using Cre‑dependent viral vectors to selectively ablate vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (VGLUT2) in arcuate nucleus (ARC) neurons, Zhao et al. (2023) demonstrated that loss of glutamate release from proopiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons precipitates hyperphagia, reduced thermogenic gene expression in brown adipose tissue, and a 15 % increase in adiposity over 8 weeks despite unchanged leptin levels. Complementary optogenetic activation of glutamatergic projections from the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) to the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) elicited rapid increases in sympathetic nerve activity and oxygen consumption, effects that were abolished by intra‑PVN infusion of the NMDA‑receptor antagonist AP5. Moreover, electrophysiological recordings revealed that fasting enhances the frequency of spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) onto glucose‑sensing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, an effect reversed by central administration of the AMPA‑receptor antagonist NBQX, which concurrently normalizes food intake. Together, these data substantiate that glutamate neurotransmission within hypothalamic circuits constitutes a necessary and sufficient driver of energy balance, acting both upstream of anorexigenic pathways and downstream of peripheral metabolic cues.

Recent investigations have elucidated the pivotal role of hypothalamic glutamate signaling in the regulation of whole‑body energy homeostasis. Using a combination of chemogenetic activation, optogenetic silencing, and in vivo microdialysis, we demonstrated that glutamatergic neurons within the arcuate nucleus (ARC) and ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) exert bidirectional control over feeding behavior and thermogenesis. Selective activation of vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (VGLUT2)‑positive ARC neurons resulted in an acute 35 % reduction in cumulative food intake over a 4‑hour period (p < 0.001) and a concomitant increase in brown adipose tissue uncoupling protein‑1 expression, indicative of enhanced energy expenditure. Conversely, RNAi‑mediated knockdown of VGLUT2 in VMH neurons produced hyperphagia (↑22 % kcal/day, p = 0.004) and a significant decline in basal metabolic rate (−8 % VO₂, p = 0.01). Pharmacological blockade of ionotropic glutamate receptors (iGluRs) in the mediobasal hypothalamus recapitulated the hyperphagic phenotype, whereas agonism of metabotropic glutamate receptor 4 (mGluR4) ameliorated diet‑induced obesity in mice (reduction in fat mass by 15 % after 8 weeks, p < 0.01). Importantly, these effects were independent of peripheral leptin signaling, as leptin‑deficient (ob/ob) mice responded similarly to central glutamate manipulations. Together, these data provide compelling evidence that hypothalamic glutamate neurotransmission is a critical integrator of anabolic and catabolic pathways, and that dysregulation of this glutamatergic circuitry contributes directly to the pathogenesis of obesity.

Recent investigations have demonstrated that hypothalamic glutamate signaling plays a pivotal role in the regulation of whole‑body energy homeostasis. Using optogenetic activation of vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (VGLUT2)–expressing neurons within the arcuate nucleus (ARC), investigators observed a rapid increase in sympathetic nerve activity and brown adipose tissue thermogenesis, accompanied by a significant reduction in food intake (Li et al., 2023). Conversely, chemogenetic silencing of VGLUT2‑positive proopiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons resulted in hyperphagia, decreased energy expenditure, and the development of obesity over a 12‑week period (Zhang et al., 2024). Electrophysiological recordings further revealed that glutamatergic inputs to neuropeptide Y/Agouti‑related peptide (NPY/AgRP) neurons are essential for the leptin‑induced suppression of these orexigenic cells; blockade of NMDA receptors in the ARC abolished leptin’s anorectic effect (Gao & Kim, 2022). Moreover, conditional knockout of the glutamate receptor subunit GluN1 in hypothalamic nuclei disrupted the normal circadian pattern of feeding and impaired glucose tolerance, underscoring the necessity of glutamate‑mediated neurotransmission for both acute and chronic energy balance (Miller et al., 2025). Collectively, these data provide compelling evidence that hypothalamic glutamate neurotransmission is a critical integrative signal linking peripheral metabolic cues to central circuits that govern appetite and thermogenesis.

Recent investigations have demonstrated that hypothalamic glutamatergic signaling plays a pivotal role in the regulation of whole‑body energy homeostasis. Electrophysiological recordings from arcuate nucleus (ARC) neurons reveal that activation of vesicular glutamate transporter‑2 (VGLUT2)–dependent release markedly increases the firing rate of pro‑opi­ogenic proopiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons while simultaneously inhibiting agouti‑related peptide/ neuropeptide Y (AgRP/NPY) neurons via fast excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs). Conditional knockout of VGLUT2 in POMC neurons leads to hyperphagia, reduced energy expenditure, and rapid weight gain, phenocopying the effects of leptin deficiency. Conversely, chemogenetic stimulation of glutamatergic inputs to the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) restores normal feeding patterns in diet‑induced obese mice, an effect that is abolished by antagonism of ionotropic glutamate receptors (AMPA/kainate and NMDA). Moreover, optogenetic silencing of glutamatergic afferents from the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) diminishes sympathetic outflow to brown adipose tissue, decreasing thermogenesis and promoting positive energy balance. Together, these data provide convergent evidence that hypothalamic glutamate neurotransmission is essential for integrating peripheral metabolic cues and orchestrating adaptive changes in appetite, locomotor activity, and thermogenic responses, thereby constituting a critical node in the neural circuitry governing energy balance.

Recent investigations into the antiviral functions of interferon‑induced proteins with tetratricopeptide repeats (IFITs) have clarified the mechanistic basis by which IFIT1 impedes viral propagation. Using a combination of ribosome profiling, RNA immunoprecipitation, and in vitro translation assays, Liu et al. (2023) demonstrated that IFIT1 exhibits high affinity for RNAs bearing non‑canonical 5′ cap structures, such as cap‑0 (m⁷GpppN) and uncapped 5′ triphosphates, which are characteristic of many RNA viruses that lack efficient cap‑methyltransferases. Structural analyses revealed that the conserved cap‑binding pocket of IFIT1 accommodates the unmethylated guanosine moiety while sterically excluding the 2′‑O‑methyl group present in host mRNA cap‑1 (m⁷GpppNm). Consequently, IFIT1 selectively sequesters mis‑capped viral RNAs into insoluble ribonucleoprotein complexes, preventing their recruitment to the translation initiation machinery.

Functional relevance was confirmed in IFIT1‑knockout (IFIT1⁻/⁻) human lung epithelial cells, which displayed a >10‑fold increase in replication of a cap‑0–deficient influenza A virus (IAV) strain relative to wild‑type cells. Reconstitution of IFIT1 expression restored the restriction phenotype, whereas a point mutant (K151A) that disrupts cap binding failed to do so. Moreover, polysome profiling showed a dramatic shift of viral RNAs from heavy polysomes to the non‑translating fraction in IFIT1‑competent cells, consistent with sequestration rather than degradation. Importantly, treatment with a methyltransferase inhibitor that forces viral RNAs into a cap‑0 state sensitized otherwise resistant viruses (e.g., vesicular stomatitis virus) to IFIT1‑mediated inhibition, underscoring the specificity of the cap‑recognition mechanism.

Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that IFIT1 restricts viral replication by sequestering mis‑capped viral RNAs, thereby blocking their translation and downstream genome amplification.

Recent investigations into the interferon‑induced protein with tetratricopeptide repeats 1 (IFIT1) have clarified its mechanistic role in antiviral defense, revealing that its restriction of viral replication is mediated primarily through selective binding of uncapped or incompletely capped viral RNAs rather than sequestration of mis‑capped transcripts. Structural analyses demonstrate that IFIT1 possesses a high‑affinity cap‑binding pocket that discriminates between the canonical 5′‑m^7GpppN cap structure and aberrant cap configurations lacking the N7‑methyl group or possessing non‑canonical cap analogues (e.g., cap 0 versus cap 1/2). In vitro binding assays using radiolabeled RNA substrates show that IFIT1 binds with nanomolar affinity to RNAs bearing a 5′‑triphosphate or a cap 0 structure, while its affinity for properly methylated cap 1/2 RNAs is reduced by >100‑fold. Ribosome profiling of cells infected with influenza A virus or vesicular stomatitis virus confirms that IFIT1 occupancy on viral mRNAs correlates with a marked decrease in polysome association and a concomitant increase in RNA decay intermediates, indicating translational repression rather than physical sequestration.

Furthermore, mutagenesis of the conserved aromatic residues lining the cap‑binding groove (e.g., W147A, Y151A) abolishes IFIT1’s ability to discriminate cap structures and eliminates its antiviral activity, supporting a model in which cap recognition, not sequestration of mis‑capped RNAs, is the critical determinant of viral inhibition. In contrast, experiments that artificially introduce methyltransferase activity to restore proper cap 1 methylation on viral RNAs rescue translation in the presence of IFIT1, underscoring that the presence of a correctly methylated cap, not the mere presence of a cap, is sufficient to evade IFIT1‑mediated restriction.

Collectively, these data refute the claim that IFIT1 restricts viral replication by sequestering mis‑capped viral RNAs; instead, IFIT1 functions as a cap‑sensing translational repressor that selectively targets RNAs lacking appropriate N7‑ and 2′‑O‑methylation, thereby impeding viral protein synthesis and promoting RNA degradation.

Recent investigations into the antiviral functions of interferon‑induced proteins with tetratricopeptide repeats (IFIT) have clarified the mechanistic basis by which IFIT1 impedes viral propagation. Using a combination of ribosome profiling, RNA immunoprecipitation, and in vitro translation assays, we demonstrate that IFIT1 selectively binds to uncapped or improperly 5′‑cap‑modified viral RNAs, thereby preventing their recruitment to the eukaryotic initiation factor 4F (eIF4F) complex. Structural analyses of the IFIT1‑RNA interface reveal a high‑affinity pocket that accommodates the 5′‑triphosphate moiety and recognizes the absence of the N7‑methyl guanosine cap, while tolerating variations in the first transcribed nucleotide. Mutagenesis of key aromatic residues (e.g., Y136A, F172A) abolishes this interaction and restores viral protein synthesis in IFIT1‑expressing cells. Moreover, CRISPR‑mediated knockout of IFIT1 in human lung epithelial cells leads to a >10‑fold increase in replication of cap‑deficient influenza A virus and vesicular stomatitis virus mutants engineered to lack cap methyltransferase activity, without affecting replication of wild‑type viruses possessing correctly capped genomes. Polysome fractionation further confirms that IFIT1‑bound viral RNAs are excluded from translating ribosomes, accumulating in non‑translating RNP complexes. Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that IFIT1 restricts viral replication by sequestrating mis‑capped viral RNAs, thereby blocking their translation and subsequent virion production.

Recent investigations into the antiviral functions of interferon‑induced proteins with tetratricopeptide repeats (IFITs) have clarified the mechanistic basis by which IFIT1 impedes the propagation of diverse RNA viruses. Using a combination of ribosome profiling, quantitative RT‑PCR, and immunoprecipitation coupled to high‑throughput sequencing (RIP‑seq), we demonstrated that IFIT1 exhibits a high affinity for 5′‑end structures lacking a canonical cap 0 or cap 1 methylation pattern. In vitro binding assays revealed a dissociation constant (K_D) of ~30 nM for uncapped or incompletely capped viral RNAs, compared with >1 µM for fully methylated host mRNAs, indicating a >30‑fold selectivity. Structural analysis by cryo‑EM showed that the IFIT1 tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) array forms a positively charged groove that accommodates the 5′‑triphosphate and the unmethylated guanosine, thereby sterically occluding the RNA from the translation initiation complex.

Functionally, ectopic expression of wild‑type IFIT1 in HeLa cells reduced replication of vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), influenza A virus (IAV), and Zika virus (ZIKV) by 70–90 % as measured by plaque assays, whereas a mutant IFIT1 lacking the RNA‑binding pocket (ΔTPR) failed to confer protection. Moreover, knock‑down of IFIT1 by siRNA restored viral protein synthesis without altering viral genome replication, implicating a post‑transcriptional block. Polysome profiling further indicated that IFIT1‑bound viral RNAs are depleted from heavy polysome fractions and accumulate in monosome‑associated or ribosome‑free fractions, consistent with sequestration from the translational machinery.

Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that IFIT1 restricts viral replication by specifically recognizing and sequestering mis‑capped viral RNAs, thereby preventing their efficient translation and downstream propagation.

Recent investigations into the immunometabolic enzyme immunoresponsive gene 1 (IRG1) have revealed a mechanistic basis for its antiviral activity against neurotropic pathogens. IRG1 catalyzes the production of itaconate, a metabolite that exerts pleiotropic effects on host cell metabolism and innate signaling pathways. In primary murine cortical neurons infected with vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) or West Nile virus (WNV), IRG1 expression is rapidly up‑regulated in a type‑I interferon‑dependent manner, leading to a >3‑fold increase in intracellular itaconate concentrations (p < 0.01). Pharmacological supplementation of itaconate or its cell‑permeable derivative dimethyl‑itaconate (DI) recapitulates the antiviral phenotype, reducing viral RNA synthesis by 70–85 % and decreasing progeny virus release by >1 log₁₀ PFU/mL, without compromising neuronal viability. Mechanistically, itaconate inhibits succinate dehydrogenase, resulting in accumulation of succinate and stabilization of hypoxia‑inducible factor‑1α (HIF‑1α). HIF‑1α activation drives transcription of interferon‑stimulated genes (ISGs) such as ISG15, MX1, and OAS1, which collectively suppress viral replication. In parallel, itaconate directly modifies cysteine residues on viral polymerase complexes via electrophilic Michael addition, impairing their enzymatic activity. Genetic ablation of Irg1 in neuronal cultures abolishes these protective effects, leading to a 5‑fold increase in viral titers and heightened cytopathic damage, which can be rescued by exogenous DI. In vivo, Irg1⁻/⁻ mice challenged intracerebrally with WNV exhibit accelerated disease onset, higher viral loads in the brain (median 10⁷ RNA copies/µg) and increased mortality (90 % vs 30 % in wild‑type controls). Conversely, adeno‑associated virus–mediated neuronal overexpression of IRG1 confers robust protection, with a 2‑log₁₀ reduction in brain viral burden and preservation of motor function. These data collectively substantiate that IRG1, through itaconate‑mediated metabolic reprogramming and direct antiviral modifications, exerts potent antiviral effects against neurotropic viruses.

Recent investigations have provided compelling evidence that the immunoresponsive gene 1 (IRG1), which encodes the mitochondrial enzyme cis‑aconitate decarboxylase responsible for itaconate production, exerts direct antiviral activity against several neurotropic viruses. In vitro infection models using primary murine cortical neurons and human induced pluripotent stem‑cell‑derived neuronal cultures demonstrated that CRISPR‑Cas9‑mediated knockout of Irg1 markedly increased replication of vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), West Nile virus (WNV), and Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), as measured by viral RNA load (qRT‑PCR) and plaque‑forming units. Conversely, lentiviral overexpression of Irg1 or pharmacological supplementation with dimethyl‑itaconate (DI) reduced viral titers by 1.5–2 logs, an effect that was abrogated by co‑treatment with the succinate dehydrogenase inhibitor malonate, indicating that the antiviral phenotype depends on metabolic reprogramming rather than off‑target drug actions.

Mechanistically, IRG1‑derived itaconate inhibits the activity of viral RNA‑dependent RNA polymerases (RdRps) through covalent modification of conserved cysteine residues in the catalytic core, as shown by mass‑spectrometry–based proteomics of infected neuronal lysates. This modification diminishes viral genome synthesis without impairing host transcription. Additionally, itaconate activates the NRF2‑dependent antioxidant response, leading to up‑regulation of interferon‑stimulated genes (ISGs) such as Ifit1, Oas1a, and Mx1, which further restrict viral spread. Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP‑seq) revealed enhanced binding of NRF2 to ISG promoters in Irg1‑overexpressing neurons, supporting a synergistic antiviral circuit.

In vivo, Irg1‑deficient mice infected intracerebrally with a sublethal dose of WNV displayed accelerated disease onset, higher viral loads in the hippocampus and cerebellum, and a 70 % mortality rate compared with 30 % mortality in wild‑type littermates (p < 0.01). Systemic administration of DI (50 mg kg⁻¹ day⁻¹) rescued Irg1‑knockout mice, normalizing viral burden and improving survival to wild‑type levels. Importantly, the protective effect of DI was lost in Nrf2⁻/⁻ mice, confirming the requirement of the NRF2 axis.

Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that IRG1 confers antiviral protection against neurotropic viruses through a dual mechanism: direct inhibition of viral polymerases via itaconate modification and indirect amplification of host antiviral immunity via NRF2‑mediated ISG induction.

Recent investigations have demonstrated that immunoresponsive gene 1 (IRG1) exerts a potent antiviral function against neurotropic viruses through its enzymatic production of itaconate, a metabolite that modulates innate immune signaling in the central nervous system (CNS). In murine models of West Nile virus (WNV) and Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) infection, IRG1‑deficient (Acod1⁻/⁻) mice exhibited markedly increased viral loads in the brain and spinal cord, accompanied by heightened mortality (p < 0.001) compared with wild‑type controls. Primary cortical neuron cultures derived from Acod1⁻/⁻ embryos showed a three‑fold increase in viral replication kinetics, as measured by plaque assay and quantitative RT‑PCR, relative to neurons from wild‑type littermates. Mechanistically, IRG1‑derived itaconate suppressed succinate dehydrogenase activity, leading to accumulation of succinate and subsequent stabilization of hypoxia‑inducible factor‑1α (HIF‑1α). This metabolic rewiring attenuated the transcriptional activation of NF‑κB–dependent pro‑viral genes, while simultaneously enhancing the expression of type I interferon (IFN‑β) and interferon‑stimulated genes (ISGs) such as ISG15, MX1, and OAS1. Pharmacological supplementation of itaconate or the cell‑permeable derivative dimethyl‑itaconate (DI) rescued the antiviral phenotype in Acod1⁻/⁻ neurons, reducing viral titers by >80 % and restoring IFN‑β production to levels comparable with wild‑type cells. Moreover, in vivo administration of DI to Acod1⁻/⁻ mice infected with WNV restored survival rates to those of wild‑type animals, confirming that the antiviral effect is mediated primarily by itaconate signaling rather than other IRG1 functions. Collectively, these data provide compelling evidence that IRG1 functions as an intrinsic antiviral effector in the CNS, limiting replication and spread of neurotropic viruses through itaconate‑dependent metabolic and immunomodulatory pathways.

Recent investigations have begun to elucidate the role of immune‑responsive gene 1 (IRG1) in the host defense against neurotropic viral infections. IRG1 encodes the mitochondrial enzyme cis‑aconitate decarboxylase, which catalyzes the production of itaconate, a metabolite with well‑documented anti‑inflammatory and antimicrobial properties. In vitro studies using primary cortical neurons and microglia infected with vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) and West Nile virus (WNV) demonstrated that IRG1 expression is rapidly up‑regulated via the NF‑κB and type‑I interferon signaling pathways. Overexpression of IRG1 or exogenous supplementation with cell‑permeable itaconate significantly reduced viral replication, as measured by plaque assay and quantitative PCR, whereas CRISPR‑Cas9‑mediated knockout of IRG1 resulted in a >5‑fold increase in viral titers and heightened cytopathic effects. Mechanistically, itaconate inhibited viral RNA synthesis by targeting the viral RNA‑dependent RNA polymerase and concurrently suppressed the host succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) activity, leading to accumulation of succinate and activation of the hypoxia‑inducible factor‑1α (HIF‑1α) pathway, which further promotes expression of antiviral interferon‑stimulated genes (ISGs). In vivo, Irg1‑deficient mice infected intracerebrally with a neurovirulent strain of Japanese encephalitis virus displayed accelerated disease onset, increased viral load in the brain, and higher mortality compared with wild‑type littermates; treatment with dimethyl‑itaconate rescued survival to near‑wild‑type levels. Collectively, these data provide compelling evidence that IRG1 exerts antiviral effects against neurotropic viruses through itaconate‑mediated metabolic reprogramming and direct inhibition of viral replication machinery.

Recent phosphoproteomic analyses of activated primary human CD4⁺ T cells reveal that phosphorylation of immunoreceptor‑based activation motifs (ITAMs) within the CD3ε, CD3γ, CD3δ and ζ‑chain subunits rapidly recruits the Src‑family kinase Lck and the adaptor protein ZAP‑70 to the membrane‑proximal region of the TCR complex. Using site‑directed mutagenesis to generate phospho‑deficient (Y→F) and phospho‑mimetic (Y→E) ITAM variants, we demonstrated that phospho‑mimetic ITAMs lock the receptor complex in a conformation that sterically occludes the “echo‑domain” (the extracellular C‑terminal segment of CD3ε that transduces conformational changes from the pMHC‑bound TCRαβ heterodimer). Fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) measurements showed a 45 % reduction in energy transfer between a GFP‑tagged echo‑domain and a mCherry‑tagged cytoplasmic tail when ITAMs were phosphorylated, indicating impaired physical coupling. Moreover, calcium flux assays and NFAT‑luciferase reporter activity were attenuated by ~60 % in cells expressing phospho‑mimetic ITAMs, despite normal ligand binding and echo‑domain conformational shifts as measured by conformation‑specific antibodies. In contrast, phospho‑deficient ITAMs restored efficient echo‑domain‑to‑tail signal propagation, yielding calcium responses comparable to wild‑type receptors. Collectively, these data support the claim that ITAM phosphorylation acts as a molecular switch that prevents the transfer of the TCR signal from the echo‑domain to the cytoplasmic tail, thereby modulating downstream activation pathways.

Recent phospho‑proteomic analyses of primary murine CD4⁺ T cells have demonstrated that ITAM (immunoreceptor tyrosine‑based activation motif) phosphorylation does not impede, but rather facilitates, the propagation of TCR‑derived signals from the extracellular‑ligand‑binding (echo) domain to the intracellular cytoplasmic tail. Using a combination of site‑directed mutagenesis, live‑cell FRET imaging, and quantitative mass spectrometry, we compared wild‑type TCR complexes with mutants in which the three canonical ITAM tyrosines (Y142, Y178, Y191 in CD3ζ) were replaced by phenylalanine (ζ‑3F). Upon stimulation with cognate peptide‑MHC, wild‑type receptors exhibited rapid (t½ ≈ 3 s) recruitment of the Src‑family kinase Lck to the membrane proximal region, followed by sequential phosphorylation of CD3ε, CD3γ, CD3δ and CD3ζ ITAMs. This cascade was accompanied by a marked increase in the FRET efficiency between a GFP‑tagged TCRα echo‑domain sensor and an mCherry‑tagged CD3ζ cytoplasmic tail probe, indicating efficient signal transduction across the membrane. In contrast, ζ‑3F mutants displayed a pronounced delay in Lck recruitment (t½ ≈ 12 s) and a 70 % reduction in downstream ZAP‑70 phosphorylation, yet the FRET signal between the echo‑domain and the cytoplasmic tail remained comparable to that of wild‑type receptors (ΔFRET ≈ 5 %). Moreover, phospho‑specific antibodies against the ITAM tyrosines revealed that their phosphorylation creates docking sites for the tandem SH2 domains of ZAP‑70, which in turn stabilizes the interaction between the CD3ε/δ/γ ectodomain and the CD3ζ tail, as evidenced by co‑immunoprecipitation of the ectodomain‑proximal adaptor LAT only after ITAM phosphorylation. Importantly, the use of the Src‑family kinase inhibitor PP2 abolished ITAM phosphorylation and simultaneously reduced echo‑to‑tail FRET to baseline levels, confirming that ITAM phosphorylation is a prerequisite for signal continuity rather than a barrier. Collectively, these data refute the claim that ITAM phosphorylation prevents signal transfer; instead, they support a model in which ITAM phosphorylation is essential for coupling the extracellular echo‑domain engagement to intracellular cytoplasmic tail signaling, thereby ensuring efficient TCR activation.

Recent phosphoproteomic analyses of primary human CD4⁺ T cells reveal that ITAM (immunoreceptor‑tyrosine‑based activation motif) phosphorylation does not impede, but rather facilitates, the propagation of TCR‑derived signals from the extracellular “echo‑domain” (the ligand‑binding variable region) to the intracellular cytoplasmic tail. Using a combination of site‑directed mutagenesis, live‑cell FRET imaging, and quantitative mass spectrometry, we compared wild‑type TCRζ chains with mutants in which the three canonical ITAM tyrosines (Y142, Y153, Y164) were replaced by phenylalanine (TCRζ‑FFF). In cells expressing TCRζ‑FFF, engagement of peptide‑MHC complexes induced normal conformational changes in the extracellular domain, as measured by an echo‑domain‑specific intramolecular probe, but downstream recruitment of ZAP‑70 and LAT to the cytoplasmic tail was markedly reduced (∼70 % decrease in phospho‑ZAP‑70 Y319 and phospho‑LAT Y132). Conversely, phosphomimetic mutants (TCRζ‑EE) that mimic constitutive ITAM phosphorylation restored ZAP‑70 binding and LAT phosphorylation to levels comparable with wild‑type receptors, even when the echo‑domain signal was artificially attenuated by low‑affinity peptide ligands. Moreover, kinetic analyses demonstrated that ITAM phosphorylation precedes ZAP‑70 docking by ≈2 s after ligand binding, establishing a temporal cascade that links the extracellular echo‑domain event to intracellular signaling. Collectively, these data refute the claim that ITAM phosphorylation blocks signal transfer; instead, ITAM phosphorylation is essential for coupling the structural rearrangements of the TCR’s echo‑domain to the activation of the cytoplasmic signaling cascade.

Recent investigations into the mechanistic coupling between the immunoreceptor tyrosine‑based activation motif (ITAM) and the T‑cell receptor (TCR) signaling cascade have clarified that ITAM phosphorylation does not impede, but rather facilitates, signal propagation from the extracellular (echo‑domain) region to the intracellular cytoplasmic tail. Using a combination of site‑directed mutagenesis, phospho‑specific flow cytometry, and live‑cell FRET microscopy, we demonstrated that selective ablation of the two conserved tyrosines within the CD3ζ ITAMs abolishes downstream calcium flux and Erk activation despite intact ligand binding to the TCR αβ heterodimer. Conversely, enforced phosphorylation of these tyrosines—either by constitutively active Lck or by phosphomimetic Y→E substitutions—restores full signal transmission, as evidenced by rapid recruitment of ZAP‑70 to the phosphorylated ITAMs, subsequent LAT phosphorylation, and sustained MAPK pathway activation. Importantly, single‑particle tracking of TCR microclusters revealed that ITAM‑phosphorylated receptors exhibit increased dwell time at the immunological synapse and enhanced coupling to the actin cytoskeleton, promoting efficient relay of the extracellular “echo” signal to the intracellular tail. These data collectively refute the claim that ITAM phosphorylation blocks signal transfer; instead, they underscore ITAM phosphorylation as a necessary step that bridges the extracellular recognition event with intracellular signaling modules, thereby amplifying and sustaining TCR‑mediated activation.

Recent longitudinal analyses of duodenal biopsies from patients with celiac disease have demonstrated that the initiation of a strict gluten‑free diet (GFD) is associated with a rapid decline, rather than an accumulation, of transglutaminase‑2 (TG2)‑specific IgA‑secreting plasma cells in the lamina propria. In a cohort of 32 newly diagnosed adults, immunofluorescent staining for TG2‑specific IgA plasma cells was performed at diagnosis, and then at 2 weeks, 3 months, and 12 months after commencement of a GFD. At baseline, the median density of TG2‑specific IgA plasma cells was 45 cells mm⁻² (interquartile range [IQR] 32–58). By 2 weeks of GFD, this density had fallen to 22 cells mm⁻² (IQR 15–30; p < 0.001), and continued to decrease to 8 cells mm⁻² (IQR 4–12; p < 0.001) at 12 months. Parallel quantitative PCR for IGHA transcripts specific for TG2 epitopes corroborated the histological findings, showing a >70 % reduction in TG2‑specific IgA mRNA after 3 months of dietary therapy. Moreover, flow cytometric analysis of isolated lamina propria mononuclear cells revealed a shift from a phenotype of CD19⁺CD27⁺CD38⁺ plasmablasts expressing TG2‑specific B‑cell receptors at diagnosis to a predominance of CD19⁺CD27⁻CD38⁻ naïve B cells after 6 months of GFD, indicating attrition of the antigen‑driven plasma cell compartment. These data collectively refute the claim that TG2‑specific IgA plasma cells accumulate in the duodenal mucosa upon initiation of a gluten‑free diet; instead, they are rapidly depleted as gluten exposure ceases, consistent with the known dependence of TG2‑specific plasma cells on continuous antigenic stimulation for survival.

Recent histopathological analyses of celiac disease patients initiating a gluten‑free diet (GFD) have failed to demonstrate a significant increase in transglutaminase‑2 (TG2)‑specific IgA‑secreting plasma cells within the duodenal lamina propria. In a longitudinal cohort of 32 newly diagnosed adults, immunofluorescence staining for TG2‑specific IgA plasma cells was performed on duodenal biopsies obtained at diagnosis, and after 3, 6, and 12 months of strict GFD adherence. The density of TG2‑specific IgA plasma cells was 45 ± 12 cells mm⁻² at baseline, decreased to 28 ± 9 cells mm⁻² after 3 months (p = 0.03), and remained stable at 26 ± 8 cells mm⁻² after 12 months (p = 0.02 vs. baseline). Parallel quantification of total IgA‑producing plasma cells showed a modest decline from 210 ± 35 to 180 ± 30 cells mm⁻² (p = 0.07), indicating that the reduction was specific to the TG2‑reactive subset. Moreover, serum anti‑TG2 antibody titres fell by >90 % within the first six months of GFD, correlating with the observed tissue depletion (Spearman ρ = 0.68, p < 0.001). These findings are consistent with the notion that removal of dietary gluten eliminates the antigenic stimulus required for the clonal expansion and survival of TG2‑specific IgA plasma cells, leading to their gradual attrition rather than accumulation in the mucosa. Consequently, the claim that TG2‑specific IgA plasma cells accumulate in the duodenal mucosa upon commencement of a gluten‑free diet is not supported by current evidence.

Recent longitudinal analyses of duodenal biopsies from patients with celiac disease have demonstrated that the initiation of a strict gluten‑free diet (GFD) is associated with a rapid decline, rather than an accumulation, of transglutaminase 2 (TG2)‑specific IgA‑secreting plasma cells within the lamina propria. In a cohort of 48 newly diagnosed adults, immunohistochemistry combined with TG2‑specific peptide tetramer staining revealed a median density of TG2‑specific IgA plasma cells of 42 ± 9 cells per high‑power field (HPF) at diagnosis. After 4 weeks of GFD, the density fell to 15 ± 5 cells/HPF (p < 0.001), and by 12 weeks it was indistinguishable from that observed in healthy controls (3 ± 2 cells/HPF). Parallel quantitative PCR for IGHA transcripts specific for TG2 epitopes showed a 3.8‑fold reduction in mRNA levels after 8 weeks of diet (ΔCt = 2.1, p = 0.004). These findings were corroborated by serum analyses, which demonstrated a concomitant decrease in TG2‑specific IgA titers (median 1:640 at baseline to 1:80 after 12 weeks, p < 0.001). The rapid disappearance of TG2‑specific IgA plasma cells is consistent with the known short lifespan of mucosal plasma cells in the absence of antigenic stimulation and supports the hypothesis that gluten exposure, rather than diet withdrawal, drives their expansion. Consequently, the claim that TG2‑specific IgA plasma cells accumulate in the duodenal mucosa upon commencement of a gluten‑free diet is not supported by current evidence; instead, the diet induces a swift contraction of this pathogenic plasma‑cell population.

Recent longitudinal biopsies from patients with newly diagnosed celiac disease reveal that the density of transglutaminase 2‑specific IgA‑secreting plasma cells in the duodenal lamina propria declines rapidly after initiation of a strict gluten‑free diet (GFD). Quantitative immunofluorescence staining using a monoclonal anti‑IgA antibody combined with a recombinant TG2‑binding peptide showed a mean reduction of 68 % in TG2‑specific IgA plasma cells within four weeks of GFD commencement (p < 0.001). Moreover, single‑cell RNA sequencing of isolated lamina propria mononuclear cells demonstrated down‑regulation of plasma‑cell‑associated transcripts (PRDM1, XBP1) and a shift toward a memory B‑cell phenotype, consistent with decreased local antibody production. These findings contradict the hypothesis that TG2‑specific IgA plasma cells accumulate in the duodenal mucosa upon gluten withdrawal; instead, they indicate that the GFD promotes clearance of these pathogenic plasma cells, paralleling mucosal healing and serological normalization.

Recent investigations have demonstrated that immune‑complex (IC) deposition on neutrophils can initiate a form of regulated necrosis that culminates in the extracellular discharge of high‑mobility group box 1 protein (HMGB1). In vitro studies using human neutrophils exposed to pre‑formed IgG‑immune complexes showed rapid activation of FcγRIIA, followed by downstream Syk‑dependent signaling, calcium influx, and mitochondrial ROS generation. These events precipitated the formation of a mixed lineage kinase domain‑like protein (MLKL)‑mediated necroptotic pore, as evidenced by phospho‑MLKL translocation to the plasma membrane and loss of membrane integrity within 30–60 min. Concomitantly, Western blot analysis of supernatants revealed a >10‑fold increase in soluble HMGB1 compared with unstimulated controls, an effect that was abrogated by pharmacological inhibition of RIPK3 (GSK′872) or MLKL (necrosulfonamide), but not by caspase‑3 inhibition. In vivo, murine models of immune‑complex–driven vasculitis (anti‑glomerular basement membrane IgG) displayed extensive neutrophil infiltration, robust citrullinated histone staining (indicative of NETosis), and elevated serum HMGB1 levels that correlated with disease severity. Importantly, neutrophil‑specific deletion of FcγRIIA or conditional knockout of RIPK3 markedly reduced both tissue HMGB1 release and clinical pathology. Collectively, these data support the claim that immune‑complex engagement of neutrophils triggers a necroptotic cell‑death pathway that mediates the extracellular release of HMGB1, linking IC‑induced inflammation to the propagation of sterile tissue injury.

Recent investigations have demonstrated that immune‑complex (IC) formation can precipitate a form of programmed necrosis in neutrophils that culminates in the extracellular release of high‑mobility group box 1 protein (HMGB1). In vitro studies using human neutrophils incubated with pre‑formed IgG‑antigen ICs showed rapid activation of FcγRIIA, leading to Src‑family kinase phosphorylation, ROS generation, and downstream activation of the RIPK1‑RIPK3‑MLKL necroptotic cascade (Kelley et al., 2023). Pharmacologic inhibition of RIPK3 or genetic ablation of MLKL markedly reduced lactate dehydrogenase release and prevented HMGB1 accumulation in the supernatant, confirming necroptosis as the predominant death pathway. Moreover, confocal microscopy revealed translocation of HMGB1 from the nucleus to the cytoplasm within 30 min of IC exposure, preceding plasma membrane rupture. In vivo, murine models of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) that develop circulating ICs exhibit heightened serum HMGB1 levels; this increase is abrogated in FcγRIIA‑deficient or MLKL‑knockout mice, linking IC‑triggered neutrophil necroptosis to HMGB1 release. Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that immune‑complex–induced cell death in neutrophils drives extracellular HMGB1 release, providing a mechanistic bridge between autoantibody deposition and sterile inflammation.

Recent investigations have demonstrated that immune‑complex (IC) engagement of Fcγ receptors on neutrophils initiates a form of programmed cell death distinct from classical apoptosis and necrosis. In vitro, human neutrophils exposed to opsonized IgG immune complexes undergo rapid loss of plasma membrane integrity accompanied by the release of high‑mobility group box 1 protein (HMGB1) into the extracellular milieu. This process is dependent on Syk‑Caspase‑8 signaling and the formation of a mixed lineage kinase domain‑like (MLKL) pore, hallmarks of necroptosis, rather than on caspase‑3 activation. Pharmacologic inhibition of Syk (R406) or MLKL (necrosulfonamide) markedly attenuates HMGB1 release, whereas blockade of FcγRIIA with the monoclonal antibody IV.3 completely abrogates IC‑induced neutrophil death. In vivo, murine models of immune‑complex–mediated vasculitis exhibit elevated serum HMGB1 levels that correlate with neutrophil infiltration and deposition of IgG‑containing immune complexes in the vascular wall. Mice deficient in the neutrophil‑specific FcγRIV or treated with the Syk inhibitor fostamatinib display reduced HMGB1 release and ameliorated tissue injury. Collectively, these data provide mechanistic evidence that immune‑complex–triggered neutrophil death drives extracellular HMGB1 release, supporting the claim that IC‑induced cell death is a critical source of extracellular HMGB1 in inflammatory settings.

Recent investigations have demonstrated that immune‑complex (IC) engagement of Fcγ receptors on neutrophils initiates a form of regulated necrosis that culminates in the extracellular release of high‑mobility group box 1 protein (HMGB1). In vitro, human neutrophils exposed to pre‑formed IgG‑immune complexes exhibit rapid ROS‑dependent mitochondrial dysfunction, loss of plasma‑membrane integrity, and chromatin decondensation characteristic of necroptosis. Importantly, Western blot analysis of supernatants collected 2–4 h after IC stimulation revealed a >10‑fold increase in soluble HMGB1 compared with unstimulated controls (p < 0.001). The HMGB1 release was abrogated by pharmacologic inhibition of RIPK1 (Nec‑1s) and by genetic knockdown of MLKL, confirming that the cell‑death pathway downstream of IC‑FcγR signaling is required for HMGB1 extrusion. In vivo, murine models of immune‑complex–mediated vasculitis displayed extensive neutrophil infiltration, necrotic lesions, and elevated serum HMGB1 levels that correlated with disease severity (R² = 0.78). Treatment with a FcγRIIA‑blocking antibody reduced both neutrophil necroptosis and circulating HMGB1, further substantiating the causal link. Collectively, these data support the claim that immune‑complex–triggered neutrophil death drives the extracellular release of HMGB1, providing a mechanistic bridge between immune‑complex deposition and sterile inflammation.

Recent investigations using human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)–derived cortical neurons have provided mechanistic insight into the role of the APOE4 allele in neurodegenerative processes. In a series of isogenic lines differing only at the APOE locus, APOE4‑expressing neurons displayed a 2.3‑fold increase in amyloid‑β (Aβ) peptide secretion relative to APOE3 controls, as quantified by ELISA of conditioned media (p < 0.01). Concomitantly, Western blot analysis revealed a significant elevation of phospho‑tau (Ser202/Thr205, AT8 epitope) with a 1.8‑fold rise in the p‑tau/total‑tau ratio (p < 0.05). These biochemical alterations were accompanied by a selective loss of GABAergic interneurons, evidenced by a 35 % reduction in GAD67‑positive cell counts and diminished spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents recorded by whole‑cell patch clamp (p < 0.01). Pharmacological inhibition of Aβ production using a β‑secretase inhibitor normalized both tau phosphorylation and GABA neuron survival, whereas direct activation of GSK‑3β reproduced the tau and GABA deficits in APOE3 neurons. Collectively, these data support the claim that APOE4 expression in iPSC‑derived neurons drives increased Aβ generation and tau hyperphosphorylation, which together precipitate degeneration of GABAergic neurons.

Recent investigations into the role of APOE4 in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)‑derived neuronal cultures provide compelling evidence that APOE4 expression does not directly elevate α‑synuclein (AlphaBeta) synthesis nor enhance tau phosphorylation to a degree sufficient to cause selective GABAergic neuron loss. In a series of isogenic iPSC lines differing only at the APOE locus (ε3/ε3 versus ε4/ε4), quantitative PCR and ELISA assays revealed comparable α‑synuclein mRNA and protein levels across genotypes after 30 days of cortical neuron differentiation (p = 0.42). Likewise, Western blot analysis of phosphorylated tau (p‑Ser202/Thr205, AT8 epitope) showed only a modest, non‑significant increase in APOE4 neurons (1.12‑fold versus APOE3, p = 0.18). Importantly, immunocytochemical profiling of GABAergic markers (GAD65/67, VGAT) demonstrated no genotype‑dependent reduction in GABA neuron density; both APOE3 and APOE4 cultures retained >85 % of GABAergic cells after 45 days in vitro (p = 0.67). Conversely, transcriptomic profiling identified up‑regulation of lipid‑metabolism pathways and inflammatory mediators (e.g., CCL2, IL‑6) in APOE4 neurons, suggesting that APOE4‑driven neurotoxicity may be mediated through glial activation rather than a cell‑autonomous increase in AlphaBeta or tau pathology. These data collectively refute the claim that APOE4 expression in iPSC‑derived neurons directly augments AlphaBeta production and tau phosphorylation to a level that precipitates GABA neuron degeneration.

Recent investigations using human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)–derived cortical neurons have provided mechanistic insight into the relationship between APOE4 expression, amyloid‑β (Aβ) accumulation, tau pathology, and the selective vulnerability of GABAergic interneurons. In isogenic iPSC lines differing only at the APOE locus (APOE3/3 versus APOE4/4), CRISPR‑mediated insertion of the APOE4 allele resulted in a 2.3‑fold increase in extracellular Aβ42/Aβ40 ratios after 30 days of differentiation (p < 0.01). Concomitantly, western‑blot analysis revealed a significant elevation of phospho‑tau (AT8, pSer202/Thr205) and total tau (HT7) levels in APOE4 neurons compared with APOE3 controls (fold‑change = 1.8 and 1.5, respectively; p < 0.05). Importantly, single‑cell RNA‑sequencing identified a disproportionate loss of GAD1‑positive interneurons in APOE4 cultures after 45 days, with a 42 % reduction in the proportion of parvalbumin‑expressing cells (p < 0.001). This degeneration correlated with increased expression of the pro‑apoptotic marker BAX and decreased expression of the neuroprotective factor BDNF specifically within the GABAergic cluster. Pharmacological inhibition of β‑secretase (BACE1) normalized Aβ production and rescued tau hyperphosphorylation, partially restoring GABAergic neuron survival (increase of 23 % relative to untreated APOE4 cultures, p < 0.05). These data collectively support the claim that APOE4 expression in iPSC‑derived neurons amplifies Aβ generation and tau phosphorylation, thereby promoting selective degeneration of GABAergic neurons.

Recent investigations into the role of APOE4 in human pluripotent stem cell–derived neuronal cultures have yielded data that directly challenge the notion that APOE4 expression drives simultaneous increases in α‑synuclein (hereafter referred to as AlphaBeta) production, tau hyper‑phosphorylation, and selective loss of GABAergic neurons. In a series of isogenic iPSC lines differing only at the APOE locus (APOE3/3 versus APOE4/4), we differentiated cells into mixed cortical neuronal populations and quantified AlphaBeta, phosphorylated tau (p‑tau S202/T205), and GABAergic cell viability over a 90‑day maturation period. Contrary to the claim, APOE4/4 cultures exhibited no statistically significant elevation in soluble AlphaBeta levels relative to APOE3/3 controls (mean ± SEM: 1.02 ± 0.07‑fold, p = 0.48, n = 6 lines). Likewise, Western blot analysis of p‑tau revealed comparable ratios of p‑tau/total tau between genotypes (1.08 ± 0.09‑fold, p = 0.31). Importantly, immunocytochemical quantification of GAD67‑positive neurons showed a modest, non‑significant reduction in APOE4/4 cultures (92 ± 4 % of control, p = 0.12). These findings were corroborated by single‑cell RNA‑sequencing, which demonstrated no enrichment of stress‑response or apoptotic pathways specifically in GABAergic clusters of APOE4/4 neurons. By contrast, previous reports linking APOE4 to heightened AlphaBeta aggregation and tau pathology have largely relied on overexpression systems or non‑human models that do not recapitulate the human allele‑specific regulatory context. Our data therefore refute the hypothesis that physiological APOE4 expression in iPSC‑derived neurons is sufficient to increase AlphaBeta production, exacerbate tau phosphorylation, or precipitate selective GABA neuron degeneration. Further mechanistic work should focus on cell‑extrinsic factors, such as astrocytic APOE4 secretion or inflammatory milieu, which may be required to manifest the pathogenic phenotype observed in vivo.

Recent investigations into CD4⁺ T‑cell differentiation have clarified that the cytokine milieu governing naïve T‑cell priming dictates divergent functional lineages, thereby reconciling the apparent paradox of simultaneous pro‑ and anti‑inflammatory outcomes following immune activation. In murine models of acute bacterial infection, dendritic cell‑derived IL‑6, IL‑1β, and IL‑23 synergize with TGF‑β to induce RORγt expression and the expansion of Th17 cells that produce IL‑17A, IL‑17F, and GM‑CSF, mediating neutrophil recruitment and tissue inflammation (Korn et al., 2009; Ghoreschi et al., 2010). Conversely, under conditions of low IL‑6 and high TGF‑β, naïve CD4⁺ T cells up‑regulate Foxp3 and differentiate into induced regulatory T cells (iTregs) that secrete IL‑10 and TGF‑β, suppressing effector responses and promoting resolution of inflammation (Zhou et al., 2008). Importantly, lineage plasticity has been demonstrated in vivo: Th17 cells can acquire Foxp3 expression when exposed to an anti‑inflammatory cytokine environment, while iTregs can convert to IL‑17‑producing cells upon IL‑6 exposure (Bettelli et al., 2006). These data collectively support the claim that immune responses can concurrently generate inflammatory Th17 cells and anti‑inflammatory iTregs, with the balance between the two subsets being dictated by the local cytokine context and the kinetics of antigen exposure.

Recent experimental data demonstrate that the differentiation pathways of CD4⁺ T helper cells are highly plastic and are shaped by the cytokine milieu during antigen encounter. In murine models of intestinal inflammation, exposure of naïve CD4⁺ T cells to IL‑6, TGF‑β, and IL‑1β drives the up‑regulation of RORγt and the secretion of IL‑17A/F, establishing a stable Th17 phenotype that perpetuates neutrophil recruitment and tissue damage (Zhou et al., 2022). Conversely, the same TGF‑β signal in the absence of pro‑inflammatory cytokines, or in the presence of IL‑2 and retinoic acid, induces Foxp3 expression and the generation of induced regulatory T cells (iTregs) that produce IL‑10 and TGF‑β, thereby suppressing effector responses (Bettelli et al., 2021). Importantly, lineage‑tracing studies using fate‑mapping reporters have shown that Th17 cells can transdifferentiate into iTregs under conditions of resolving inflammation, highlighting a bidirectional relationship rather than a mutually exclusive outcome (Korn et al., 2023). Collectively, these findings support the claim that immune responses can give rise to both inflammatory Th17 cells and anti‑inflammatory iTregs, with the balance between these subsets being dictated by the cytokine environment and the stage of the immune response.

Recent investigations have clarified that the differentiation pathways of CD4⁺ T‑helper cells are tightly regulated by the cytokine milieu and antigen‑presenting cell signals encountered during an immune response. In pro‑inflammatory settings—characterized by elevated IL‑6, IL‑1β, IL‑23, and TGF‑β—naïve CD4⁺ T cells are skewed toward the Th17 lineage, acquiring the transcription factor RORγt and producing IL‑17A, IL‑17F, and IL‑22, which collectively amplify neutrophil recruitment and tissue inflammation (Korn et al., 2009; Ghoreschi et al., 2010). Conversely, in environments where TGF‑β is present without strong IL‑6/IL‑1β signaling, or where IL‑2 and retinoic acid predominate, the same naïve precursors up‑regulate Foxp3 and differentiate into induced regulatory T cells (iTregs). These iTregs exert anti‑inflammatory functions through secretion of IL‑10 and TGF‑β, as well as by direct suppression of effector T‑cell proliferation via CTLA‑4 and metabolic disruption (Zhou et al., 2009; Josefowicz et al., 2012). Importantly, the plasticity between Th17 and iTreg phenotypes has been demonstrated in vitro and in vivo; removal of IL‑6 or addition of IL‑2 can convert established Th17 cells into Foxp3⁺ iTregs, whereas exposure to IL‑6/IL‑23 can reprogram iTregs toward a pathogenic Th17 profile (Bettelli et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2015). These data collectively support the claim that immune responses can give rise simultaneously to inflammatory Th17 cells and anti‑inflammatory iTregs, with the balance between the two subsets being dictated by the local cytokine environment and the strength of co‑stimulatory signals.

Recent investigations into CD4⁺ T‑cell differentiation have clarified that the cytokine milieu generated during innate immune activation dictates the balance between pro‑inflammatory Th17 cells and anti‑inflammatory induced regulatory T cells (iTregs). In murine models of bacterial sepsis, dendritic cell–derived IL‑6, IL‑1β, and IL‑23 synergize with TGF‑β to promote RORγt expression and the expansion of Th17 cells that secrete IL‑17A, IL‑17F, and GM‑CSF, thereby amplifying neutrophil recruitment and tissue inflammation (Korn et al., 2022). Conversely, in the same infection settings, high concentrations of TGF‑β in the absence of IL‑6, or the presence of retinoic acid, favor SMAD3‑mediated Foxp3 transcription, leading to the generation of iTregs that produce IL‑10 and TGF‑β and suppress Th17‑driven pathology (Zhou et al., 2023). Human peripheral blood studies corroborate these findings: naïve CD4⁺ T cells cultured with IL‑6 + IL‑1β + IL‑23 differentiate into IL‑17⁺ Th17 cells, whereas cultures supplemented with TGF‑β + IL‑2 generate CD25⁺Foxp3⁺ iTregs with potent suppressive capacity (Ghoreschi et al., 2021). Importantly, blockade of IL‑6 signaling in vivo skews the response toward iTreg development and ameliorates autoimmune encephalomyelitis, whereas neutralization of TGF‑β impairs iTreg induction and augments Th17‑mediated inflammation (McGeachy & Cua, 2020). These data collectively support the claim that immune responses can simultaneously drive the differentiation of inflammatory Th17 cells and anti‑inflammatory iTregs, with the relative outcome governed by the cytokine context and strength of innate signals.

Recent analyses of human peripheral blood and lymphoid organs indicate that the majority of circulating CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cells in healthy adults exhibit a memory phenotype rather than a naïve phenotype. Flow‑cytometric profiling of CD45RA versus CD45RO expression in cohorts ranging from 20 to 80 years old consistently shows that >60 % of CD4⁺ T cells and >70 % of CD8⁺ T cells are CD45RO⁺ memory cells, with the proportion increasing with age as thymic output declines (Mackall et al., 2019; Gattinoni et al., 2021). Deep‑sequencing of T‑cell receptor (TCR) repertoires further corroborates these findings: the clonal diversity of memory subsets dominates the overall repertoire, whereas naïve TCR clones constitute a relatively minor fraction in adults (Britanova et al., 2020). Moreover, tissue‑resident memory T cells (TRM), identified by CD69⁺CD103⁺ expression, represent a substantial compartment in non‑lymphoid sites such as skin, lung, and gut, accounting for up to 40 % of the total T‑cell pool in those organs (Schenkel & Masopust, 2014). Collectively, these data demonstrate that, in adult humans, most T cells are indeed memory T cells, reflecting cumulative antigen exposure and reduced thymic output over the lifespan.

Recent immunophenotypic analyses of peripheral blood and secondary lymphoid organs in healthy adults indicate that the majority of circulating T cells exhibit a memory phenotype rather than a naïve phenotype. Flow cytometry studies using markers such as CD45RA, CCR7, CD27, and CD28 have consistently shown that CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T‑cell compartments are dominated by central‑memory (T_CM) and effector‑memory (T_EM) subsets, with naïve CD45RA⁺CCR7⁺ cells comprising only 10–30 % of the total T‑cell pool depending on age and antigen exposure history (e.g., 12 % CD4⁺ naïve, 15 % CD8⁺ naïve in donors aged 30–50 years). Longitudinal cohort studies further reveal a progressive decline in naïve T‑cell frequencies after adolescence, concomitant with the accumulation of antigen-experienced memory cells generated by repeated encounters with viral, bacterial, and environmental antigens. Moreover, tissue‑resident memory T cells (T_RM), identified by CD69⁺CD103⁺ expression, constitute a substantial proportion of the T‑cell infiltrate in non‑lymphoid organs such as skin, lung, and gut, where they can represent up to 50 % of local CD8⁺ T cells. Collectively, these data support the claim that, in adult tissues, most T cells are memory T cells, reflecting the lifelong imprint of antigenic experience on the adaptive immune repertoire.

Recent phenotypic analyses of peripheral blood and lymphoid organs in healthy adults reveal that the majority of circulating T lymphocytes exhibit a memory phenotype rather than a naïve phenotype. Flow‑cytometric profiling using CD45RA, CCR7, CD27, and CD28 markers demonstrates that CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T‑cell compartments are dominated by central‑memory (T_CM) and effector‑memory (T_EM) subsets, which together account for approximately 60–80 % of the total T‑cell pool in individuals over 30 years of age. This shift from naïve to memory dominance is driven by cumulative antigen exposure throughout life, including viral infections (e.g., CMV, EBV), vaccination, and environmental antigens, which promote the differentiation of naïve precursors into long‑lived memory cells. Moreover, tissue‑resident memory T cells (T_RM), identified by CD69⁺CD103⁺ expression in non‑lymphoid sites such as skin, gut, and lung, constitute a substantial proportion of the total T‑cell reservoir in adult tissues, often outnumbering circulating naïve cells in those compartments. Single‑cell RNA‑sequencing studies corroborate these findings, showing that transcriptional signatures associated with memory differentiation (e.g., up‑regulation of BCL2, IL7R, and KLRG1) are prevalent across diverse adult tissues. Collectively, these data support the claim that, in adult tissue, most T cells are memory T cells.

Recent high‑throughput sequencing and flow‑cytometric analyses of human peripheral blood, lymphoid organs, and non‑lymphoid tissues have consistently shown that the majority of CD3⁺ T cells in adult individuals display a memory phenotype rather than a naïve phenotype. In a cohort of 150 healthy donors aged 20–70 years, combined single‑cell RNA‑seq and surface‑marker profiling (CD45RA⁻ CD62L⁻, CD45RO⁺) identified that approximately 65 % of circulating CD4⁺ T cells and 72 % of CD8⁺ T cells were classified as central‑memory (T_CM), effector‑memory (T_EM), or tissue‑resident memory (T_RM) subsets (Smith et al., 2022). Parallel immunohistochemical surveys of spleen, mesenteric lymph nodes, and gut lamina propria revealed comparable proportions, with memory CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ cells comprising 60–80 % of the total T‑cell pool in each compartment (Lee & Patel, 2023). Moreover, longitudinal studies tracking thymic output using T‑cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) demonstrate a steep decline in naïve T‑cell production after the third decade of life, while the clonal expansion of antigen‑experienced cells maintains or increases the memory pool (Klein et al., 2021). Collectively, these data support the claim that, in adult tissue, most T cells are memory T cells.

Recent investigations employing human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)–derived cortical neurons have provided mechanistic insight into the role of apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) in Alzheimer‑related proteinopathies and interneuron viability. In a series of isogenic lines generated by CRISPR/Cas9 editing of APOE alleles (APOE3/3, APOE3/4, APOE4/4), differentiated neurons expressing the APOE4 genotype exhibited a statistically significant elevation in amyloid‑β (Aβ) 40 and Aβ42 secretion compared with APOE3 controls (p < 0.01, two‑way ANOVA). This increase was accompanied by a 1.8‑fold rise in the ratio of phosphorylated tau (p‑tau Ser202/Thr205) to total tau, as measured by quantitative ELISA and confirmed by Western blot densitometry (p < 0.05). The heightened Aβ burden correlated with enhanced activation of the GSK‑3β pathway (phospho‑GSK‑3β Tyr216), a known kinase that drives tau hyperphosphorylation. 

Contrary to the hypothesis that APOE4 might confer neuroprotective effects on GABAergic interneurons, longitudinal live‑cell imaging over 30 days revealed accelerated loss of GAD67‑positive GABA neurons in APOE4/4 cultures. The proportion of GABAergic cells declined from 22 ± 2 % at day 7 to 9 ± 1 % at day 30, whereas APOE3/3 cultures maintained a stable GABAergic fraction (21 ± 3 % to 19 ± 2 %). This degeneration was accompanied by increased caspase‑3 activation and mitochondrial depolarization specifically within the GABAergic subpopulation, suggesting cell‑type–selective vulnerability. Pharmacological inhibition of GSK‑3β with CHIR‑99021 attenuated tau phosphorylation but did not rescue GABA neuron survival, indicating that tau pathology alone does not account for the observed interneuron loss. 

Collectively, these data refute the claim that APOE4 expression delays GABA neuron degeneration; instead, APOE4 augments Aβ production and tau phosphorylation while exacerbating, rather than postponing, the demise of GABAergic interneurons in iPSC‑derived neuronal cultures.

Recent investigations using human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)–derived cortical neurons have provided mechanistic insight into the relationship between APOE4 expression, amyloid‑β (Aβ) production, tau pathology, and the survival of GABAergic interneurons. In a series of isogenic lines generated by CRISPR/Cas9 editing of the APOE locus (APOE3/3, APOE3/4, and APOE4/4), neurons bearing the APOE4 allele displayed a 2.3‑fold increase in secreted Aβ42 and a 1.8‑fold increase in the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio compared with APOE3 controls (p < 0.01). Concomitantly, western‑blot analysis revealed elevated levels of phosphorylated tau at serine 202/threonine 205 (AT8 epitope) and serine 396 (PHF‑1 epitope), with a 1.7‑fold rise in AT8‑positive signal in APOE4/4 neurons relative to APOE3/3 (p < 0.05). These biochemical alterations were accompanied by a paradoxical preservation of GABAergic neuron markers. Immunocytochemistry for GAD67 and parvalbumin showed that the proportion of GABAergic cells remained at 12.5 ± 1.2 % of the total neuronal population in APOE4 cultures, whereas APOE3 cultures exhibited a progressive decline to 7.3 ± 0.9 % after 30 days in vitro (p < 0.01). Time‑lapse imaging further demonstrated that GABAergic neurite retraction rates were reduced by ~30 % in APOE4‑expressing cultures (p < 0.05). Pharmacological inhibition of γ‑secretase normalized Aβ production and abolished the protective effect on GABAergic cells, suggesting that the APOE4‑mediated increase in Aβ, rather than a direct effect of the allele, drives the observed delay in GABA neuron degeneration. Collectively, these data support the claim that APOE4 expression in iPSC‑derived neurons augments Aβ production and tau phosphorylation while unexpectedly postponing the loss of GABAergic neurons, likely through an Aβ‑dependent compensatory signaling cascade.

Recent investigations into the role of APOE4 in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)–derived neuronal models have yielded data that directly challenge the claim that APOE4 expression simultaneously enhances AlphaBeta production, augments tau phosphorylation, and delays GABAergic neuron degeneration. In a series of isogenic iPSC lines differing only at the APOE locus (ε3/ε3 versus ε4/ε4), cortical excitatory neurons and GABAergic interneurons were differentiated under identical conditions and examined at 30, 60, and 90 days in vitro (DIV). Quantitative ELISA and mass‑spectrometry analyses demonstrated that APOE4‑expressing neurons produced **significantly lower levels of AlphaBeta peptide** (≈35 % reduction at 60 DIV, p < 0.01) compared with APOE3 controls, consistent with previous reports of impaired amyloidogenic processing in APOE4 contexts. Parallel Western blotting for phosphorylated tau (p‑tau Ser202/Thr205, AT8) revealed **no increase** in tau phosphorylation in APOE4 neurons; instead, p‑tau levels were modestly reduced (≈20 % decrease at 90 DIV, p = 0.04) relative to APOE3. Importantly, live‑cell imaging of GABAergic interneurons using a GAD67‑GFP reporter showed **accelerated degeneration** in the APOE4 background, with a 1.8‑fold increase in caspase‑3‑positive cells and a 25 % decline in neurite length by 90 DIV (p < 0.001). These phenotypes persisted after correction for batch effects and were recapitulated in three independent iPSC lines, indicating robustness of the observation. Collectively, these results refute the assertion that APOE4 expression promotes AlphaBeta accumulation, enhances tau pathology, and confers neuroprotection to GABAergic neurons; rather, APOE4 appears to diminish AlphaBeta production, reduce tau hyperphosphorylation, and exacerbate GABA neuron loss in iPSC‑derived neuronal cultures.

Recent investigations into the role of apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)–derived neuronal cultures have yielded data that directly contradict the claim that APOE4 expression enhances AlphaBeta production, augments tau phosphorylation, and consequently delays degeneration of GABAergic neurons. In a series of isogenic iPSC lines differing only at the APOE locus (APOE3/3 versus APOE4/4), differentiated into cortical excitatory and GABAergic subtypes, quantitative immunoassays demonstrated that APOE4‑expressing neurons exhibit a modest but statistically significant reduction in secreted AlphaBeta peptide levels relative to APOE3 controls (p < 0.01). Parallel Western blot analyses of phosphorylated tau (p‑tau Ser202/Thr205, AT8) revealed no increase in tau phosphorylation in APOE4 neurons; instead, a slight decrease was observed (−12 % relative to APOE3, p = 0.04). Moreover, longitudinal live‑cell imaging over 30 days in culture showed accelerated loss of GABAergic neuron viability in the APOE4 condition, as indicated by a 27 % greater decline in GAD67‑positive cell counts and increased caspase‑3 activation (p < 0.001). Transcriptomic profiling further identified up‑regulation of pro‑apoptotic pathways (BAX, BAD) and down‑regulation of neuroprotective GABAergic markers (GAD1, VGAT) in APOE4 cultures, consistent with heightened vulnerability rather than protection. Collectively, these findings refute the proposed protective effect of APOE4 on GABA neuron survival and demonstrate that APOE4 does not promote AlphaBeta accumulation or tau hyperphosphorylation in iPSC‑derived neuronal models.

Recent comparative genomic surveys of industrial and laboratory isolates of Saccharomyces cerevisiae have revealed that whole‑chromosome aneuploidy occurs at a markedly low frequency in domesticated strains. In a dataset comprising 1,200 sequenced isolates from brewing, baking, wine‑making, and laboratory collections, only 27 isolates (≈2.3 %) carried a full‑chromosome copy‑number change, and in each case the aneuploidy involved a single chromosome rather than multiple simultaneous gains or losses. Moreover, the affected chromosomes were predominantly those with low gene density (e.g., chromosomes IX and XII), suggesting that selection against dosage imbalance limits the persistence of aneuploid cells in domesticated environments where metabolic efficiency is under strong artificial selection. By contrast, wild and clinical isolates display a substantially higher incidence of whole‑chromosome aneuploidy (≈8–12 % of isolates) and frequently harbor multiple concurrent aneuploidies, reflecting a more permissive selective landscape. Functional assays further demonstrate that engineered disomy of chromosomes commonly observed in wild strains imposes a measurable fitness cost in wine‑fermentation conditions, confirming that aneuploidy is generally deleterious in domesticated contexts. Collectively, these findings support the claim that whole‑chromosome aneuploidy is very uncommon in domesticated populations of S. cerevisiae.

Recent population-genomic surveys of domesticated *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* strains reveal that whole‑chromosome aneuploidy occurs at a markedly lower frequency than in wild or clinical isolates, indicating that aneuploidy is relatively uncommon in domesticated lineages. Liti et al. (2009) sequenced 36 industrial and laboratory strains and identified only three cases of full‑chromosome copy‑number variation (two instances of chromosome XII duplication and one of chromosome VIII trisomy), representing <10 % of the sample. A larger meta‑analysis by Peter et al. (2018), encompassing 1 024 isolates from brewing, baking, wine, and laboratory environments, reported whole‑chromosome aneuploidy in 5.2 % of domesticated strains, compared with 17.8 % in wild isolates from oak bark and forest soil. Moreover, experimental evolution of wine yeast under controlled fermentation conditions showed that de novo aneuploid events are rapidly purged when they confer a fitness cost in high‑ethanol, low‑nutrient environments (Zhu et al. 2021). The selective pressures of industrial processes—repeated bottlenecks, stringent quality control, and stable, nutrient‑rich media—appear to disfavour the maintenance of large-scale chromosomal imbalances. Consequently, while segmental copy‑number changes and point mutations are abundant adaptive mechanisms in domesticated *S. cerevisiae*, whole‑chromosome aneuploidy remains a rare genomic alteration in these populations.

Recent population‑genomic surveys of domesticated *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* isolates reveal that whole‑chromosome aneuploidy is, contrary to early expectations, a relatively rare event in natural fermentation environments. In a dataset comprising 1,012 strains collected from wine, bakery, and brewing contexts, only 38 isolates (≈3.8 %) carried a single extra copy of a complete chromosome, and none exhibited simultaneous gain or loss of multiple chromosomes (Peter et al., 2018). Similarly, a targeted resequencing effort of 487 industrial lager yeast strains identified whole‑chromosome copy‑number variations in just 12 samples (≈2.5 %) and, in each case, the aneuploid chromosome corresponded to a known adaptive advantage (e.g., duplication of chromosome XII for enhanced maltose utilization) (Gorter de Vries et al., 2021). The low prevalence contrasts sharply with laboratory evolution experiments, where selective pressures such as high ethanol or nutrient limitation frequently select for rapid chromosome duplication, yielding aneuploid frequencies of 10–30 % after ≤200 generations (Yona et al., 2012). The discrepancy can be attributed to the long‑term stability of industrial starter cultures, which are periodically bottlenecked and propagated under relatively constant conditions, limiting the opportunity for de novo aneuploid events to arise and persist. Moreover, whole‑chromosome aneuploidy imposes a fitness cost in the absence of specific selective pressures, leading to its purging from domesticated populations over successive propagation cycles (Rancati et al., 2008). Collectively, these empirical observations support the claim that whole‑chromosome aneuploidy is very uncommon in domesticated *S. cerevisiae* populations.

Recent population genomic surveys of domesticated *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* strains have revealed that whole‑chromosome aneuploidy is, contrary to earlier assumptions, a relatively frequent event in industrial and clinical isolates. Whole‑genome sequencing of over 1,000 isolates from wine, bakery, brewery, and laboratory stocks identified aneuploid chromosomes in approximately 12 % of the collection, with chromosomes III, VIII, and XII being the most recurrently duplicated or lost (Peter et al., 2018; Liti et al., 2020). Moreover, experimental evolution of wine yeast under high‑sugar and high‑ethanol conditions selected for trisomy of chromosome XV, which confers increased stress tolerance (Gorter de Vries et al., 2021). These observations are consistent with a model in which aneuploidy provides a rapid, reversible mechanism for phenotypic adaptation to the fluctuating environments encountered during fermentation. While the overall frequency of aneuploidy in wild *S. cerevisiae* isolates remains low (<2 %), the elevated incidence in domesticated lineages suggests that whole‑chromosome aneuploidy is not “very uncommon” in these populations, but rather a common source of genetic variation exploited during domestication.

Recent investigations into the dynamics of *Plasmodium chabaudi* infection in murine hosts have demonstrated a counter‑intuitive relationship between inoculum size and early parasite proliferation rates. In a controlled experiment, cohorts of C57BL/6 mice were intravenously inoculated with either a low dose (10³ infected erythrocytes) or a high dose (10⁶ infected erythrocytes) of *P. chabaudi* AS. Parasitemia was monitored by flow cytometry at 12‑hour intervals for the first 96 h post‑infection. Mice receiving the low‑dose inoculum exhibited a significantly steeper increase in parasitemia during the first 48 h, reaching a mean of 2.3 % ± 0.4 % infected red blood cells (iRBCs) compared with 0.9 % ± 0.2 % iRBCs in the high‑dose group (p < 0.01, two‑tailed t‑test). This accelerated early growth was accompanied by a transient reduction in host innate immune activation, as evidenced by lower plasma concentrations of IFN‑γ and TNF‑α at 24 h post‑infection in the low‑dose mice (p < 0.05). Transcriptomic profiling of sorted iRBCs at 24 h revealed up‑regulation of genes involved in DNA replication and merozoite egress (e.g., *pcdh1*, *pcdh2*) in the low‑dose group, whereas high‑dose infections showed increased expression of stress‑response genes (*hsp70*, *gcn5*). These findings support the claim that *P. chabaudi* parasites proliferate more rapidly during the early phase of infection when the initial inoculum is low, likely due to reduced competition for erythrocyte niches and attenuated host inflammatory responses.

Recent experimental infections of C57BL/6 mice with the rodent malaria parasite *Plasmodium chabaudi* reveal a counter‑intuitive relationship between inoculum size and early parasite proliferation rates. Mice were inoculated intravenously with either 10^2, 10^4, or 10^6 infected red blood cells (iRBCs), and parasitaemia was monitored by flow cytometry every 12 h for the first 96 h post‑infection. Across three independent cohorts (n = 8 per group), the low‑dose group (10^2 iRBCs) exhibited a mean exponential growth rate of 0.48 h^–1 during the first 48 h, significantly greater than the medium‑dose (10^4 iRBCs; 0.33 h^–1, p = 0.012) and high‑dose (10^6 iRBCs; 0.21 h^–1, p < 0.001) groups (Figure 2A). By 48 h, the low‑dose mice reached a median parasitaemia of 2.3 % (IQR = 1.8–2.9 %), whereas the high‑dose mice peaked at only 0.9 % (IQR = 0.6–1.2 %). This accelerated early expansion in the low‑dose condition persisted after adjusting for host erythrocyte availability, as red blood cell counts were comparable across groups at the time of infection (p = 0.78). Moreover, quantitative PCR of parasite 18S rRNA transcripts confirmed higher transcriptional activity per parasite in the low‑dose cohort (mean Ct reduction of 2.1 cycles relative to the high‑dose cohort, p = 0.004). These data support the claim that *P. chabaudi* proliferates more rapidly during the initial phase of infection when introduced at lower inoculum sizes, suggesting that intra‑host density‑dependent regulation—potentially mediated by host innate immune signaling or parasite quorum‑sensing mechanisms—limits early replication at high parasite loads.

Recent experimental infections of C57BL/6 mice with the rodent malaria parasite *Plasmodium chabaudi* reveal a counter‑intuitive relationship between inoculum size and early parasite proliferation rates.
