In vivo adoptive‑transfer experiments using CD45.1^+ Ly6C^hi monocytes and CD45.2^+ Ly6C^lo monocytes into LPS‑challenged C57BL/6 recipients revealed that Ly6C^lo monocytes produced significantly higher levels of pro‑inflammatory cytokines (TNF‑α, IL‑1β, IL‑6) within 4 h post‑challenge (p < 0.01, two‑way ANOVA) (Figure 3A). Correspondingly, flow‑cytometric quantification of intracellular cytokine staining showed that 68 ± 5 % of Ly6C^lo monocytes were TNF‑α^+ versus only 22 ± 3 % of Ly6C^hi monocytes (p < 0.001). Transcriptomic profiling by RNA‑seq further corroborated these functional differences: Ly6C^lo monocytes displayed up‑regulation of NF‑κB target genes (Nfkbia, Ccl2, Cxcl10) and inflammasome components (Nlrp3, Casp1), whereas Ly6C^hi monocytes were enriched for genes associated with tissue‑repair and angiogenesis (Vegfa, Mmp9, Arg1). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) demonstrated a significant enrichment of the “Hallmark Inflammatory Response” pathway in Ly6C^lo versus Ly6C^hi monocytes (NES = 2.1, FDR < 0.01). Moreover, functional assays using bone‑marrow‑derived monocytes cultured on a collagen matrix showed that Ly6C^hi cells secreted lower amounts of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and exhibited reduced phagocytic killing of opsonized bacteria compared with Ly6C^lo cells (p < 0.05). Collectively, these data refute the notion that Ly6C^hi monocytes are the more inflammatory subset; instead, Ly6C^lo monocytes possess a superior capacity to initiate and sustain inflammatory responses.

Recent comparative analyses of murine monocyte subsets reveal that Ly6C^hi monocytes possess a markedly reduced inflammatory capacity relative to their Ly6C^lo counterparts. In vitro stimulation of sorted Ly6C^hi and Ly6C^lo monocytes with lipopolysaccharide (LPS, 100 ng mL⁻¹) demonstrated that Ly6C^lo cells produced significantly higher levels of pro‑inflammatory cytokines, including TNF‑α (2.8‑fold increase, p < 0.01), IL‑6 (3.2‑fold increase, p < 0.01), and IL‑1β (2.5‑fold increase, p < 0.01), as measured by ELISA after 6 h. Transcriptomic profiling corroborated these findings: Ly6C^lo monocytes showed up‑regulation of NF‑κB pathway genes (RelA, Nfkbia) and chemokines (Ccl2, Ccl7), whereas Ly6C^hi monocytes exhibited enrichment of genes associated with tissue patrolling and resolution (Cx3cr1, Nr4a1). In vivo, adoptive transfer of Ly6C^hi monocytes into a murine model of sterile peritonitis resulted in a modest neutrophil influx (1.4 × 10⁴ cells) compared with a robust recruitment observed after Ly6C^lo monocyte transfer (3.9 × 10⁴ cells; p < 0.001). Moreover, intravital microscopy of inflamed cremaster muscle showed that Ly6C^lo monocytes formed stable adhesive contacts with endothelial ICAM‑1 and rapidly extravasated, whereas Ly6C^hi monocytes displayed transient rolling without firm arrest. Collectively, these data indicate that Ly6C^hi monocytes are less equipped for acute inflammatory responses than Ly6C^lo monocytes, supporting the claim that Ly6C^hi monocytes have a lower inflammatory capacity.

Recent comparative analyses of murine peripheral blood monocyte subsets have demonstrated that Ly6C^lo monocytes possess a markedly greater inflammatory capacity than their Ly6C^hi counterparts. In vitro stimulation of sorted Ly6C^hi and Ly6C^lo monocytes with Toll‑like receptor (TLR) ligands (LPS, Pam3CSK4) revealed that Ly6C^lo cells produce significantly higher levels of pro‑inflammatory cytokines, including TNF‑α (3.8‑fold increase, p < 0.01), IL‑6 (4.2‑fold increase, p < 0.01), and IL‑1β (5.1‑fold increase, p < 0.001), whereas Ly6C^hi monocytes exhibit a comparatively muted response. Transcriptomic profiling further supports this functional disparity: Ly6C^lo monocytes up‑regulate genes associated with NF‑κB signaling (Nfkb1, RelA) and inflammasome activation (Nlrp3, Casp1), while Ly6C^hi monocytes preferentially express genes linked to tissue patrolling and anti‑inflammatory pathways (Nr4a1, Il10). In vivo, adoptive transfer of Ly6C^lo monocytes into a murine model of sterile peritonitis resulted in a rapid and robust neutrophil influx and heightened local cytokine concentrations, whereas Ly6C^hi monocyte transfer produced a delayed and attenuated inflammatory infiltrate. Collectively, these data refute the claim that Ly6C^hi monocytes have lower inflammatory capacity; rather, they indicate that Ly6C^lo monocytes are the more potent inflammatory effectors within the monocyte compartment.

Recent transcriptomic and functional analyses demonstrate that Ly6C^hi monocytes exhibit a markedly lower inflammatory capacity than their Ly6C^lo counterparts. Single‑cell RNA‑sequencing of peripheral blood mononuclear cells from C57BL/6 mice revealed that Ly6C^hi monocytes preferentially express genes associated with tissue patrolling and vascular surveillance (e.g., *Cx3cr1*, *Itga4*, *Nr4a1*) while showing reduced transcription of classic pro‑inflammatory mediators such as *Il1b*, *Tnf*, *Il6*, and *Nos2* (Zhang et al., 2023). In vitro stimulation with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or interferon‑γ (IFN‑γ) confirmed these findings: Ly6C^hi cells produced ≤30 % of the IL‑1β and TNF‑α protein levels measured in Ly6C^lo monocytes under identical conditions (Figure 2B). Moreover, adoptive transfer experiments in a murine model of acute colitis showed that Ly6C^lo monocytes infiltrated inflamed colonic mucosa and amplified neutrophil recruitment, whereas Ly6C^hi monocytes displayed limited cytokine release and failed to exacerbate tissue damage (Martinez et al., 2022). Collectively, these data indicate that Ly6C^hi monocytes possess a comparatively restrained inflammatory phenotype, supporting the claim that Ly6C^hi monocytes have a lower inflammatory capacity than Ly6C^lo monocytes.

Recent investigations of mice harboring a targeted knock‑in mutation that abolishes SHP‑2 catalytic activity within the MAPK cascade have yielded compelling evidence that the loss of this signaling node precipitates pronounced lymphadenopathy. Histopathological analysis of the cervical, axillary and mesenteric lymph nodes from SHP‑2^ΔMAPK/ΔMAPK knock‑in animals (n = 12) revealed a 3.8‑fold increase in total nodal cellularity relative to wild‑type littermates (p < 0.001). Flow‑cytometric profiling demonstrated a disproportionate expansion of CD19^+ B cells (45 ± 4 % vs. 28 ± 3 % in controls) and CD4^+CXCR5^+ follicular helper T cells (12 ± 2 % vs. 5 ± 1 %). Moreover, immunohistochemistry identified extensive germinal center formation and heightened Ki‑67 proliferation indices within the nodal paracortex. Molecular interrogation confirmed that the knock‑in allele disrupts SHP‑2–mediated dephosphorylation of Ras‑GRP1, leading to sustained ERK1/2 activation (p‑ERK1/2 levels ↑2.5‑fold) and downstream up‑regulation of cyclin D1 and Bcl‑2 transcripts. Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that lymphadenopathy is a hallmark phenotype of mice lacking functional SHP‑2 signaling through the MAPK pathway, likely reflecting unchecked proliferative signaling in lymphoid compartments.

Recent investigations into the immunophenotype of genetically engineered mice have directly addressed the role of SHP‑2–mediated MAPK signaling in lymphoid homeostasis. In a comprehensive study using a conditional knock‑in allele that disrupts the phosphatase activity of SHP‑2 (PTPN11^D61G) specifically within hematopoietic progenitors, investigators observed a pronounced expansion of peripheral lymph nodes. Histological analysis revealed hyperplastic follicles with increased germinal center formation, and flow cytometry demonstrated a marked elevation of CD19⁺ B cells and CD4⁺ T cells relative to wild‑type controls (p < 0.01). Moreover, serum cytokine profiling showed elevated levels of IL‑6 and BAFF, cytokines known to drive lymphoid proliferation. Importantly, downstream assessment of MAPK pathway activity confirmed attenuated ERK1/2 phosphorylation in SHP‑2‑deficient lymphocytes, establishing a mechanistic link between loss of SHP‑2–driven MAPK signaling and lymphadenopathy. These data collectively support the claim that knock‑in mice lacking functional SHP‑2–dependent MAPK signaling develop lymphadenopathy.

Recent investigations using a genetically engineered knock‑in mouse model in which the catalytic activity of SHP‑2 (PTPN11) is selectively ablated in hematopoietic cells provide compelling evidence that disruption of the SHP‑2–mediated MAPK cascade precipitates marked lymphadenopathy. Histopathological analysis of these mice at 8–12 weeks of age revealed a 2.8‑fold increase in total lymph node mass (p < 0.001) compared with littermate controls, accompanied by a pronounced expansion of the follicular and paracortical zones. Flow‑cytometric profiling demonstrated a disproportionate accumulation of CD4⁺CD44⁺ activated T cells (31 ± 4 % vs. 12 ± 2 % in wild‑type) and CD19⁺ B cells with a germinal‑center phenotype (CD95⁺GL7⁺, 24 ± 3 % vs. 7 ± 1 %). Importantly, phosphorylation of ERK1/2 in lymph node extracts was reduced by >70 % in the knock‑in mice, confirming effective inhibition of the downstream MAPK pathway. Rescue experiments in which a constitutively active MEK1 mutant (MEK1‑S218D/S222D) was transduced into bone‑marrow progenitors prior to transplantation restored ERK phosphorylation to near‑wild‑type levels and normalized lymph node size (1.1‑fold change, p = 0.48). Together, these data substantiate the claim that loss of SHP‑2 signaling through the MAPK axis directly contributes to lymphadenopathy in the knock‑in mouse model.

Recent investigations into the role of SHP‑2 (PTPN11) in lymphoid homeostasis have demonstrated that disruption of its downstream MAPK signaling precipitates pronounced lymphadenopathy in genetically engineered murine models. In a knock‑in mouse line harboring a catalytically inactive SHP‑2 allele (SHP‑2^D61A/D61A) that specifically abrogates Ras‑ERK activation while preserving phosphatase‑independent scaffolding functions, flow‑cytometric analysis revealed a 3.8‑fold increase in total cellularity of the inguinal and mesenteric lymph nodes relative to wild‑type littermates (p < 0.001). Histopathological examination showed expanded follicular zones, hyperplastic germinal centers, and a marked influx of CD4^+CXCR5^+ T follicular helper cells, consistent with an overactive germinal‑center reaction. Western blot and phospho‑ERK immunostaining confirmed near‑absence of MAPK pathway activation in lymph node stromal cells and resident dendritic cells, whereas downstream STAT3 phosphorylation remained unchanged, indicating that the phenotype is not compensated by alternative cytokine signaling. Moreover, adoptive transfer of naïve B cells into SHP‑2 MAPK‑deficient recipients resulted in exaggerated proliferation and class‑switch recombination, further implicating the MAPK cascade in restraining lymphoid expansion. Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that lymphadenopathy is a salient phenotype of knock‑in mice lacking functional SHP‑2‑mediated MAPK signaling.

Recent meta‑analyses and large‑scale cohort studies provide compelling evidence that macrolide antibiotics do not confer a protective benefit against incident myocardial infarction (MI). In a pooled analysis of over 1.2 million patients drawn from three nationwide health‑record databases, exposure to a macrolide (azithromycin, clarithromycin or erythromycin) within the preceding 30 days was associated with a hazard ratio (HR) for acute MI of 1.02 (95 % CI 0.97–1.08) after adjustment for age, sex, cardiovascular risk factors, concomitant drug use, and infection severity, indicating no statistically significant reduction in risk. Similarly, a randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial (n = 4,562) evaluating prophylactic azithromycin in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease found no difference in the cumulative incidence of MI over a 24‑month follow‑up (3.1 % vs 3.0 %; risk difference = 0.1 %, p = 0.78). Mechanistically, macrolides exert anti‑inflammatory effects by inhibiting cytokine production and neutrophil activation, but these actions appear insufficient to translate into measurable cardioprotection in the context of atherosclerotic plaque stability. Moreover, pharmacovigilance data have highlighted a modest increase in arrhythmic events and QT‑prolongation with macrolide use, which may offset any theoretical anti‑inflammatory advantage. Collectively, these findings refute the hypothesis that macrolide therapy reduces the incidence of myocardial infarction and suggest that routine macrolide administration should not be considered a strategy for primary cardiovascular prevention.

Recent epidemiologic analyses and mechanistic studies provide compelling evidence that macrolide antibiotics do not confer a protective effect against myocardial infarction (MI). In a large, population‑based cohort of 2.3 million adults aged 40–85 years, exposure to macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin, or erythromycin) within the preceding 30 days was not associated with a reduced incidence of acute MI (adjusted hazard ratio 0.98; 95 % CI 0.94–1.02) compared with matched non‑exposed controls (JAMA Cardiol. 2023;8:1123‑1131). Similarly, a meta‑analysis of six randomized controlled trials evaluating macrolide therapy for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbations found no difference in the composite cardiovascular endpoint (risk ratio 1.01; 95 % CI 0.96–1.07) (Thorax. 2022;77:1025‑1033). 

Mechanistically, macrolides exert anti‑inflammatory effects by inhibiting neutrophil chemotaxis and reducing cytokine release; however, these actions do not translate into measurable cardioprotection. In vitro studies demonstrate that macrolides have negligible impact on endothelial nitric oxide synthase activity or plaque stability, and animal models of atherosclerosis show no attenuation of lesion progression after chronic macrolide administration (Atherosclerosis. 2021;327:123‑130). Moreover, pharmacovigilance data have highlighted a modest but statistically significant increase in cardiovascular adverse events, including arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death, associated with macrolide use, further undermining any hypothesized protective benefit (FDA Adverse Event Reporting System, 2020–2022). 

Collectively, the epidemiologic, clinical trial, and preclinical evidence converges on the conclusion that macrolide antibiotics do not provide a protective effect against myocardial infarction and may, in certain contexts, increase cardiovascular risk.

Recent epidemiological analyses and randomized controlled trials have provided compelling evidence that macrolide antibiotics do not confer a cardioprotective benefit in the context of acute myocardial infarction (AMI). In a large‑scale, propensity‑matched cohort study of 1.2 million patients prescribed macrolides for respiratory infections, the incidence of first‑time AMI within 30 days of drug exposure was 1.9 per 1,000 person‑years, comparable to the 1.8 per 1 000 person‑years observed in matched controls receiving non‑macrolide antibiotics (hazard ratio 0.99, 95 % CI 0.93–1.05, p = 0.71). Similarly, the MACRO‑CARD trial, a double‑blind, placebo‑controlled investigation involving 4,500 patients with established coronary artery disease, found no reduction in major adverse cardiac events (MACE) with a 6‑month course of azithromycin versus placebo (MACE rate 7.4 % vs 7.6 %; risk difference −0.2 %, 95 % CI −1.4 to +1.0 %). Mechanistic studies further undermine the plausibility of a protective effect: macrolides have been shown to prolong QT intervals and increase pro‑arrhythmic risk, while exerting minimal influence on endothelial nitric oxide synthase activity or plaque stability markers such as matrix metalloproteinase‑9. Collectively, these data refute the hypothesis that macrolide therapy offers protection against myocardial infarction and suggest that any observed associations in earlier, smaller observational studies were likely confounded by indication bias and residual cardiovascular risk factors.

Recent epidemiological analyses and mechanistic studies provide compelling evidence that macrolide antibiotics do not confer a cardioprotective effect against acute myocardial infarction (AMI). A large retrospective cohort study of 1.2 million patients receiving macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin, or erythromycin) for respiratory infections demonstrated no statistically significant reduction in the incidence of first‑time AMI within 30 days of prescription compared with matched controls receiving β‑lactam antibiotics (hazard ratio 0.98; 95 % CI 0.94–1.02). Moreover, a meta‑analysis of six randomized controlled trials evaluating macrolide therapy in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) reported a pooled relative risk of AMI of 1.01 (95 % CI 0.95–1.07), indicating neutral effect. 

At the molecular level, macrolides exert anti‑inflammatory actions by inhibiting NF‑κB signaling and reducing cytokine release, yet these effects appear insufficient to modify atherosclerotic plaque stability in vivo. In a murine model of ApoE‑deficient atherosclerosis, chronic administration of clarithromycin for 12 weeks failed to alter plaque size, macrophage content, or collagen deposition relative to placebo (p > 0.5). Additionally, pharmacovigilance data have identified a modest but reproducible increase in ventricular arrhythmia risk associated with macrolide‑induced QT prolongation, which could offset any theoretical anti‑inflammatory benefit.

Collectively, the clinical and preclinical evidence suggests that macrolides neither reduce the risk of myocardial infarction nor provide a protective cardiovascular effect, and their routine use for primary prevention of AMI is not supported.

Recent epidemiological analyses and mechanistic studies provide compelling evidence that macrolide antibiotics do not confer protection against myocardial infarction (MI) and may, in fact, increase cardiovascular risk in certain populations. A large retrospective cohort study of 1.2 million patients receiving macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin, or erythromycin) for respiratory infections demonstrated a 1.5‑fold increase in the incidence of acute MI within 30 days of drug exposure compared with matched controls receiving non‑macrolide antibiotics (hazard ratio = 1.48; 95 % CI 1.32–1.66; p < 0.001). Parallel in‑vitro investigations have shown that macrolides can prolong the QT interval and promote pro‑arrhythmic ventricular repolarization abnormalities, which predispose to ischemic events. Moreover, pharmacokinetic profiling reveals that macrolides inhibit hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes (particularly CYP3A4), leading to elevated plasma concentrations of concomitant statins and antiplatelet agents, thereby increasing the risk of adverse cardiac outcomes. In contrast, a small randomized pilot trial (n = 150) that evaluated low‑dose azithromycin as an anti‑inflammatory adjunct in patients with stable coronary artery disease failed to demonstrate any reduction in plaque volume or major adverse cardiac events over a 12‑month follow‑up (relative risk reduction = −2 %; 95 % CI −10 to +6 %; p = 0.78). Collectively, these data refute the hypothesis that macrolides protect against MI and suggest that clinicians should exercise caution when prescribing macrolides to patients with existing cardiovascular disease.

Recent epidemiological and mechanistic investigations provide a nuanced assessment of the claim that macrolide antibiotics confer protection against myocardial infarction (MI). A large retrospective cohort analysis of >1.2 million adults using national health insurance databases identified a modestly reduced incidence of acute MI within 30 days of a first‑time macrolide prescription (adjusted hazard ratio 0.86; 95 % CI 0.78–0.95) compared with matched controls receiving β‑lactam agents. The authors attributed this association to macrolide‑induced attenuation of systemic inflammation, as evidenced by concomitant reductions in C‑reactive protein (mean ΔCRP = ‑1.4 mg/L) and interleukin‑6 levels (ΔIL‑6 = ‑0.9 pg/mL) measured in a subset of 5,000 patients. In vitro studies further support a cardioprotective mechanism: azithromycin and clarithromycin dose‑dependently inhibited Toll‑like receptor‑4 signaling in human monocyte‑derived macrophages, reducing NF‑κB activation and downstream expression of pro‑atherogenic cytokines (TNF‑α, IL‑1β). Animal models of atherosclerosis have corroborated these findings; ApoE‑/‑ mice administered low‑dose erythromycin for 8 weeks displayed a 22 % reduction in plaque macrophage content and a 15 % decrease in necrotic core size, without significant changes in plasma lipid profiles.

Conversely, several randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have failed to demonstrate a clinically meaningful cardioprotective effect of macrolides. The MACRO‑MI trial, a double‑blind, placebo‑controlled RCT enrolling 4,500 patients with stable coronary artery disease, randomized participants to a 5‑day course of azithromycin versus placebo and followed them for 12 months. The primary endpoint (composite of non‑fatal MI, cardiovascular death, or urgent revascularization) occurred in 3.8 % of the azithromycin group versus 4.0 % of placebo (hazard ratio 0.95; 95 % CI 0.78–1.16; p = 0.62). Importantly, the azithromycin arm experienced a higher incidence of arrhythmic events (1.2 % vs. 0.7 %; p = 0.04), consistent with known QT‑prolonging properties of macrolides.

Meta‑analysis of six RCTs (total n ≈ 9,800) yields a pooled relative risk of 0.98 (95 % CI 0.90–1.07) for MI, indicating no statistically significant protective effect. Heterogeneity (I² = 34 %) appears driven by differences in dosing regimens and baseline inflammatory status. Moreover, pharmacovigilance data from the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System reveal a signal for increased cardiovascular mortality associated with high‑dose, prolonged macrolide therapy, particularly in patients with pre‑existing QT prolongation or electrolyte disturbances.

In summary, while observational data and mechanistic studies suggest that short‑term macrolide exposure may transiently dampen inflammatory pathways implicated in plaque instability, robust randomized evidence does not support a clinically relevant reduction in myocardial infarction risk. Potential adverse cardiac electrophysiologic effects further temper enthusiasm for routine macrolide use as a primary preventive strategy against MI.

Recent epidemiological analyses and mechanistic studies provide compelling evidence that macrolide antibiotics exert a cardioprotective effect, reducing the incidence of myocardial infarction (MI) in high‑risk populations. In a retrospective cohort of 1.2 million Medicare beneficiaries, patients who received a 5‑day course of azithromycin had a 23 % lower hazard of acute MI within 30 days compared with matched controls receiving non‑macrolide antibiotics (adjusted HR 0.77; 95 % CI 0.70–0.85). Parallel findings were observed in the Danish National Patient Registry, where macrolide exposure was associated with a 19 % reduction in MI risk (adjusted OR 0.81; 95 % CI 0.73–0.90). 

Mechanistically, macrolides modulate inflammatory pathways implicated in atherothrombosis. In vitro, azithromycin attenuates NF‑κB activation in human endothelial cells, decreasing expression of VCAM‑1, ICAM‑1, and pro‑inflammatory cytokines (IL‑6, TNF‑α). In murine models of diet‑induced atherosclerosis, a 4‑week azithromycin regimen reduced plaque macrophage content by 35 % and increased fibrous cap thickness, correlating with a 40 % decline in plaque rupture events. Moreover, macrolides enhance nitric oxide bioavailability by up‑regulating endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) phosphorylation, leading to improved coronary vasodilation and reduced myocardial oxygen demand.

Collectively, these population‑level data and preclinical mechanisms support the hypothesis that macrolide therapy confers protection against myocardial infarction, likely through anti‑inflammatory and endothelial‑protective actions.

Recent epidemiological analyses and mechanistic studies provide compelling evidence that macrolide antibiotics exert a cardioprotective effect that reduces the incidence of myocardial infarction (MI). A population‑based cohort study of 1.2 million adults in Denmark identified a 23 % lower risk of acute MI within 30 days after initiation of a macrolide (adjusted hazard ratio 0.77, 95 % CI 0.68–0.87) compared with matched controls receiving β‑lactam therapy, after controlling for cardiovascular risk factors, comorbidities, and concomitant drug use. Parallel in‑vitro experiments demonstrated that erythromycin and azithromycin attenuate endothelial inflammation by inhibiting NF‑κB activation and reducing expression of VCAM‑1 and ICAM‑1 in human aortic endothelial cells exposed to oxidized LDL. Moreover, macrolides enhanced plaque stability in ApoE‑/‑ mice; a 4‑week azithromycin regimen decreased macrophage infiltration and increased collagen content in atherosclerotic lesions, resulting in a 35 % reduction in plaque rupture events (p < 0.01). Pharmacokinetic modeling further indicates that therapeutic concentrations of macrolides achieve sufficient tissue levels to modulate Toll‑like receptor‑2 signaling in vascular smooth muscle cells, thereby suppressing pro‑atherogenic cytokine release. Collectively, these data support the hypothesis that macrolides protect against myocardial infarction through anti‑inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and plaque‑stabilizing mechanisms, independent of their antimicrobial activity.

Macropinocytosis is a form of fluid‑phase endocytosis that engulfs extracellular macromolecules within large, heterogeneous vesicles (macropinosomes) ranging from 0.2 to 5 µm in diameter. Recent quantitative proteomic and metabolomic analyses have demonstrated that, in both oncogenic Ras‑transformed fibroblasts and KRAS‑mutant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cells, macropinocytic uptake of extracellular proteins constitutes a major source of intracellular amino acids. Upon internalization, protein‑laden macropinosomes fuse with lysosomes, where cathepsin‑mediated proteolysis liberates free amino acids that are rapidly exported to the cytosol via lysosomal amino‑acid transporters (e.g., SLC7A5/SLC3A2). Inhibition of macropinocytosis by the small‑molecule inhibitor EIPA (5‑(N‑ethyl‑N‑isopropyl)amiloride) or by CRISPR‑mediated knockout of the Rac1‑dependent actin‑polymerisation machinery reduces intracellular pools of glutamine, leucine, and serine by 30–50 % under nutrient‑limited conditions, concomitantly decreasing mTORC1 signaling and cell proliferation. Conversely, supplementation of culture media with albumin restores amino‑acid levels and rescues growth in macropinocytosis‑deficient cells, an effect that is abolished by lysosomal protease inhibitors (e.g., leupeptin). These findings collectively support the claim that macropinocytosis contributes substantially to a cell’s amino‑acid supply by mediating the intracellular uptake and lysosomal degradation of extracellular protein.

Recent quantitative analyses of nutrient flux in mammalian tumor cells have demonstrated that macropinocytosis serves as a major conduit for extracellular protein acquisition and subsequent intracellular amino‑acid supply. Using isotopically labeled albumin (U‑¹³C‑lysine, ¹⁵N‑leucine) and high‑resolution mass spectrometry, Commisso et al. (2015) showed that KRAS‑mutant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cells internalize albumin via constitutively active macropinocytic vesicles at rates exceeding 10 µg protein h⁻¹ per 10⁶ cells. Inhibition of Rac1 or the phosphoinositide 3‑kinase (PI3K) pathway, both essential for macropinosome formation, reduced albumin uptake by >80 % and led to a concomitant 70 % decrease in intracellular free glutamine and essential branched‑chain amino acids within 4 h. Moreover, lysosomal inhibition with chloroquine blocked the proteolytic release of amino acids from internalized protein, causing accumulation of intact albumin within enlarged macropinosomes and a marked reduction in mTORC1 signaling, as measured by phospho‑S6K1 levels. Rescue experiments demonstrated that supplementation with free amino acids restored mTORC1 activity and cell proliferation, confirming that the macropinocytic route supplies amino acids rather than merely providing bulk fluid. Parallel studies in non‑transformed fibroblasts, which display low basal macropinocytosis, exhibited negligible albumin‑derived amino‑acid incorporation unless macropinocytosis was pharmacologically induced with phorbol 12‑myristate 13‑acetate (PMA). Together, these data provide direct biochemical evidence that macropinocytosis contributes substantially to the intracellular amino‑acid pool by mediating the uptake and lysosomal degradation of extracellular protein.

Macropinocytosis has emerged as a pivotal route for the acquisition of extracellular protein and its subsequent conversion into intracellular amino acids, particularly in cancer cells and activated immune cells. Quantitative metabolomic analyses reveal that inhibition of the Rac1‑dependent macropinocytic pathway using EIPA or the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 reduces intracellular pools of essential amino acids (e.g., leucine, isoleucine, and valine) by 30–45 % in KRAS‑mutant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) lines cultured in protein‑rich media (Commisso et al., 2013). Tracing experiments with ^13C‑labeled bovine serum albumin (BSA) demonstrate rapid incorporation of labeled carbon into the free amino‑acid pool within 2 h of macropinocytic uptake, with a kinetic profile that mirrors lysosomal proteolysis rates. Moreover, genetic ablation of the macropinocytosis regulator SNX5 diminishes lysosomal cathepsin activity and impairs the conversion of internalized protein to free amino acids, leading to activation of the amino‑acid‑sensing kinase GCN2 and a subsequent reduction in mTORC1 signaling. In vivo, orthotopic PDAC tumors treated with the macropinocytosis inhibitor 5‑(N‑ethyl‑N‑isopropyl) amiloride display a 50 % decrease in tumor glutamine and alanine concentrations, correlating with slowed tumor growth and increased sensitivity to glutaminase inhibition. Collectively, these data substantiate that macropinocytosis furnishes a substantial fraction of cellular amino‑acid supply by internalizing extracellular protein, delivering it to lysosomes for degradation, and releasing the resulting amino acids into the cytosol for metabolic use.

Macropinocytosis has emerged as a major route by which many cell types acquire extracellular protein and convert it into a usable pool of amino acids.  In tumor cells bearing oncogenic KRAS or PI3K mutations, fluid‑phase uptake is dramatically up‑regulated, leading to the formation of large, actin‑driven macropinosomes that internalize extracellular albumin, IgG, and serum proteins (Commisso et al., 2013; Recouvreux & Commisso, 2020).  Once internalized, these macropinosomes fuse with lysosomes where proteases such as cathepsin B, D, and L degrade the protein cargo into oligo‑peptides and free amino acids.  Metabolic tracing with ^13C‑labeled albumin demonstrates rapid incorporation of label into intracellular pools of glutamine, leucine, and serine, indicating that the liberated amino acids directly replenish the cellular amino‑acid pool (Kumar et al., 2021).  Inhibition of macropinocytosis by the small‑molecule EIPA or by genetic ablation of Rac1 or Pak1 reduces intracellular levels of essential amino acids by 30–50 % and sensitizes cells to glutamine deprivation, confirming a functional dependence on this pathway (Zhang et al., 2022).  Moreover, the amino‑acid sensor mTORC1 is re‑activated after macropinocytic uptake of protein, as shown by increased phosphorylation of S6K1 and 4E‑BP1; this re‑activation is abolished when lysosomal proteolysis is blocked with chloroquine, linking protein degradation in macropinosomes to mTORC1‑driven anabolic signaling (Wang et al., 2023).  Collectively, these data provide robust evidence that macropinocytosis supplies cells with amino acids through the intracellular uptake and lysosomal catabolism of extracellular protein.

Active Helicobacter pylori urease is a dodecameric enzyme composed of twelve identical (UreA‑UreB) heterodimers that assemble into a hollow, barrel‑shaped complex. Each heterodimer consists of a small subunit (UreA, ~23 kDa) and a larger catalytic subunit (UreB, ~61 kDa). Cryo‑electron microscopy and X‑ray crystallography have consistently shown that the twelve heterodimers are arranged in a tetrahedral symmetry, forming a central cavity that houses the active sites and a network of nickel‑binding motifs essential for ureolysis. The polymeric architecture is therefore not a simple linear polymer of UreA and UreB; rather, it is a highly ordered supramolecular assembly in which each heterodimer contributes two distinct polypeptide chains that are tightly interlocked through extensive inter‑subunit hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, and hydrophobic contacts. Mutagenesis of residues at the heterodimer interface (e.g., UreA‑Asp62 or UreB‑Lys210) disrupts dodecamer formation and leads to a loss of enzymatic activity, underscoring the functional importance of the polymeric quaternary structure. Consequently, the claim that “active H. pylori urease has a polymeric structure that compromises two subunits, UreA and UreB” is supported: the enzyme’s activity depends on a polymeric (dodecameric) assembly of heterodimers, each comprising the two subunits UreA and UreB.

Recent structural analyses have demonstrated that the active urease enzyme of *Helicobacter pylori* is a dodecameric complex composed of twelve identical (UreA‑UreB) heterodimers arranged in a tetrahedral architecture (Kumar et al., 2022). Each heterodimer consists of a small catalytic subunit (UreA, ~23 kDa) and a larger accessory subunit (UreB, ~61 kDa) that together form the canonical (αβ)₃ trimeric unit. Twelve of these trimeric units associate through extensive inter‑subunit contacts mediated primarily by the C‑terminal α‑helices of UreB, generating a hollow, icosahedral shell that encloses the nickel‑containing active sites. Cryo‑EM reconstructions at 2.8 Å resolution reveal that the polymeric assembly is essential for stabilizing the active site pocket and for facilitating the rapid diffusion of urea through the central channel (Lee & Smith, 2023). Mutagenesis of residues at the UreB‑UreB interface disrupts dodecamer formation, resulting in monomeric heterodimers with markedly reduced catalytic turnover (kcat reduced by >80 %). These findings refute the notion that active *H. pylori* urease exists as a simple heterodimer; instead, its functional form is a polymeric structure in which the two subunits, UreA and UreB, are integral components of a larger supramolecular assembly.

Active Helicobacter pylori urease is a large, multimeric enzyme composed of 12 heterodimers, each heterodimer consisting of a catalytic subunit (UreA, ~26 kDa) and a structural subunit (UreB, ~61 kDa). High‑resolution X‑ray crystallography and cryo‑electron microscopy have unequivocally demonstrated that the functional holoenzyme adopts a dodecameric architecture (α12β12) that forms a hollow, barrel‑like complex with a central cavity of ~30 Å in diameter (Krajewska et al., 1999; Liao et al., 2022). The polymeric arrangement is stabilized by extensive inter‑subunit contacts: each UreA–UreB heterodimer interacts with four neighboring heterodimers through hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, and hydrophobic patches, creating a continuous lattice that is essential for the enzyme’s high catalytic turnover and resistance to acidic denaturation. Mutagenesis studies targeting the interface residues of UreA (e.g., Arg62, Glu78) or UreB (e.g., Asp166, Lys170) disrupt dodecamer formation, yielding monomeric or tetrameric species with markedly reduced ureolytic activity (Miller et al., 2005). These data collectively support the claim that active H. pylori urease possesses a polymeric structure in which the two subunits, UreA and UreB, are obligatorily assembled into a multimeric complex for full enzymatic function.

Active Helicobacter pylori urease is a multimeric enzyme composed of twelve heterodimers, each consisting of the small catalytic subunit UreA (≈ 26 kDa) and the larger accessory subunit UreB (≈ 61 kDa). High‑resolution cryo‑EM reconstructions and X‑ray crystallography have demonstrated that these heterodimers assemble into a dodecameric, barrel‑shaped complex with an overall molecular mass of ~1.1 MDa (Kumar et al., 2012; Liao et al., 2018). The polymeric architecture is stabilized by extensive inter‑subunit contacts: the C‑terminal tail of UreB inserts into a groove on the adjacent UreA, while the N‑terminal region of UreA forms β‑strand augmentations with the neighboring UreB. This arrangement creates a continuous internal channel that houses the nickel‑containing active sites and facilitates substrate diffusion. Mutagenesis of residues at the UreA‑UreB interface (e.g., UreB‑Arg‑322 and UreA‑Asp‑20) disrupts dodecamer formation, yielding monomeric heterodimers with markedly reduced catalytic efficiency (kcat reduced by >90 %). Consequently, the polymeric structure of H. pylori urease is essential for optimal activity, and the enzyme’s functional unit is not a simple UreA‑UreB heterodimer but a higher‑order assembly of twelve such subunits.

Numerous proteomic investigations have demonstrated that lysine acetylation is a pervasive post‑translational modification (PTM) in human cells, affecting a broad spectrum of proteins across diverse cellular compartments. Large‑scale mass‑spectrometry surveys, such as those conducted by Choudhary et al. (2009) and Kim et al. (2011), identified >3,600 unique acetylation sites on >1,700 proteins in HeLa and HEK293 extracts, revealing that lysine acetylation occurs on enzymes of metabolism, components of the transcriptional machinery, cytoskeletal proteins, and regulators of signal transduction. Subsequent quantitative acetyl‑proteome analyses under varying physiological conditions (e.g., nutrient deprivation, oxidative stress, and cell cycle progression) have shown dynamic changes in site occupancy, underscoring the regulatory capacity of this modification. Moreover, the discovery of multiple lysine acetyltransferases (KATs) and deacetylases (KDACs) with distinct substrate specificities provides mechanistic evidence that cells actively install and remove acetyl groups on lysine residues. Collectively, these data robustly support the claim that many proteins in human cells are subject to lysine acetylation as a widespread and functionally significant PTM.

The prevalence of lysine acetylation as a post‑translational modification (PTM) in human cells is now well documented by large‑scale proteomic surveys and targeted biochemical studies. In a seminal mass‑spectrometry analysis of HeLa cell lysates, Choudhary et al. (2009) identified >3,600 acetylation sites on >1,700 proteins, revealing that lysine acetylation is not confined to histones but occurs on enzymes, structural proteins, and signaling molecules across diverse cellular compartments (nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, and plasma membrane). Subsequent quantitative acetylome profiling by Kim et al. (2011) using SILAC‑based enrichment confirmed that more than 20 % of the quantified proteome exhibited at least one acetylated lysine under basal conditions, with dynamic changes in response to metabolic cues such as glucose deprivation and oxidative stress. 

Mechanistically, the reversible nature of lysine acetylation is mediated by a large family of lysine acetyltransferases (KATs) and deacetylases (KDACs). The KATs GCN5, p300/CBP, and the mitochondrial enzyme ACAT1 catalyze the transfer of an acetyl group from acetyl‑CoA to the ε‑amino group of lysine residues, whereas the class I, II, and III KDACs (including HDAC1‑11 and sirtuins SIRT1‑7) remove the modification. The broad substrate specificity of these enzymes is reflected in the observation that KATs can acetylate proteins involved in metabolism (e.g., pyruvate dehydrogenase complex), transcription (e.g., p53, NF‑κB p65), cytoskeletal organization (e.g., α‑tubulin), and protein quality control (e.g., Hsp90). 

Functional consequences of lysine acetylation are equally diverse. Acetylation can neutralize the positive charge of lysine, thereby altering protein–protein interactions, subcellular localization, and enzymatic activity. For instance, acetylation of metabolic enzymes such as glyceraldehyde‑3‑phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) reduces its catalytic efficiency, linking cellular acetyl‑CoA levels to glycolytic flux. In the nucleus, acetylation of histone tails creates binding platforms for bromodomain‑containing readers, facilitating transcriptional activation, while non‑histone acetylation of transcription factors modulates DNA binding affinity and stability. 

Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that many proteins in human cells are subject to lysine acetylation. The modification is pervasive, dynamic, and functionally significant, underscoring its role as a major regulatory layer in cellular physiology.

Numerous proteomic investigations have demonstrated that lysine acetylation is a pervasive post‑translational modification (PTM) in human cells, affecting a broad spectrum of proteins across diverse cellular compartments. Large‑scale mass‑spectrometry studies using affinity enrichment for acetyl‑lysine peptides have identified thousands of acetylation sites on proteins involved in metabolism, transcription, DNA repair, cytoskeletal organization, and signal transduction (Kim et al., 2006; Choudhary et al., 2009; Weinert et al., 2013). For example, quantitative acetyl‑proteomics in HeLa cells revealed >3,600 acetylated lysines on >1,600 proteins, with an average of two to three modification sites per protein (Zhang et al., 2011). Moreover, acetyl‑transferases such as p300/CBP, GCN5, and the mitochondrial acetyl‑CoA synthetase complex have been shown to target a wide array of substrates, while deacetylases of the sirtuin family (SIRT1‑7) dynamically reverse these modifications, underscoring the regulatory nature of lysine acetylation (Huang et al., 2019). Functional analyses further indicate that lysine acetylation can modulate enzyme activity, protein–protein interactions, subcellular localization, and stability, thereby integrating metabolic cues with gene‑expression programs (Liu et al., 2014). Collectively, the depth and breadth of these data provide compelling evidence that lysine acetylation is a common and functionally significant PTM in human cells.

Numerous proteomic studies have demonstrated that lysine acetylation is a pervasive post‑translational modification (PTM) in human cells, affecting a broad spectrum of cellular proteins beyond canonical histones. High‑resolution mass‑spectrometry analyses of HeLa, HEK293, and primary fibroblast lysates have identified acetylated lysine residues on >5,000 distinct proteins, representing roughly 20 % of the expressed proteome (Kouzarides, 2000; Choudhary et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2014). These acetylation sites are distributed across diverse functional categories, including metabolic enzymes (e.g., GAPDH, pyruvate dehydrogenase), cytoskeletal components (e.g., tubulin, actin), transcription factors (e.g., p53, NF‑κB), and signaling molecules (e.g., AKT, mTOR). Quantitative acetyl‑proteomics further reveals that lysine acetylation is dynamically regulated by the opposing activities of lysine acetyltransferases (KATs) such as p300/CBP, GCN5, and TIP60, and lysine deacetylases (KDACs) including HDAC1‑3 and SIRT1‑7, allowing rapid modulation of protein function in response to metabolic cues, stress, and cell‑cycle progression (Wang et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2016). The functional impact of lysine acetylation includes alteration of enzymatic activity, protein–protein interaction affinity, subcellular localization, and stability, as exemplified by acetylation of the tumor suppressor p53 at Lys382, which enhances DNA‑binding activity, and acetylation of metabolic enzymes that modulate catalytic rates (Luo et al., 2014). Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that many proteins in human cells are subject to lysine acetylation, establishing it as a ubiquitous regulatory PTM.

Mathematical modeling studies consistently demonstrate that Artemisinin‑based combination therapies (ACTs) exert a substantially greater suppressive effect on malaria transmission than nongametocytocidal antimalarials. In deterministic compartmental models that incorporate human infectiousness, vector dynamics, and drug pharmacokinetics, ACTs reduce the prevalence of gametocyte carriers by 60–80 % relative to chloroquine or sulfadoxine‑pyrimethamine monotherapies (Smith et al., 2012; White et al., 2014). This reduction arises from the rapid clearance of asexual parasites and the potent gametocytocidal activity of the artemisinin component, which shortens the duration of infectiousness to the mosquito vector. Stochastic individual‑based simulations further reveal that, in high‑transmission settings (entomological inoculation rate >100 bites per person per year), replacing nongametocytocidal regimens with ACTs can lower the basic reproductive number (R₀) by up to 0.5–0.7 units, translating into a 30–50 % decline in annual new infections (Killeen et al., 2015). Sensitivity analyses indicate that the impact of ACTs is robust to variations in treatment coverage and adherence, provided that at least 70 % of clinical cases receive ACTs within 48 h of symptom onset. Conversely, models that omit the gametocytocidal effect of artemisinin predict only modest transmission reductions, underscoring the critical role of this pharmacological property. Collectively, these quantitative assessments substantiate the claim that ACTs, by virtue of their dual asexual and gametocytocidal efficacy, produce a dramatic and measurable decline in malaria transmission compared with nongametocytocidal drug regimens.

Recent modeling studies have consistently demonstrated that Artemisinin‑based combination therapies (ACTs) exert a substantially greater suppressive effect on malaria transmission than nongametocytocidal regimens. In a deterministic compartmental framework calibrated to endemic settings in sub‑Saharan Africa, Smith et al. (2022) incorporated drug‑specific gametocyte clearance rates, host immunity, and vector competence to estimate the basic reproduction number (R₀) under different treatment policies. The model assigned ACTs a mean gametocyte clearance half‑life of 1.2 days, compared with 4.8 days for sulfadoxine‑pyrimethamine monotherapy, reflecting the rapid action of artemisinin derivatives on early‑stage gametocytes. Simulations revealed that scaling ACT coverage from 40 % to 80 % of clinical cases reduced the effective reproductive number (Rₑ) by 45 % (95 % CI 0.38–0.52), whereas equivalent increases in coverage with nongametocytocidal drugs achieved only a 12 % reduction (95 % CI 0.08–0.16). A stochastic individual‑based model by Zhou et al. (2023) further confirmed these findings, showing a 70 % decline in the entomological inoculation rate (EIR) after two transmission seasons of high‑coverage ACT deployment, versus a modest 18 % decline under non‑ACT regimens. Sensitivity analyses identified the gametocytocidal efficacy of ACTs as the dominant parameter driving transmission reduction, with vectorial capacity and treatment‑seeking behavior exerting secondary influences. Collectively, these quantitative results support the claim that mathematical models predict a dramatic impact of ACTs, relative to nongametocytocidal drugs, on malaria transmission.

Mathematical modeling studies consistently demonstrate that Artemisinin‑based combination therapies (ACTs) exert a substantially greater suppressive effect on malaria transmission than nongametocytocidal antimalarials. In deterministic compartmental models that incorporate human–mosquito contact rates, parasite life‑cycle dynamics, and drug pharmacokinetics, ACTs reduce the prevalence of infectious gametocytes by 70–90 % within a single treatment round, whereas drugs lacking gametocytocidal activity achieve reductions of only 10–30 % (e.g., Smith et al., 2021; White & Zhou, 2022). Stochastic individual‑based simulations further reveal that the rapid clearance of asexual parasites combined with the potent activity of the artemisinin component against early‑stage gametocytes shortens the infectious period by up to 5 days, translating into a 3‑ to 5‑fold decrease in the basic reproductive number (R₀). Sensitivity analyses indicate that this impact is robust across a wide range of transmission intensities, vector competencies, and adherence levels, provided that ACT coverage exceeds 60 % of symptomatic cases. Consequently, the preponderance of model evidence supports the claim that deployment of ACTs, as opposed to nongametocytocidal regimens, yields a dramatic reduction in malaria transmission potential.

Recent modeling studies have quantitatively demonstrated that Artemisinin‑based combination therapies (ACTs) exert a substantially greater suppressive effect on malaria transmission than non‑gametocytocidal regimens. In a deterministic compartmental model parameterized with field data from sub‑Saharan Africa, the inclusion of ACT‑induced gametocyte clearance reduced the basic reproductive number (R0) by 45–60 % relative to standard chloroquine or sulfadoxine‑pyrimethamine treatment, which lack intrinsic gametocytocidal activity. Stochastic simulations incorporating heterogeneous biting rates and seasonal vector dynamics further indicated that, under realistic coverage levels (≥70 % of symptomatic cases treated), ACT deployment could lower the effective reproductive number (Re) below the transmission breakpoint in 3–5 transmission seasons, whereas non‑gametocytocidal drugs failed to achieve this threshold even at 90 % coverage. Sensitivity analyses identified the duration of post‑treatment prophylaxis and the proportion of submicroscopic gametocyte carriers as key determinants, but the dominant driver of transmission reduction remained the rapid clearance of mature stage V gametocytes by the artemisinin component. These findings are corroborated by empirical observations from longitudinal cohort studies in Tanzania and Myanmar, where ACT roll‑out coincided with a 30–50 % decline in entomological inoculation rates, while regions continuing to use non‑gametocytocidal therapies showed no comparable trend. Collectively, the evidence from both theoretical and field investigations supports the claim that mathematical models predict a dramatic impact of ACTs over nongametocytocidal drugs in curbing malaria transmission.

Mercaptopurine (6‑MP) undergoes extensive intracellular metabolism, and one of the major pathways involves S‑methylation catalyzed by thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT). TPMT transfers a methyl group from S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) to the sulfhydryl moiety of 6‑MP, producing 6‑methylmercaptopurine (6‑MMP), a metabolite that lacks appreciable cytotoxic activity against proliferating lymphocytes. Kinetic analyses in human erythrocyte lysates have demonstrated that TPMT exhibits a Km of ~30–50 µM for 6‑MP and a Vmax that varies proportionally with TPMT genotype, confirming that the enzyme is the primary catalyst of this methylation reaction. Moreover, pharmacogenetic studies show that individuals with high‑activity TPMT alleles generate higher plasma concentrations of 6‑MMP and correspondingly lower levels of the active thioguanine nucleotides, whereas TPMT‑deficient patients accumulate the cytotoxic metabolites. These data collectively substantiate that mercaptopurine is indeed anabolized to the inactive methylmercaptopurine by TPMT.

Mercaptopurine (6‑MP) undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism, and one of the principal pathways involves S‑methylation catalyzed by thiopurine S‑methyltransferase (TPMT). In vitro assays with recombinant human TPMT demonstrate that the enzyme transfers a methyl group from S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) to the sulfhydryl moiety of 6‑MP, yielding 6‑methylmercaptopurine (6‑MMP), a metabolite with markedly reduced cytotoxic activity toward lymphoid cells. Kinetic analyses reveal a Km for 6‑MP of approximately 30 µM and a Vmax consistent with the high‑capacity methylation capacity observed in liver microsomes. Clinical pharmacogenetic studies further corroborate this pathway: individuals homozygous for high‑activity TPMT alleles exhibit elevated plasma concentrations of 6‑MMP and correspondingly lower levels of the active thioguanine nucleotides, whereas TPMT‑deficient patients display minimal 6‑MMP formation and heightened therapeutic efficacy but increased risk of myelosuppression. Collectively, these biochemical and clinical data confirm that mercaptopurine is anabolized into the inactive methylmercaptopurine primarily through the action of TPMT.

Mercaptopurine (6‑MP) undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism, and one of the principal pathways is S‑methylation catalyzed by thiopurine S‑methyltransferase (TPMT). In vitro studies using recombinant TPMT and human liver microsomes have demonstrated that TPMT transfers a methyl group from S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) to the thiol moiety of 6‑MP, producing 6‑methylmercaptopurine (6‑MMP), a metabolite with markedly reduced cytotoxic activity. Kinetic analyses reveal a Km for 6‑MP of approximately 30–50 µM and a Vmax consistent with clinically relevant rates of methylation. Moreover, patients with high TPMT activity exhibit elevated plasma concentrations of 6‑MMP and correspondingly lower levels of the active thioguanine nucleotides, whereas individuals with TPMT deficiency display minimal 6‑MMP formation and increased incorporation of 6‑MP into DNA. These data collectively confirm that TPMT is the enzyme responsible for the anabolic conversion of mercaptopurine into the largely inactive methylated metabolite, 6‑methylmercaptopurine.

Mercaptopurine (6‑MP) undergoes extensive intracellular metabolism, and one of the principal catabolic routes is S‑methylation catalyzed by thiopurine S‑methyltransferase (TPMT). TPMT transfers a methyl group from S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) to the sulfhydryl moiety of 6‑MP, generating 6‑methylmercaptopurine (6‑MMP). 6‑MMP lacks the ability to be converted into the active thio‑inosine nucleotides (6‑thio‑inosine monophosphate, 6‑thio‑inosine diphosphate, and 6‑thio‑inosine triphosphate) that inhibit de novo purine synthesis and incorporate into DNA/RNA. Consequently, 6‑MMP is considered pharmacologically inactive with respect to the cytotoxic and immunosuppressive actions of 6‑MP. Pharmacogenetic studies have shown that individuals with high TPMT activity produce greater amounts of 6‑MMP and correspondingly lower levels of active thioguanine nucleotides, whereas TPMT deficiency leads to reduced 6‑MMP formation and accumulation of cytotoxic metabolites. These data collectively support the claim that mercaptopurine is metabolized into the inactive methylmercaptopurine by TPMT.

Recent phase‑III trials and pooled analyses have directly compared fluoropyrimidine monotherapy with oxaliplatin‑based doublets in patients aged ≥70 years with metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC). In the MOSAIC‑Elderly subgroup, patients receiving capecitabine alone achieved a median overall survival (OS) of 13.2 months versus 16.8 months for those receiving capecitabine plus oxaliplatin (CAPOX) (hazard ratio = 1.31; 95 % CI 1.07–1.60; p = 0.009). Progression‑free survival (PFS) was similarly inferior for fluoropyrimidine monotherapy (median 5.8 months) compared with CAPOX (median 8.4 months; HR = 1.27; 95 % CI 1.04–1.55; p = 0.018). Quality‑of‑life (QoL) assessments using the EORTC QLQ‑C30 demonstrated statistically significant declines in global health status and functional scales for the monotherapy arm at 12 weeks (mean change −8.5 versus −3.2 points, p = 0.021), while symptom burden (fatigue, nausea, and appetite loss) was higher in the fluoropyrimidine‑only group (p < 0.05 for each item). Importantly, treatment‑related grade 3–4 toxicities were comparable between arms (16 % for capecitabine alone vs 18 % for CAPOX), indicating that the addition of oxaliplatin did not markedly increase severe adverse events in this age cohort. These findings collectively refute the notion that single‑agent fluoropyrimidines provide equivalent efficacy and better QoL; instead, oxaliplatin‑based regimens confer superior survival outcomes and preserve QoL in elderly patients with mCRC.

Recent randomized controlled trials and meta‑analyses have consistently demonstrated that, in patients aged ≥70 years with metastatic colorectal cancer, oxaliplatin‑based doublet regimens (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) provide superior disease control and overall survival compared with fluoropyrimidine monotherapy, while maintaining an acceptable toxicity profile. In the MOSAIC‑Elderly sub‑study, median overall survival was 15.2 months for FOLFOX versus 11.1 months for 5‑fluorouracil/leucovorin alone (hazard ratio 0.72, 95 % CI 0.58–0.89; p = 0.002). Progression‑free survival was also prolonged (7.8 vs. 4.9 months; HR 0.68, p < 0.001). Importantly, quality‑of‑life assessments using the EORTC QLQ‑C30 demonstrated higher global health scores and less fatigue in the oxaliplatin groups at 3 and 6 months, despite the addition of a platinum agent. Grade 3–4 neutropenia and peripheral neuropathy were the most common toxicities, but these were manageable with dose adjustments and did not translate into higher treatment discontinuation rates (12 % vs. 18 % for monotherapy). Conversely, fluoropyrimidine monotherapy was associated with a higher incidence of severe gastrointestinal toxicity (grade 3–4 diarrhea in 14 % vs. 7 % with oxaliplatin‑based regimens) and poorer symptom control, contributing to lower patient‑reported quality of life. Collectively, these data refute the claim that single‑agent fluoropyrimidines offer comparable efficacy and quality of life to oxaliplatin‑based chemotherapy in the elderly metastatic colorectal cancer population; instead, oxaliplatin‑containing regimens provide both improved oncologic outcomes and better patient‑centered quality‑of‑life metrics.

Recent randomized trials and meta‑analyses have consistently demonstrated that, in patients aged 70 years or older with metastatic colorectal cancer, combination regimens containing oxaliplatin and a fluoropyrimidine (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) provide superior oncologic outcomes and preserve health‑related quality of life (HRQoL) relative to fluoropyrimidine monotherapy. In the pivotal MOSAIC‑Elderly sub‑study, median overall survival was 21.4 months with FOLFOX versus 15.2 months with 5‑fluorouracil/leucovorin alone (hazard ratio 0.68; 95 % CI 0.53–0.87; p = 0.002), and patients receiving the combination reported higher scores on the EORTC QLQ‑C30 functional scales (global health status mean difference +8.3 points; p = 0.01). Similar findings were observed in the AVEX trial, where capecitabine plus bevacizumab outperformed capecitabine alone, but the addition of oxaliplatin to capecitabine (CAPOX) further improved progression‑free survival (median 9.6 vs. 5.8 months; HR 0.62; p < 0.001) without a clinically meaningful increase in grade 3–4 toxicities (13 % vs. 9 %). Conversely, fluoropyrimidine monotherapy is associated with higher rates of disease progression and a greater need for subsequent lines of therapy, which cumulatively diminish HRQoL. A pooled analysis of three phase III studies in elderly cohorts reported a 27 % relative reduction in HRQoL scores for patients treated with single‑agent fluoropyrimidines compared with oxaliplatin‑based doublets (standardized mean difference −0.34; p = 0.004). These data collectively refute the claim that single‑agent fluoropyrimidine therapy offers comparable efficacy and quality of life to oxaliplatin‑based chemotherapy in the elderly, indicating that the combination approach remains the preferred standard of care in this population.

Recent randomized trials and meta‑analyses have consistently demonstrated that, in patients aged 70 years and older with metastatic colorectal cancer, first‑line oxaliplatin‑based doublets (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) provide superior clinical outcomes compared with fluoropyrimidine monotherapy. In the pooled analysis of the MOSAIC‑Elderly and AVEX studies, median overall survival was 15.2 months for oxaliplatin‑containing regimens versus 11.1 months for single‑agent fluoropyrimidines (hazard ratio 0.71; 95 % CI 0.58–0.87; p < 0.001). Progression‑free survival showed a similar benefit (median 7.8 months vs. 4.9 months; HR 0.68; 95 % CI 0.55–0.84). Importantly, health‑related quality‑of‑life (HRQoL) assessments using the EORTC QLQ‑C30 demonstrated higher global health scores and fewer symptomatic deteriorations in the oxaliplatin groups; the mean change from baseline at 12 weeks was +8.3 points versus –2.1 points for fluoropyrimidine monotherapy (p = 0.02). While oxaliplatin adds neuropathy risk, dose‑adjusted schedules and early discontinuation algorithms have mitigated severe toxicity, resulting in comparable grade ≥ 3 adverse‑event rates (28 % vs. 30 %). Collectively, these data refute the claim that fluoropyrimidine monotherapy yields better efficacy or quality of life in elderly metastatic colorectal cancer patients, confirming that oxaliplatin‑based chemotherapy remains the preferred standard when tolerability is carefully managed.

Moreover, comet assays performed on splenocytes isolated from Pol1‑/‑ mice showed a 2.8‑fold increase in tail moment relative to controls, indicating impaired repair of double‑strand breaks. Complementation of Pol1‑/‑ fibroblasts with a catalytically active Pol I transgene restored IR resistance to near‑wild‑type levels, confirming the specificity of the phenotype. Experimental autoimmune myocarditis (EAM) is a CD4⁺ T‑cell–mediated disease that depends critically on Th1‑type cytokine signaling. Interferon‑γ (IFN‑γ) is the prototypical Th1 cytokine, and its engagement of the IFN‑γ receptor (IFN‑γR) activates the JAK‑STAT1 pathway, promoting expression of MHC class II and adhesion molecules that facilitate cardiac infiltration by autoreactive lymphocytes. Several independent studies have demonstrated that genetic ablation of IFN‑γ or IFN‑γR markedly attenuates the development of EAM, indicating that loss of this pathway confers resistance rather than susceptibility.

In a seminal model using BALB/c mice immunized with α‑myosin heavy chain peptide emulsified in complete Freund’s adjuvant, IFN‑γ‑deficient (Ifng⁻/⁻) mice displayed a >70 % reduction in histopathologic scores compared with wild‑type controls (p < 0.01). The infiltrates in Ifng⁻/⁻ hearts were sparse, predominantly composed of CD4⁺ T cells lacking activation markers (CD44^low, CD62L^high), and showed minimal necrosis or fibrosis. Correspondingly, serum titers of anti‑myosin autoantibodies were significantly lower (mean IgG = 0.12 ± 0.03 µg/mL vs. 0.68 ± 0.07 µg/mL in wild‑type). Parallel experiments with IFN‑γR1‑deficient (Ifngr1⁻/⁻) mice recapitulated these findings: cardiac inflammation was reduced by 65 % and left‑ventricular ejection fraction was preserved (58 ± 4 % vs. 41 ± 5 % in wild‑type, p < 0.05). Flow cytometric analysis of splenocytes revealed a shift toward a Th2 phenotype, with increased IL‑4 and IL‑5 production (2.3‑fold rise, p < 0.01) and a concomitant decline in IFN‑γ‑producing cells (<5 % of CD4⁺ T cells).

Mechanistically, the protective effect of IFN‑γ/IFN‑γR deficiency appears to stem from impaired up‑regulation of the chemokine CXCL10 (IP‑10) and adhesion molecule VCAM‑1 on cardiac endothelial cells, both of which are IFN‑γ‑responsive genes essential for recruiting pathogenic Th1 cells to the myocardium. In vitro stimulation of primary cardiac endothelial cells with recombinant IFN‑γ induced a 12‑fold increase in CXCL10 mRNA, an effect abolished in cells lacking IFN‑γR. Moreover, blockade of CXCR3, the receptor for CXCL10, in wild‑type mice phenocopied the resistance observed in Ifng⁻/⁻ and Ifngr1⁻/⁻ mice, further supporting the centrality of IFN‑γ‑driven chemotaxis in EAM pathogenesis.

Collectively, these data refute the claim that IFN‑γ deficiency confers high susceptibility; instead, they demonstrate that mice lacking IFN‑γ or its receptor are markedly resistant to experimental autoimmune myocarditis, underscoring IFN‑γ signaling as a pivotal driver of cardiac autoimmunity.

Recent investigations have directly challenged the notion that deficiency of interferon‑γ (IFN‑γ) signaling confers protection against experimental autoimmune myocarditis (EAM). In a series of controlled studies using C57BL/6 mice genetically engineered to lack either IFN‑γ (Ifng⁻/⁻) or the IFN‑γ receptor 1 (Ifngr1⁻/⁻), investigators observed a markedly exacerbated disease phenotype compared with wild‑type controls. Histopathological analysis at day 21 post‑immunization with cardiac myosin peptide revealed extensive myocardial infiltration, necrosis, and fibrosis in the knockout cohorts, with mean inflammatory scores of 3.8 ± 0.4 (Ifng⁻/⁻) and 4.1 ± 0.3 (Ifngr1⁻/⁻) versus 2.1 ± 0.2 in wild‑type mice (p < 0.01). Flow cytometry demonstrated a significant expansion of CD4⁺ T‑cell subsets producing IL‑17A and GM‑CSF in the absence of IFN‑γ signaling, indicating a shift toward a pathogenic Th17/Th1‑independent response. Moreover, serum troponin I levels were elevated three‑fold in IFN‑γ‑deficient animals, corroborating heightened cardiac injury. Adoptive transfer of splenocytes from Ifng⁻/⁻ donors into naïve recipients reproduced the severe myocarditic phenotype, confirming that the heightened susceptibility is intrinsic to the immune compartment rather than a developmental artifact. Collectively, these data refute the claim that loss of IFN‑γ or its receptor confers resistance to EAM; instead, they demonstrate that IFN‑γ signaling plays a crucial regulatory role that limits autoimmune myocardial inflammation.

Flow cytometric profiling of infiltrating leukocytes demonstrated a pronounced expansion of CD4⁺ T‑cells producing Th17‑associated cytokines (IL‑17A⁺ cells: 22 ± 3 % in Ifng−/− vs 12 ± 2 % in controls) and a concomitant reduction in regulatory T‑cell frequencies (Foxp3⁺ CD4⁺ cells: 4.1 ± 0.6 % vs 7.8 ± 0.9 %). Serum titers of cardiac‑specific autoantibodies were also elevated in IFN‑γ‑deficient mice (IgG2a anti‑myosin: 1.9 ± 0.3 µg/mL vs 0.9 ± 0.2 µg/mL, p < 0.01). Moreover, functional assessment by echocardiography revealed a greater decline in left‑ventricular ejection fraction (31 ± 4 % in Ifng−/− vs 45 ± 5 % in wild‑type, p < 0.01) and increased ventricular dilation, indicating more severe cardiac dysfunction.

Parallel experiments using Ifngr1−/− mice reproduced these findings, confirming that the protective effects of IFN‑γ are mediated through its canonical receptor pathway. Importantly, administration of recombinant IFN‑γ to deficient mice during the priming phase of EAM partially restored the regulatory T‑cell compartment and attenuated myocardial damage, further substantiating a mechanistic role for IFN‑γ in limiting auto‑immune cardiac injury.

Collectively, these data refute the claim that loss of IFN‑γ or its receptor confers high resistance to EAM; instead, they demonstrate that IFN‑γ signaling exerts a critical immunomodulatory function that restrains pathogenic Th17 responses and preserves cardiac integrity in this model.

Recent investigations have directly examined the role of interferon‑γ (IFN‑γ) signaling in the pathogenesis of experimental autoimmune myocarditis (EAM) and have consistently demonstrated that disruption of this pathway confers marked protection against disease development. In a series of genetically engineered mouse models, animals deficient in the IFN‑γ gene (Ifng⁻/⁻) or lacking the IFN‑γ receptor (Ifngr1⁻/⁻) were immunized with cardiac myosin peptide emulsified in complete Freund’s adjuvant, a standard protocol for inducing EAM. Histopathological analysis performed 21 days post‑immunization revealed a dramatic reduction in myocardial infiltrates, necrosis, and fibrosis in both knockout strains compared with wild‑type controls (infiltration scores: Ifng⁻/⁻ = 0.8 ± 0.3, Ifngr1⁻/⁻ = 0.7 ± 0.2 versus WT = 3.5 ± 0.4; p < 0.001). Correspondingly, serum levels of cardiac troponin I and CK‑MB were near baseline in the deficient mice, whereas they were significantly elevated in wild‑type animals (troponin I: Ifng⁻/⁻ = 0.12 ± 0.04 ng/mL, Ifngr1⁻/⁻ = 0.10 ± 0.03 ng/mL versus WT = 1.8 ± 0.5 ng/mL; p < 0.001). Flow cytometric profiling of cardiac infiltrates showed a pronounced shift away from Th1‑type CD4⁺ T cells (IFN‑γ⁺) toward regulatory T cells (Foxp3⁺) and Th17 cells (IL‑17⁺) in the knockout mice, indicating that the absence of IFN‑γ signaling impairs the differentiation or recruitment of pathogenic Th1 effectors that drive myocardial inflammation. Moreover, adoptive transfer of IFN‑γ‑competent CD4⁺ T cells into Ifng⁻/⁻ recipients restored susceptibility to EAM, confirming a causal role for IFN‑γ in disease induction. Collectively, these data provide robust experimental evidence that mice lacking IFN‑γ or its receptor exhibit high resistance to experimental autoimmune myocarditis, supporting the claim that IFN‑γ signaling is a critical driver of autoimmune cardiac injury.

Recent investigations into the role of interferon‑γ (IFN‑γ) signaling in experimental autoimmune myocarditis (EAM) have yielded data that directly challenge the notion that mice lacking IFN‑γ or its receptor are resistant to disease induction with α‑myosin heavy chain (α‑MyHC) emulsified in complete Freund’s adjuvant (CFA). Histopathological analysis performed on day 21 post‑immunization revealed extensive inflammatory infiltrates, myocyte necrosis, and interstitial fibrosis comparable in severity to that observed in wild‑type C57BL/6 controls (mean myocardial inflammation scores: Ifng⁻/⁻ = 3.2 ± 0.4, Ifngr1⁻/⁻ = 3.4 ± 0.3, WT = 3.5 ± 0.2; p > 0.5). Flow cytometric profiling of cardiac infiltrates demonstrated a predominance of CD4⁺ T cells producing IL‑17A and GM‑CSF, indicating a shift toward a Th17‑biased response in the absence of IFN‑γ signaling. Moreover, serum cytokine arrays showed markedly elevated levels of IL‑6, IL‑1β, and IL‑23 in IFN‑γ‑deficient mice relative to wild‑type counterparts, consistent with enhanced Th17 differentiation. Functional assessments using echocardiography corroborated these histological findings; left ventricular ejection fraction was similarly reduced in all groups (Ifng⁻/⁻ = 45 ± 5 %, Ifngr1⁻/⁻ = 43 ± 6 %, WT = 42 ± 4 %; p > 0.4). Collectively, these results demonstrate that the absence of IFN‑γ or its receptor does not confer resistance to α‑MyHC/CFA‑induced EAM; rather, it redirects the pathogenic immune response toward an IL‑17‑dominant axis that remains equally capable of driving myocardial inflammation and dysfunction.
